9.t: Signing up for the USO tour under Jesse Stone and manager Sylvester Lewis
9.s: After the war ended in 1945 he signed up for a USO tour; Jesse Stone was leader, but Sylvester Lewis, an ex-trumpeter, was manager.
9.q: band, but Sylvester Lewis was the manager of the show. He's the one that had the say. He run everything, Sylvester. When the show left New York, Jesse Stone had no more to say whatsoever. He had no more to say than me or anybody else. But it was supposed to be his band.

9.t: The USO band and trumpeter Nelson Williams
9.s: Holmes lists the USO band including Dave McRae and Louis Bacon, and trumpeter Nelson Williams, who had served in the Pacific.
9.q: : Dave McRae. He was an alto player. The tenor player was from Chicago, a ...(?)... He's still going, I guess; plays clarinet and tenor. I can't think of his name right offhand. The drummer, I don't know what his name is. He's from Brooklyn. He was not what you would call a real legitimate drummer.…

9.t: Promised Spam, the greatest trip of his life
9.s: The six-month trip took them through the Philippines and Okinawa, where Spam was daily fare and supplies were short.
9.q: : A lot of things happened on that, and that's the greatest trip I ever had. They told me it would be, and it was a great trip -- for me anyway. Because I hadn't done much traveling before that. I had only been around the country about forty times. Yeah, that was the greatest... They told me…

9.t: Herbie Cowens and Jesse Stone: how he signed up for the USO
9.s: Holmes thought Herbie Cowens had invited him to Japan but ended up signing with Jesse Stone for a USO tour, rehearsing for pay.
9.q: This is, oh, around September 1945. I meet Herbie Cowens, a drummer, who I had worked with many a time, who had been doing a lot of USO work. So Herbie asked me would I like to make a trip to Europe? Not in Europe, I'm sorry. He asked me if I'd like to make a trip to Japan. And I told him, "Sure!"…

9.t: The USO show format and rehearsals at Noll Studios
9.s: The thirteen-person show ran an hour with an MC, three women and an eight-piece band, rehearsed at Noll Studios.
9.q: : To the USO. So I'm rehearsing with Jesse Stone every day. And there would be different units in the billing where we was rehearsing that. We was rehearsing at Noll Studios downtown on 52nd Street, I think...51st and Broadway. We rehearsed there. And there was a lot of bands rehearsing in there…

9.t: USO show personnel and three months of rehearsal
9.s: He names the reeds, brass, rhythm and singers, and says the timed show could not be changed and was rehearsed for three months.
9.q: No, just the alto. And there was Franz Jackson on tenor saxophone. And Dave McRae, who played alto and baritone saxophone. In fact, he could play them all. He played clarinet.

9.t: Leaving New York by train in USO uniforms, November 30, 1945
9.s: The show left Jersey by train for San Francisco in new Eisenhower-jacket uniforms with USO patches.
9.q: : Oh yeah, they knew the time. They knew the time. There was timing. That's why they had to rehearse. Now, we rehearsed... Although the show was complete and everything, we had to rehearse until it was time for us to leave. We didn't know when we were going to leave. So consequently, we... We're…

9.t: The bucket-seat flight to Honolulu
9.s: They flew twelve or thirteen hours on a cargo plane with steel side seats to hot Honolulu in winter clothing.
9.q: : So we stayed around Frisco for about four or five days or a week, then we got our orders to fly out. So we left one night at nine o'clock. And I never will forget what Louis Bacon, the trumpet player, said. We got in the plane. It was a bucket job, what they call a bucket job in the plane, which…

9.t: Waikiki Beach disappoints, then shipped to Guam
9.s: Waikiki looked worse than Jones Beach to Holmes, and orders sent the show on to Guam.
9.q: : So we're lookin' the place the place over and one-thing-or-another. The hotel is nice. The next day, Sylvester says, "Charlie, let's go out to Waikiki Beach," and I said, "Okay." So he got four or five of us together, and we got a jeep, and we made our way to Waikiki Beach. I

9.t: Guam: missing his brother and Howard Johnson
9.s: On a stopover in Guam they visited a New York band and found that Holmes's brother and Howard Johnson had just left.
9.q: : And we're on our way to Manila, but we stopped over in Guam. And that's where the rest of the show caught up with us the next day. They caught up with us. Well, Guam wasn't no big deal. The only thing about it, one of the outfits was there that I... Well, we all knew quite a few of the fellows in…

9.t: Arriving in Manila in rain and mud
9.s: The show landed at the back of Manila in thick mud and slept in tents with mosquito bars.
9.q: : now was traveling to Manila. We were making stopovers. So anyway, we got into Manila, in the back end of it someplace, and it ended up raining like it always does over there, is rain -- nothin' but mud. It was thick with mud. We had on boots and things, but it was still mud to me. I wasn't used…

9.t: Weeks of waiting in the Manila staging area for instruments
9.s: Their instruments went missing for two or three weeks, during which about fifty shows lived like a family in the staging area without working.
9.q: : Well, they got set up there, and we are just browsing around, waiting for orders. No orders have come in. And then we come to find the plane with the instruments and things hadn't shown up. We were there, but the plane with the instruments, they hadn't shown up. They don't know where the…

9.t: New Year's Eve in a quonset hut with White officers
9.s: Moved into a hut with drinking White officers, the Black performers were tense until an officer gave them whiskey and let Bacon fire a .45.
9.q: So I'll never forget, they changed from where we were stationed... This is right after Christmas. They moved us from where we were stationed in Manila to another part of town, from ...(?)... Why do they want to change us way over there? You know, we was right at home where we was at. So anyway, we…

9.t: Pre-dawn orders and a rainy truck ride on Leyte
9.s: Woken at three after little sleep, the show flew to the island of Lahti in downpours and rode standing in an open truck.
9.q: like a ton of bricks. Now, you've gone to bed and your head is like that. I had slept about two hours, and here comes Sylvester waking everybody up: "Pack up." So we packed up. We had to meet the plane at about six o'clock. Oh, brother, my head was bustin' open, and I know some of the rest of them…

9.t: Playing in the rain for soldiers who had waited for hours
9.s: Soldiers sat on stumps in the rain since afternoon, so Holmes agreed to perform on their homemade stage.
9.q: it here to the island." "Oh yeah." He says, "Do you know, they're waiting out there in the theatre for you now." And this was about four o'clock in the afternoon. He said, "They're waiting in the theatre, they're waiting now." Gee, in all that rain, we got to go through all that rain to get to the…

9.t: Sixteen days of rain and the whiskey he gave away
9.s: It rained fourteen of sixteen days; Holmes gave away his three bottles of stateside whiskey and disliked that others sold theirs.
9.q: Well, we stayed on Lahti(?) sixteen days. And of those sixteen days we stayed there, it stopped raining two days. It stopped raining two days of the sixteen days we were there. The Sun came out. And when the Sun came out, it would be so hot, you would wish for it to rain again. So

9.t: Touring Philippine islands and crossing to Japan with Herbie Cowens
9.s: They played many islands; after a show's plane vanished at sea, shows went by boat, and Sylvester Lewis impressed him as manager.
9.q: : Well, we did a lot of gettin' around in the Philippines. I don't know where. We did so many islands and things, I can't even remember the names of them. We went to Sabu(?), this (?) called Sabu. All of them. I can't even think of the names of them.

9.t: Okinawa: bombed landscape and thirty days of Spam
9.s: Supplies failed so they ate C-rations and Spam on Okinawa among shot-off trees and empty highways, and he was eager to go home.
9.q: : There wasn't too much to talk about at Okinawa, except the food supply didn't come in, and we had to eat C-rations and Spam, the Spam that they told us we would eat til it run out of our ears... But we did on Okinawa. We ate Spam just about thirty days. That was bad. That was the bad part of the…

9.t: First impressions of Tokyo, the Ginza and a surprise modern city
9.s: Tokyo amazed him with subways, steam trains run by children, stores and a theatre where he played the pipe organ.
9.q: : So anyway, we go into Yokohama, they put us off the boat in Yokohama, and take us over into...was it Tokyo...? They take us into Tokyo. And they put us up in a hotel, and we come out the hotel and we looken the town over. It's just like you'd come from out in the country somewhere and the first…

9.t: Touring Japan but not performing in Tokyo
9.s: Troops weren't allowed in Tokyo, so the show played Kyoto and cities across Honshu.
9.q: : I don't think we played in Tokyo. We played at the (?). Now, we performed all over Japan. But I don't think we did a show in the city of Tokyo.

9.t: The mountain hotel at Kanazawa and Japan as the trip's best part
9.s: A hot-springs mountain hotel gave a sukiyaki dinner; Holmes liked Japan most, preferring not to be stationed in Tokyo like Herbie Cowens's group.
9.q: : Then we had a little vacation. They sent us to a hotel in Kanizawa(?) where we spent, I don't know, about five or six days there -- a beautiful hotel on the side of a

9.t: Boat home to Seattle and news of his brother's burial
9.s: After eleven days at sea and a train to New York, his landlady told him to call his mother: his youngest brother had just been buried.
9.q: : That's when our contract ran out. And we left Japan, and they put us on a boat to come back here. It taken us eleven days to get to Seattle, Washington. Eleven

9.t: The original Ink Spots
9.s: Holmes lists the Ink Spots members, Bill Kenney, Deek Watson and Hobby, and notes Charlie Fuqua had gone into the Army.
9.q: There was Bill Kenney and Pete Watson and the one who played the bass, Hobby... And let me see... The guitar player... Yeah, that was the original. Except for Charlie Fuqua. He was the short one... But he wasn't with them. He went in the Army. I don't think he ever come back with them after he come…

99.t: Charles's 1942 draft, Spike, and Norris Turney
99.s: They sort out the order of personnel changes, Charles entering service in September 1942 and Norris Turney joining later in the Club Riviera days.
99.q: Norris Turney, he's from Wilmington, Ohio. Wilmington. Turney came in later. He came in during the Club Riviera days. But nothing happened too exciting with the band, other than the band kept up with current music and see, we were playing every night. We had no nights off. And this is

99.t: Playing for troops at Jefferson Barracks and losing musicians to the services
99.s: They play free shows at Jefferson Barracks, then lose Charles, Chester Lane and others to the Navy at Great Lakes in September 1942.
99.q: In the meantime, we had been taking our band down to the Jefferson Barracks, playing for the troops about twice a month, free of charge. We would take the entire show and band down, and the troops seemed like they enjoyed it so much. And we enjoyed doing it. The latter part of 1942, we began losing

99.t: Pillars is rejected by the draft board
99.s: After telling the examining officers about his band's free shows for the troops, Pillars is rejected from the Army and is happy to be.
99.q: In the meantime, the Army was gradually taking fellows. I've had several guys -- I'd call up, they would say Yes, they could join the band, and then they'd call back and say they received their greetings. '43 was a rough year, personnel-wise. But we stuck it out. And we stuck it out. In the…

99.t: Joining the USO through Dick Campbell
99.s: After his father-in-law's death Pillars visits USO talent coordinator Dick Campbell, who signs the band, and they travel to New York by Pullman.
99.q: by and see a fellow named Dick Campbell who was the coordinator of talent for the USO camp shows. I had met Dick when we were playing the Apollo Theater. So I went down to the USO camp shows, and Dick was glad to see me. And he said, "By the way, Pillars, how would you like to come with the USO?"…

99.t: Rehearsing at Nola Studio and first USO dates
99.s: They build a 59-minute show at Nola Studio, play for troops in Pennsylvania and New England, and are offered a trip to Asia.
99.q: They had a big room for us to rehearse the band, rehearsed and he brought in some show people, some acts, and we rehearsed and then he had us to play some band tunes, which we did. So we put together a show that lasted in there in about 59 minutes. And we hung around there about a week, rehearsing,…

99.t: San Francisco and the flight to Honolulu through a storm
99.s: After sightseeing in San Francisco they fly in a bucket-seat plane through a storm to Honolulu, with the brothers disagreeing over whether General Marshall bumped their plane.
99.q: We got to San Francisco, they were very nice to us. They took us sightseeing, took us to see the bridge, took us up on Nob Hill. And a few historical spots. Then they took us out to Hamilton Field and told us not to leave because we were on alert, see. In about a day and a half, we got ready to fly…

99.t: Island hopping to Guam and the whiskey ban for enlisted men
99.s: They refuel on Johnston Island, Kwajalein and Guam, where a G.I. says enlisted men cannot buy a drink, so Pillars shares a bottle with him.
99.q: MR. PILLARS: Johnson Island, Kwajalein, and Guam. Now, Kwajalein is where that experimented with that atomic bomb, remember? Kwajalein Island. With those islands, you could --

99.s: They reach hot Manila, are billeted, and play around the area and at Batangas.
99.q: Hot, man, so we -- they were waiting for us. And they took us somewhere in that town to billet And after we were there a couple of days, they started booking us out to different places to play. And we played the whole area of Manila and we went to one little town called Batangas.

99.t: A trip to Mindoro Island with Lieutenant MacLauren
99.s: A black lieutenant with a Ph.D. takes the show by yacht to Mindoro, where they wade ashore to a tree-house village and relax with the chief's whiskey.
99.q: And I ran into a fellow there, his name was MacLauren, from Oklahoma. He had his Ph.D. in economics. And he was a first lieutenant, black fellow. And he was in the

99.t: USO billets in Manila and Charles's gambling luck
99.s: The USO troupe lives behind barbed wire in Manila, where Charles and Crack Stanley lose in the big crap games.
99.q: Anyway, we came back. And we spent several days down in Batangas, and back to Manilla. WE played in and around Manilla. We had a regular stage area where all the USO personnel lived. But everybody was billetted, men on one side of the barbed wire fence, and women on the other side. You come in at…

99.t: Cheap whiskey and the rough boat voyage to Yokohama via Okinawa
99.s: They stock up on $1.35 whiskey and sail a troop liberty ship through rough water at Okinawa, kept below deck for four days.
99.q: -- we left Manila by boat. Before leaving, we were able to get our share of liquor. We could do that -- they brought some liquor in, we could go down and buy liquor, so we -- I stocked up with V.O. and I think it was only $1.35 a bottle. Real cheap, you know. That's what we got it for. And... I had…

99.t: Yokohama and Tokyo: a Japanese band and Meiji Park
99.s: Billeted at the Mitsubishi yards he hears a Japanese band swing 'The Sergeant Was Shy', then the band stays at Meiji Park in Tokyo.
99.q: MR. PILLARS: -- in Yokahama, and we were billeted in the office of the Mitsubishi yards. The shipbuilding yards. We were billeted right there. And one night, we were walking down the street, and we heard a band playing, and we walked into this barroom, and there was a band playing, swinging like…

99.t: Hot spring baths in northern Japan
99.s: In Hokkaido's ski resort area he describes the communal hot baths and bathing customs.
99.q: Yeah, anyway, we went to northern Japan where there was a ski resort. And where they have this hot water, you could take those baths. And the women would bathe you, you know what I mean, and they would wash you before you got into the big pool. They would wash you, and they'd take a bamboo bucket…

99.t: Kyoto show for Eisenhower, Kobe, Nagoya and a birthday in Tokyo
99.s: Their unit plays a Kyoto theater for General Eisenhower, then Kobe and Nagoya, and celebrates his birthday and Jeter's son's birth at the Ernie Pyle Theater.
99.q: So then we left Tokyo, and went to Kyoto, southern Japan, all the way down to Kyoto. We caught that fast train. The train at that time wasn't as fast as the modern trains they have now. But it was one of those kind of trains that never was off time. It always was on time. Kyoto, Japan, was a shrine…

99.t: Voyage home to Seattle and meeting Duke Ellington's band
99.s: After leaving Japan in June they return by Victory ship to Seattle, listen to the Louis Conn fight, meet Ellington's band, and go home by train.
99.q: And our stay in Japan lasted until about the second, third week in June. Second week in June, because we were three weeks --

99.t: Assembling the USO band; Charles returns from the Navy
99.s: Two sidemen fail the physical, he hires replacements in New York including bassist Carl Pruitt, and Charles, just discharged, rejoins in November 1945.
99.q: But we got processed for this trip. Then I found I had two men in the band who couldn't pass the examination. One was Bill Martin. He had a heart murmur. And the other was Amos Woodruff, who had a bad ticker, and he was fat and a little bit overweight. So they sent them back to St. Louis.

99.t: Refused a meal at Takikawa Air Base and the MacArthur directive
99.s: Officers deny the black troupe dinner at the officers' mess, so they cancel the show, nearly causing a riot, and MacArthur's office orders respectful treatment of USO shows.
99.q: : (We ran into it) (Unintelligible) up there. We left Tokyo too early to eat dinner. We got up there, the enlisted men had eaten and closed the dining room. What we did, we went to the officers' mess. That's where we usually ate, you know what I mean, the officers' mess. Officers sent us over to…

99.t: Otis stays home; the band's private train car to San Francisco
99.s: Otis White declines the USO trip because of a girl; the band travels west in a private car with a drawing room and plays all night.
99.q: Otis didn't want to go. Otis had just gotten married. Otis had -- either he had just gotten married or he was going with this girl.

100.t: German occupation of Denmark and escape to Sweden; father's flight via Varian Fry
100.s: He recalls the Nazi arrival in Vienna and Copenhagen, the 1943 rescue of Danish Jews to Sweden, and his father's escape through France and Lisbon to the US.
100.q: Yeah. Well actually, this is April 9th is not? It is April 9th today? April 9th was the day that the Germans occupied Denmark. April 9, 1940. I remember it very well because it was the second time in my life that Nazis marched into a city that I was living in. When I was in Vienna I had scarlet…

100.t: Reunion with father and arrival in the US in 1947
100.s: He reached the US on April 21, 1947, and praises the Danes for rescuing nearly everyone.
100.q: So since he came here in ’41 he became a citizen after five years, in ’46, and then he was able to get my mother and I to come here in ’47. So I arrived in the U.S.A. in April, April 21st, 1947.

100.s: Waking to German planes and leaflets, the quick Danish surrender, and the Danish jazz scene with Svend Asmussen.
100.q: We’re on the top floor, the fifth floor. It wasn’t a very tall building. I remember waking up that morning, because there were suddenly a lot of planes in the sky, and looking up. There were the Germans. You could recognize them with that black cross that they had on the wings. They were all these…

100.t: The air raid on Copenhagen and the warning of the roundup of Jews
100.s: Watching British Mosquitos bomb the harbour, then the underground man's instructions to leave that night with a small bag.
100.q: There was one incident that I clearly remember that was the only incidence while I was in Denmark – there was some more trouble later, but – the only air raid. It happened on a sunny afternoon. This was in ’43, but before – it was the summer, not the fall. My best friend and I, we had a – we were…

100.t: Hiding in a fisherman's attic and being passed between helpers
100.s: The crowded train, the attic hideout, separation from his mother, nights with strangers and his friend's family, and reunion at a station.
100.q: But it became clear to us, on the journey, that there were far too many people on this train, including some people that I knew. There were friends of the family. There were too many people on this train. Clearly what had happened was that, in spite of being told not to tell friends and relatives,…

100.t: Crossing to Sweden by fishing boat, October 1943
100.s: Drifting past a German patrol boat in the fog, being welcomed to Sweden, and arriving in Trelleborg.
100.q: over water than where we were originally supposed to leave from. This time it worked. So I arrived in Sweden in mid-October of 1943. There was a hairy moment, going across. Originally when we left it was bright moonlight, which was not good. Then it got cloudy and foggy. A small fishing boat, and…

100.t: Basic training at Fort Benning and the Dr. Jive record store
100.s: The segregated Army, a pot-smoking friend, buying LPs in Columbus's black district and being picked up by detectives.
100.q: Rome, Georgia, and another in Columbus. So there was some footnote there to jazz history. In any case, being in the South, that was an education in itself. I got to know a couple of people who were jazz fans. One was a guy from Brooklyn who was a – he worked in the garment district. He was a…

100.t: The detectives' warning, Charlie Barnet, battery clerk and shipping to Germany
100.s: A police warning, seeing Barnet's band, becoming the clerk instead of learning to drive, and the ruins of Mannheim.
100.q: town. While they were doing that, one of them gave us a nice lecture, with a pronounced Southern drawl, which I won’t try to imitate. He said, “We don’t care what you do where you’re from.” He said, “But down here” – he said, “we have certain ways of doing things.” To make a long story short, he…

100.t: The Munich club for black GIs and Jutta Hipp's Frankfurt quartet
100.s: His nickname Drac, Max Gregor's band, then a trip to Frankfurt to hear Jutta Hipp and Hans Koller and find his family grave.
100.q: That was short for Count Dracula. There’s two Italians, Inbimbio and Branfiglio. They were like a comedy team. One was short and the other one was tall. They had a great sense of humor. They said that my eyes were – they said that I had piercing eyes, and they reminded them of Count Dracula, so…

100.t: Army integration, Colonel Jones and discharge
100.s: The integration of his unit, a deranged battalion commander, low IQ scores that proved misleading and his discharge.
100.q: wanted to talk a little bit to them in German, so I was privy to this. But you could see it anyway. He bounced this thing off his snare, and he caught it. That was the best live jazz I heard in Germany. The Army was integrated during my term of service there. That was very interesting, because we…

100.t: Returning home and his father's choice of Brandeis
100.s: A visit to his grandmother and Denmark, GI Bill tests, and his father enrolling him at Brandeis.
100.q: in Bavaria. So of course I visited there. I also made a brief visit to Denmark, where I hadn’t been for a few years. So that was my return to Europe, unexpected, and then back here. I had taken a couple of – the Army had these tests, so I did a two-year college equivalent thing, which I passed with…

100.s: Everything was found untouched in 1945 thanks to friends in the underground.
100.q: The thing is – I was going to come back to that – when we came back in 1945, after the war in Europe ended, everything was just the way we left it. That was our friends, by way of the underground. Everybody had taken care of that. It was quite remarkable. We didn’t lose anything. That is another…

100.t: Father escapes the camp and leaves Europe with Varian Fry's help
100.s: The German army's lax camp commander, flight to Marseilles, a Honduran passport and arrival in New York in April 1941.
100.q: So he called in the leaders of the various factions in the camp – there’s Social Democrats, orthodox Jews, and communists. There were also real Germans, some of whom were Nazis who had been rounded up. A bit of everything. And Slovak. All sorts of things. He told these people – he said that within…

100.t: Time Inc., the New York Times, the draft and Brandeis jazz concerts
100.s: He wanted to be a journalist, worked at Time Inc. and the Times, was drafted, then at Brandeis edited the paper and arranged jazz via George Wein's Storyville.
100.q: not much more than a glorified messenger but I got to meet a lot of people and actually was talked into running for office at the American Newspaper Guild, a pretty left wing thing. I was a Wallace — Henry Wallace was running for president. That was that famous election when Truman — Truman and…

100.t: Dachau post, Munich bands and exposure to country music
100.s: Quartered in former SS barracks, GI bands playing In the Mood and listening to country radio at Fort Benning.
100.q: Dachau, not far from where the concentration camp had been. Where we were quartered, in very solid buildings, had been the SS barracks. So that was a nice note. I went once to see Dachau, which had been turned into kind of a museum, but I never spent any time in that small town. I had no eyes for…

100.t: Jazz under the Nazis, a schoolboy record collection and the underground's knock
100.s: How jazz flourished in occupied countries, German pressing plants, lending records at parties, an older collector, and the underground visitor in October 1943.
100.q: titles of the things, but the Germans didn’t know anyway. Actually the Germans, interestingly enough – Germany was the major producer of recordings in Europe. That is to say, they had the major pressing plants. For years, even after the Nazi takeover, German pressing plants were still pressing…

100.t: Father in France: internment and the visa problem
100.s: Contact with his father again from Sweden; French internment of German and Austrian refugees and the stateless visa maze.
100.q: This is a very good question. When my father – we should attend to him now, because once we arrived in Sweden, we were able to communicate with him again. When he arrived after many adventures in France, where the French were not so nice. We know that the French interned, when the war broke out,…

101.t: Great Lakes Navy band and its sports stars
101.s: Terry's 1942-45 Navy service at Great Lakes with Gerald Wilson and many bandmates, plus the base football and baseball stars.
101.q: Gerald Wilson, Willie Smith, Flocks McConnell, Big George Matthews, Joe Bardussen, Ernie Wilkins, Jimmy Wilkins, Jimmy Kennedy, the whole schmear, man. Paul Campbell, super human. We had quite a motley crew there.

101.t: Camp Robert Smalls and Commander Eddie Peabody's minstrel idea
101.s: Black sailors were segregated at Camp Robert Smalls; they refused Commander Peabody's plan for a blackface minstrel show.
101.q: Well our camp was Camp Robert Smalls, and all of the black enlisted men in the Naval services were relegated to this camp. And there were six other camps, Caucasian camps you know, so we were all there in our little space you know, in our little camp, Camp

101.t: The barracks bigot and the Battle of Great Lakes
101.s: A racist commander picked a fight with a former Joe Louis sparring partner; the men escaped marches through a hole in the fence.
101.q: It was funny though. We had one commander who literally hated black people. He came through the barracks every night to make sure that everything was in order. Anything that was out of order was referred to as a “holiday.” If there was a speck on the window he’d say, “get that holiday off of…

101.t: Joining the Navy and going to Great Lakes
101.s: A recruiter organized Black musicians from St. Louis, including the Wilkins brothers, rather than wait for the Army.
101.q: There was a recruiting officer that came to – that went to the major cities. The one that came through St. Louis for some strange reason got a hold to Len Bowden, and Len would give him the chore of soliciting interesting people who might want to go into the Navy, because at this point – up until…

101.t: Camp Robert Small and the plantation-style indignities
101.s: Barracks 1812, the vocal chief's plantation singing for a visit, and the banjo-playing lieutenant's minstrel plan.
101.q: Camp Robert Small was the only camp in all of Great Lakes that was geared to – that was dedicated to black sailors. After a while they opened up Moffett and Lawrence and a couple of others, but from the beginning, Barracks 1812, Camp Robert Small, that was the band barracks, and all the other…

101.t: The importance of the Great Lakes bands
101.s: Black musicians shown to be capable of organized work, with radio broadcasts and parades.
101.q: I think it was very, very important, because there were some of the musicians who were totally unheard of before. Nobody ever knew them in the capacity of a public or an organization – government thing, that you could get that many black people

101.t: Other musicians stationed at Great Lakes
101.s: Names include Ross McConnell, Gerald Wilson, Al Grey, Lou Donaldson, Osie Johnson.
101.q: Yeah. There was Gerald Wilson. There was Paul Campbell, who used to play with Lester Young. There were so many cats in there . . .

101.t: The Great Lakes ship's company band: saxes and rhythm section
101.s: The Batchman brothers, Willie Smith, Pee Wee Claybrook, and the rhythm section of the first recruited band, which trained others.
101.q: In St. Louis. Those two were in that recruited bunch too, Ed Batchman, and Cliff Batchman was the alto player that played like Willie Smith. As a matter of fact, in that band at Great Lakes, he and Willie Smith sat side by side. He – the band there at Great Lakes was he, Willie Smith, and Charles…

101.t: Daily routine and weekends in Chicago
101.s: Raising the flag, teaching hammock routines, and Chicago hospitality for servicemen including Bennie Green.
101.q: A typical day was to get up in the morning, raise the flag, and, at one point, just jam all day long. We had section people coming in from everywhere, and until they got things organized, had more people coming in and forming more bands, then we had to work with teaching people the routines, how to…

101.t: Ernie and Jimmy Wilkins and the Sumner High band
101.s: The Wilkins brothers ask Terry to join their band; they all enter the Navy in 1942.
101.q: Ernie Wilkins and Jimmy Wilkins were brothers, and they were two of my choice buddies. When I was a member of the Tom Powell Drum and Bugle Corps once, they showed up at one of our rehearsals. We rehearsed at [the] Tom Powell Drum and Bugle Corps Building, which was 3900 on Enright [Street], which…

101.t: Who passed through Great Lakes: Dave Young and the California contingent
101.s: Len Bowden's ship's company, the West Coast musicians, and Gerald Wilson's writing.
101.q: Dave Young was a saxophone player from Chicago, and as I mentioned earlier in our discussion, the group that came into Great Lakes from St. Louis under the leadership of – the old fox, we used to call him – Len Bowden.

101.t: Running the jam sessions and what Great Lakes meant to him
101.s: Buddy Collette recalls Terry running things; Terry says the pool and mixing with players broadened him.
101.q: It was – we had in those days, when we were forming bands, what they called the pool. Everybody was in the pool, and out of the pool we chose people to put together – to form bands to send to various places. I was young and an eager beaver, so I was involved in most of the sessions. I don’t know. I…

101.t: Luther Henderson and Dudley Brooks, Great Lakes arrangers
101.s: The two staff arrangers and Terry's nickname habit.
101.q: Luther Henderson and Dudley Brooks were two of our chief arrangers on staff at Great Lakes. Of course Dudley Brooks had been ensconced in the Hollywood scene, so he was doing a lot of writing for movies, etc., in Hollywood, but Luther – Luke, I used to call him – he’s an East Coaster. He’d been…

101.t: Robert Russell, Wilbur Baranco, Andy Anderson and Stack Walton
101.s: Terry does not remember some names, and recalls the m.c. Stack Walton.
101.q: Andy Anderson. The only Andy Anderson I ever remember was a little short cat who sang in Hathcock’s vocal group, which was at the Great Lakes, in barracks 1812. I don’t know if that’s the same Andy Anderson or not. But he was a sort of a nondescript person. No particular indulgence in one thing.…

101.t: The old Chief Petty Officer who never saluted
101.s: A closing Navy memory, then a pause in the recording.
101.q: The only thing that I can remember is that we had a little Chief Petty Officer. He had – every four years or so you get a stripe for service. He had stripes all up his – he must have been born in – and all of the officers for long enough to get their degree and get their officer’s stripes – your…

101.t: Willie Smith turns down an officer's commission
101.s: Willie Smith, lead alto, chose to stay with his Black colleagues.
101.q: Willie Smith was the lead alto player. We got him out of boot camp and brought him over there. When we got him over there and they found out who they had – they didn’t know what – he was just another dude that was in the Navy. When we got him over there, they found out he played with Jimmie…

28.t: Arthur Briggs gets him a job at the Ostend casino
28.s: Back in Paris with no summer work, trumpeter Arthur Briggs found him a job at the Ostend/Knokke casino, where he sang English songs with Red de Broy's group.
28.q: and when it's hot in Paris, you really hot, man. Things was very bad, so, a fellow named Briggs, Arthur Briggs, a trumpet player, he was a great trumpet player.

28.t: The German commandant, the brewery and a ration card
28.s: In an occupied Dutch/Belgian hotel he faced the arriving German command, who learned he had picked up German at Chris Hart's brewery in Washington and gave him a ration card.
28.q: Now here's where I said well, if they are going to do me in, I'm going to get pretty I decided -- well, I got my suit on and so, I was -- what do you call the big hotel there -- the Metropole They are saying all this Dutch and, the Dutchland so, they said, all citizens stay in the house.

28.t: Buerman's help and the plan to escape north
28.s: Buerman warns him after seeing a woman dragged away, and offers to help him reach Sweden, Norway or Canada via Gothenburg and Iceland.
28.q: So, I said well -- I went there that next day and there was a woman protesting about her son. They took her son away and I said, well, I don't know nothing and she was saying who was no good and everybody so -- all of a sudden four soldiers come and grabbed the woman and took her out.

28.t: Arriving in Norway on a military plane and the officer's glove slap
28.s: Flying to Norway with a German colonel's escort, Butler was refused entry for lack of a visa until the officer slapped the customs man; Crouch presses him to clarify who slapped whom.
28.q: And he gave me a tiloten. The right /To get off the boat, I mean, to get on the plane to go to Norway. And so I got to Norway and they said, man, you can't come in here.

28.t: Working at Oslo's Metropole Hotel despite the American Consul
28.s: He found a singing job at the Metropole Hotel the first night, got no help from the American Consul, and obtained working papers from the German consul, playing for sunk-ship crews.
28.q: So, I got a room in a hotel/on---- and the next day, I went to the American Consulate. I went to the American Consulate and he says well, I -- by the way, I had gotten a job that night.

28.t: The Black Prince of Norway and a jazz chapter
28.s: For eleven months he was a big man in Norway, nicknamed the Black Prince, taught audiences to clap and swing, and organised a jazz society with British trumpeter Roland Greenberg.
28.q: Until one day, they said you got to leave man, because this is it. I went to Fenmark -- it's way up there -- lapland is there. You couldn't get no boats coming out --

28.t: Free passage to New York and the ship that was blown up
28.s: He got a free ship passage from Oslo to New York, brought the crew to Harlem, and learned the ship was blown up on its way back with everyone lost.
28.q: Now, what happened then, I got a note in my hotel up in Fenmark and I was lucky enough to come back to -- Oslo, and I got a ship -- it was going to America.

28.s: Back in New York he was summoned for the draft, ordered to Pennsylvania Station, and subjected to an exam.
28.q: Now, I'm in New York and I was saddened about affairs. Now, I said, well, I guess I gotta sort of remass myself and/plan out a of what I must do.

28.t: Seeking a Norwegian ship job and the translation
28.s: He tried to get work on a Norwegian ship because he spoke the language and knew how to catch Germans by a word, and recalls translating for a Norwegian ship.
28.q: Now, I'm finished with that. I said, well, I'd like to get a job -- on a Norwegian ship because there was a lot of Germans come in there and and they didn't know they was Germans. There was some words in Norwegian that a German will be caught up on and the word is Jasca han las...oun..."(?) "Jasca…

28.t: Wartime gigs with Cass Carr and Buddy Walker; going to Canada
28.s: With friends in the army, he gave up shipyard work for music, played with Cass Carr and Buddy Walker, then made an act and went to Canada for about two years.
28.q: So then, I started meeting friends. All of them were gone to the army, or trying to keep from going -- and the state of affairs, I said, well, man, I think I'd better go to the shipyard and do something there, but no, it wasn't no good for me.

28.t: The army takes the musicians; trombonist Frank Johnston
28.s: The army, especially the tank corps with many Indian Canadians such as the Kahnawake trombonist Frank Johnston, was draining Rockhead's of players by 1942-43.
28.q: So, everything is going on beautiful, beautiful, beautiful, then they start with going to the army and most of them was in the tank corps.

28.t: Singing Sonny Boy for the Germans; Hans Buerman
28.s: He sang Sonny Boy and German songs for the officers' club, and a soldier who had heard him play at Knokke as a teenager, Hans Buerman, offered papers.
28.q: And he says, can you sing and I says yes, I think so and I know the songs that he, that German club -- so, first they love "Sonny Boy."

28.t: War declared; trenches, Pops Foster and fleeing toward Dunkirk
28.s: In September 1939 his Swedish girlfriend could not cross the border; a comedian Pops Foster warned him, he found trenches outside, raised money and tried to reach a ship at Dunkirk as the Germans arrived.
28.q: That night, of August -- was it August or September, I think it was September 2nd, there was a long distance call from Sweden because my Swedish girl was supposed to come down and visit me.

28.t: The visiting star, a dressing-room razor fight and the anthems
28.s: A star and a dancer called Flash fought in the dressing room; when the star demanded God Bless America before the British anthem, Butler calmed disorderly soldiers.
28.q: So, I joined their local and we was wailing so much up there and you see, it's very, very cold As you know. Andif you don't wear rubbers, you just gone -- you die. Now, you can go up there and be cute if you want to but -- and so we're playing and at that time the war's on and a certain big star,…

28.t: Freddie Blackburn, the Gene Krupa record and the knife
28.s: Freddie drank, played along to a Krupa record, and during a number Bill Kurzie pulled a bowie knife to calm him before both were drafted.
28.q: I said, well, I'm -- I ain't getting all those dollars up there and I can't drink all my Mol$en (phonetic) and, but, speaking of Freddie.

28.t: The trombonist John Degrass and Norwegian ladies
28.s: Butler marvels at trombonist John Degrass and drummer Walter Johnson picking up women at a Norwegian hotel while the Cubans quarrelled over them; they left in July 1939.
28.q: John, he played the trombone. John could snatch more women. John culd snatch more women in the a street called Radhust Gaten hotel -- we was living in/ (inaudible) and John opened the door and the chick, he snatch her and close the door and then, about an hour later, because those people are very…

6.t: War years: Procope's draft and Billy Kyle going into the army first
6.s: Procope was drafted in September 1943 after Pearl Harbor; pianist Billy Kyle went first, and the band kidded him with songs about the army.
6.q: Pearl Harbor Day was December the 7th, 1941, and I was drafted in the army in October, 19 -- September, 1943. So I had those years. And those are very good years, because --

6.t: The blocked Copacabana contract in Rio and the band's decline
6.s: The band had a one-year Rio de Janeiro contract just as the war began but were not allowed to leave the country, which started the band's downgrade as members were lost.
6.q: And if you remember, Nelson Rockefeller was in charge of Latin affairs at that time, and so we went around and we all did this together, Kirby and everybody, and we pulled all sorts of strings to get out of the country, down on this job. Because we had it all figured out. We could go down there,…

6.t: Hearing the Kirby band without him at the Academy of Music
6.s: In rain gear, stationed at 110th Street, he sat in the audience and found the band had lost its sound and precision, which depressed him.
6.q: Well, not all at once, because they played a theater down at 14th Street, the Academy of Music. Used to be a theater down -- they still had vaudeville, sort of. And there was a fellow named Johnson who took my place, so then he -- so then that was two of the group that were out, Billy Kyle and…

6.t: Being drafted: induction physical and a request to be stationed at 110th Street
6.s: He didn't try to dodge; he had never been sick, passed the physical, and a friend arranged to have him at 110th Street, and he asked for the Army not the Navy.
6.q: Oh, goodness no. Goodness, no. No. I didn't volunteer at all, not at all. The only thing I remember about the Army now, I had sense enough to know that, you know, you can't -- I mean you can't fight these things. If you have to go in the Army you have to go in the Army. And I wasn't about to harm…

6.t: Ten months in a band at 110th Street, then shipped to Kentucky
6.s: He lived at home on a daily pass while in the 372nd Infantry's band; when the unit moved to Camp Breckenridge the Colonel had arranged for his place.
6.q: So I was at 110th Street, and I was at 110th Street about 10 months, and it was beautiful, because I played in a band and every day at 5:00 o'clock I'd get what you call your Class A pass, and I'd go home. Yeah.

6.t: The troop train and Colonel Ned Gardine of the 372nd Infantry
6.s: The long troop train trip to Kentucky; the all-Black 372nd under Colonel Gardine, a Howard athlete and lawyer, and a pointed protocol moment on arrival.
6.q: So we were at Breckenridge, all the same, and I'll tell you this, a little side story. Of course when the regiment got on this troop train, that was a good experience too, this troop train. I didn't like it, but I liked the

6.t: The unauthorized regimental band and running a barrack of forty
6.s: He was attached to the band by the Colonel's grace, ended up second in charge as a Technician 5th Grade, and ran the barrack of a marching band.
6.q: Well, I'll tell you, the Army band, the Army had authorized bands which consisted of 28 pieces and a director who was an officer, an officer. He wasn't a Lieutenant. He was just a step below a Lieutenant. Funny how these things escape you. Well, anyway, so we were all attached. When you came into…

6.t: Fort Huachuca staging area and the regiment broken up
6.s: The regiment was moved to Arizona to prepare for overseas, but the Battle of the Bulge brought orders that broke up the outfit and band.
6.q: We had a pretty good band, too, down there in Breckenridge. And that's the second band I was in. So after that, they were readying -- getting ready to go

6.t: Going AWOL on the post after the band broke up
6.s: Strained by night duty, he simply started walking off to the movies and cafeteria each day, slipping back to sleep, for two weeks, until he decided to report himself.
6.q: So anyway, while we were there they broke it up, so I said now I'm going to have to do something. So this particular day I just got up -- they were doing different things. They were coming around and giving you different duties and so on.

6.t: Facing the review board: a Major who was a Kirby fan
6.s: Before three white officers, he claimed headaches and sore feet, and the Major quipped they didn't bother him with John Kirby, which took the pressure off.
6.q: So I went in front of this Board. It was all white, and there was a Colonel, a Major and a Captain. Oh, they were heavy. Soldiers from Texas. Oh, my goodness. You're talking about soldiers, they were three soldiers. I mean soldiers. They didn't care. They didn't care what, they were soldiers, and…

6.t: The Colonel's untouchables, the medics, and his brother's warning from Patton's army
6.s: The Colonel kept him as an untouchable and transferred him to the Medical Corps, which he loved; his brother in Patton's army wrote telling him to avoid going overseas at any cost.
6.q: But as it turned out I went back to my regiment and the Colonel -- the Colonel had what everyone called untouchables. I was one of the Colonel's untouchables. When you came to get soldiers, he had a file on this side that was the untouchables, and there was a file on that side which was the…

6.t: Colonel Gardine sends him to the old post in the bushes
6.s: The Colonel visited the field camp, picked Procope and told him he'd be sent to the old post, free to take others, but his comrades wanted to stick together.
6.q: So he said, 'Well, you'll hear from them.' Then he left. So I went -- I was so happy, I told some of the fellows sitting around, I said, 'The Colonel's going to transfer me up to the old post, with the band.' I said, 'Any of you fellows want to go with me? You can if you want to, you know.' And I…

6.t: Life at the old Fort Huachuca post for the rest of the war
6.s: He describes the cavalry-era barracks, horses and later missile base, the soldiers' good health, and his duties of one weekly rehearsal and a Saturday parade.
6.q: Now, the old post, like I told you before, you know, was an old -- old Army, regular Army installation, which went way back to the Indian fighting. They met some of the wagons. The still kept up the tradition of horses and wagons and the fellows used to get the horses out and hitch them up on…

6.t: Playing dance jobs and USO shows on the side; avoiding the Navy
6.s: Most famous drafted musicians went to Great Lakes Navy, which he abhorred; in Kentucky small bands played $5 USO and club dates in nearby towns with an army truck.
6.q: Well, no, not in the -- most of the well known musicians who were drafted into the armed services were sent to Great Lakes.

6.t: Leaving the Army in October 1945 and readjusting
6.s: After two years, he found leaving the Army a bigger adjustment than going in and wanted to regain lost time.
6.q: Well, I puttered around, you know. I was so glad to get out of the Army. I was free as a bird. I could flap my wings, you know. And it's quite an adjustment. And I think coming out of the Army was more of an adjustment than it was going in the Army, because you want to do so much.

6.t: A Small's Paradise gig for Charlie Holmes and Army pay
6.s: Charlie Holmes gave him a gig at Small's Paradise days after discharge; Procope notes his Army pay was $20 a month after the allotment and the family sent money.
6.q: So anyway, I started just free lancing around, you know, getting jobs. I remember about the third or fourth day I was out of the Army, Charlie Holmes, you know, he came up to my house and he had a gig for me, which was, oh, beautiful, you know. I worked at Small's Paradise.

102.t: Morgan State football and letting the Army draft him
102.s: He made first string on the Morgan Bears for one season, then let himself be drafted because Black men had few opportunities beyond delivering mail.
102.q: So, I said, “Don’t, don’t hug her.” So, the next thing I knew, I was drafted. I deliberately let the Army draft me. I say deliberately because I’d enrolled in the—I just had to play football with the Morgan Bears. Morgan had the reputation, like Brandon, of state winners and whatever. I just wanted…

102.t: Basic training and arriving in Germany
102.s: He recalls Baltimore theatres he was not allowed to visit, then Le Havre, the box cars into Germany, a laundry company and the devastation. These shaped his view of evil.
102.q: I played guard, pulling guard. Anyways, I thoroughly enjoyed it and playing with the big boys. Then I was drafted and I was sent to Germany. I had basic training in Alabama. My father, when I was in Baltimore, I knew about Count Basie, Duke Ellington and all the major jazz guys, Fats Waller. They…

102.t: Laundry company musicians and carrying the tuba
102.s: Three musicians in the laundry led him to the post band and Sergeant Allen Tinney. His first gig was carrying a tuba for a parade before Japanese troops.
102.q: Oh, yes, right. Thank you. So, there were three musicians there. We got the worst job in my life washing clothes for soldiers everyday. So, I used to see these guys, after hours they would take their instruments out and play. One played guitar, one played the trumpet and another played the…

102.t: Teaching himself tuba, 'Estrellita' and the new Army band audition
102.s: He learned tuba fingerings from a bandmate, heard 'Estrellita' played by a soulful trombonist and chose trombone. Ernest Outlaw told him about the audition for Truman's new Army band.
102.q: drop and he calls me and said, “Look, you did us a big favor. Now it’s my time to do you a favor.” He says, “I’ll let you stay in the band if you learn how to play some marches on that tuba.” I said, “Wow! Here’s my shot! At last, I’m going to get a break!” So, the band had two clubs in town. You…

102.t: The Red Mitchell audition and later reunion
102.s: A sergeant who gave up his Christmas vacation passed him on tone. Years later he learned the auditioner was Red Mitchell and thanked him at a club.
102.q: “I gotta go see that.” My conscience says, “Don’t you dare go into that theatre. Go into that rehearsal hall and get ready for the audition.” So, I went there. A sergeant came, and he was a very pleasant guy, but he was very serious. He was angry because he had to give up his Christmas vacation to…

102.t: Jeanie Olham and the decision to go to Juilliard
102.s: A schoolgirl, Jeanie Olham, told him about Juilliard. Rising to master sergeant, he decided not to stay in the Army and later enrolled.
102.q: So, I caught up with her and I said, “Hi, how are you doing?” I became aggressive, “What’s you name.” “Jeanie Olham.” Boy, what a strange name. I thought, I’d accept that beautiful girl and I could see that she’s very intelligent. I said that I have to appear intelligent. So I said, “You’re…

102.t: Juilliard conductor and pitching Truman's band as a film
102.s: He praises the Juilliard orchestra's conductor, then lays out his film story of Truman's all-Black band as a weapon against segregation during the Cold War.
102.q: Well, they had a first class symphony orchestra. The student orchestra was superb. They could play with—because they had a superb conductor. The man who conducted the orchestra, he worked at the Met. He could have been a conductor for any major orchestra, but his thing was he treated musicians…

102.t: Cutting the string: the segregated mess hall
102.s: A string divided the mess hall until someone cut it, and Colonel Bilbo Jr. arrived. He credits Truman with desegregation and explains his nickname 'Money'.
102.q: Theodore Bilbo Senior made a career of preaching hatred in the US Senate. Here comes his son in charge of this situation. Guys start to get nervous and anxious and the more moderate ones say, “Oh, man. This is the Army, c’mon.” “No, no, no! Wake up! When did you see a white man that has the…

102.t: Truman's band becomes a conservatory at Dachau
102.s: Truman had the barracks turned into a conservatory. General Huebner enlarged the band to 82 and Frankfurt Symphony teachers were paid in cigarettes, chocolate and stockings.
102.q: I think it’s important to know that President Truman came to believe strongly that all the accomplishments of the allied victory over Nazi Germany would be ridiculed by Adolf Hitler from his grave, as long as people remembered the Holocaust over the allied victory. He wanted to do something to put…

102.t: Desegregation of the armed forces began with the band
102.s: He argues the band showed Black musicians' capability, proved a model, and that Truman then outlawed segregation without using the word.
102.q: think we knew, our barracks was arranged like a first class conservatory of music. We kept ordering, walking from class to class, from this hour of this, to musical instruction. Then we had musical history, then we had musical personal instruction. Each member had to spend an hour everyday. We…

102.t: Mrs. Campbell, Frita Jones and the 'Estrellita' trombonist
102.s: He regrets losing touch with Mrs. Campbell and Jeanie, then recounts hearing 'Estrellita' sung by Frita Jones and played in the Army dance band.
102.q: I just heard this guy play, that’s all. I told you I had a voice scholarship. My high school teacher, junior high school, after the failed ordeal with the bass drum, my father told me to get rid of the bass drum. Then, she wasn’t satisfied and she goes and gets me this scholarship. There was this…

102.t: Leaving the Army for Juilliard on the G.I. Bill
102.s: He planned a safe 20 years of Army service as a master sergeant, then chose Juilliard instead of being a big fish in a little pond.
102.ch: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
102.q: Yes, what’s significant about me coming out the Army is that I gave up what I thought I was going to do. You know, you start—at some point in your life you start thinking about security. How are you going to provide a living for Tom McIntosh? I recognized early on that a musician is the second most…

102.t: The soldier who painted himself to live in Africa
102.s: A funny tale of a soldier who darkened his skin with shoe polish to desert and live in Africa, and was caught because he swatted flies.
102.ch: Bags Jackson, Army tales and Gordon Parks films
102.q: America at one time was purely black America and white America. So, here we are in the band, well this is before the band. There was one guy who decides he’s not going to put up with it anymore. Now that the band and now that black American troops are sent to Africa, he feels like he’s in the…

102.t: Soviet agents targeting the Army band
102.s: He says Soviet agents targeted complaining members of Truman's band for Radio Moscow, and that he blends fact and imagination in his film story.
102.ch: Bags Jackson, Army tales and Gordon Parks films
102.q: See, but it’s a fact that several of the people who were primary proponents of the Soviet Union, all of them defected and came to the U.S. Because of them having first hand knowledge of what it was all about, the U.S. made them turn into first class consultants about all that. The next thing you…

102.s: Willie Cox asked Soviet agents what car Stalin drove and, hearing no Cadillac, left them with nothing to offer.
102.ch: Bags Jackson, Army tales and Gordon Parks films
102.q: Oh yes, okay. So, the sergeant that was in charge of—our spiritual leader. He discovered that the Soviet Union had put wires in our rooms to eavesdrop on conversation. They were after this guy who had the malaria because he was constantly complaining. His name was Buck Dyson. The man that they were…

103.t: Leaving for the Army; Shadow Wilson subs; Walter Page sent home
103.s: He left the Lincoln Hotel for the Army, with Shadow Wilson playing for a week, while Walter Page was sent home to settle family troubles.
103.q: Shadow Wilson. I had him to play in my place for one week because I went down to Washington. They wanted me to go into the Navy Band but Mr. Glenn Miller had sent a brown envelope- you know, Glenn had the overlay for the musicians going into the Army and he was placing various peoples. Shadow was…

103.t: Glenn Miller's Navy Band offer; Lester and Jones drafted days apart
103.s: Jones turned down a Navy Band post arranged by Glenn Miller, and he and Lester entered the Army in 1944, days apart.
103.q: Glenn had a card for me and I was supposed to go the Washington to join the Navy Band, because they was going to make it very racial, that I was going to be the first black in the Navy Band and all they wanted me to do was to stay in Washington. I said no and I got Shadow to work in my place for a…

103.t: How the Army treated Lester; "Break up Basie"; Jones as infantry soldier
103.s: Jones says the Army treated Lester Young shamefully and suggests an effort to break up Basie's band; he himself chose infantry and refused to play drums.
103.q: Of course not, what did he have to do. He had nothing to do with that. All I know is, with 5 1/2 million people in the Army at that particular time, there's no way

103.t: Lester's treatment at Fort McClellan: the photo of his white wife
103.s: He says Lester was punished after a footlocker search found his wife was white, and Jones was made his guard; Ken Bluett is identified.
103.q: Of course not. Three people are alive that will tell you the way they treated Lester Young was horrible. The thing that happened with Lester -

103.t: Billy Goodall and Lester's treatment in Georgia
103.s: Jones recalls a bass player guarding Lester at gunpoint to make him play, and Lester's transfer to Camp Stewart.
103.q: You know Billy Goodall that was playing bass with Joe Bushkin before you got there. He has 9 children. He's right out of Baltimore and Washington right now.

103.t: The trumpet-player MP who had to insult Lester for show
103.s: Jones describes a white trumpet player-turned-MP who had to insult Lester before black prisoners to keep up appearances.
103.q: But this trumpet player with tears in his eyes had to call Lester a nigger and Lester had to say, 'Yessir boss,' because in front of the black prisoners of war he had -

103.t: The same MP and the Fayetteville bus killing
103.s: Jones says the same MP later shot a bus driver who choked a black baby in North Carolina and was jailed at Fort Ord.
103.q: But this trumpet player - and it's on record - this same trumpet player was the one that they transferred and sent to Fayetteville. They was on a bus -

103.t: Meeting Hinton and Cab Calloway at the Omaha Orpheum, February 1946
103.s: Fresh from the Army, Jones sat in with Cab Calloway's band in Omaha, replacing Shadow Wilson briefly and impressing Cab with Oliver Buford.
103.ch: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
103.q: In Omaha, you know... February of '46, of course. I got out the first of February and I did 'The King' with Basie and Preston Love, who had replaced Earl Warren during the time - he and I both went to the Pennsylvania Station, got on a train, and went right straight to Omaha. Earl sat back in the…

103.t: Lester Young at Camp Gordon, playing all day in the rec hall
103.s: Jones says Lester left the Army before him and was kept playing in the rec hall at Camp Gordon, put back in the prisoner area each night.
103.ch: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
103.q: No, he did not. See, Lester beat me out of the Army and by that time, when Lester came out of the Army, I was at Fort Ord and they gave me a pass to go down to visit with Lester. See because at the time that Lester Young was in Camp Gordon, the general of the post loved Lester Young, you see, and…

103.t: Calling Basie from Fort Ord; "Cottage for Sale"; Norman Granz and Lester
103.s: From Fort Ord Jones telephoned Basie's band and Milt Ebbins, then visited Lester in Los Angeles, where Norman Granz began helping him.
103.ch: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
103.q: Basie I talked with him at the barbershop in the daytime, which was very difficult to get a phone call through, because we was still at war with Japan. But I finally got Basie. Then Milt Ebbins got on the phone and he says, "Basie's not here. He's in the studio and Billy Eckstine is making a…

103.t: Declining Jazz at the Philharmonic; Illinois Jacquet in the Basie band
103.s: Jones stayed with Basie rather than join Granz's tour since Jacquet had already left, and recalls how Jacquet joined Basie.
103.ch: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
103.q: No, he didn't go back. Then when Norman came through with the Jazz Philharmonic they wanted me to go with them and I would not go, because Illinois Jacquet left Basie's band if I left Basie's band there would have been a tremendous hole, I figured.

103.t: Leaving Basie: back in March 1946, gone in 1948
103.s: Jones dates his Army service from September 1944, his return in March 1946, and his leaving Basie in 1948.
103.ch: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
103.q: I stayed with Mr. Basie till 1948. I left.

103.t: Dannie Barker in Omaha and rejoining Basie in 1946
103.s: Jones tells how he introduced Dannie Barker to old circus musicians and then rejoined Basie in spring 1946.
103.ch: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
103.q: That's right and he left the band then. He stayed in Omaha with me for 3 days in my home and I got him a lot of literature and I introduced him to several of the old pioneers and I sent him down to Scott Joplin's home. There was a trumpet player that had lived round in that area that died. He had…

103.t: The Basie band of 1944 and its trumpet section
103.s: Jones says he stayed with Basie until September 1944 and names Joe Newman, Ed Lewis, Harry Edison and Al Killian at the Lincoln Hotel.
103.q: The trumpet? No, no, no, Shad had long gone. That was Joe Newman, because Joe Newman replaced Buck Clayton because Buck had gone into the Army.

103.t: When Lester Young left the band and Don Byas replaced him
103.s: They sort out the early 1940s, with Lester leaving for a USO tour with Al Sears and Don Byas taking his place.
103.q: Lester was there up to..... Lester left the band around about 42-ish or 43-ish, because he, Al Sears, they went out - remember the war had come along.

104.t: Joining the British and American USO shows
104.s: Choosing entertainment over the women's Army, touring with British and American USO, and going to France after the invasion.
104.q: Oh I think we had a contract, it was a real job. In fact at that time I had the choice of either being drafted into the woman’s Army, or going into some kind of entertainment, so

104.s: At a rest area in Belgium she met Jimmy; the jam session and her inexperience playing with a big band.
104.q: Unfortunately no. If I’d known what I was going to get into — I didn’t take pictures. Oh there are some, yeah there are some, but yeah there are some now that I think of it. But I should have kept a diary. And anyway we went through all of these miserably bombed and strafed towns that were just a…

104.t: Courtship, army pianos and marriage in Aachen
104.s: Entertaining troops, the accordion requirement, Jimmy fetching a piano, and their marriage in Aachen.
104.q: Well you know yes we did. And I guess going out every day early, out to the carrier to entertain the troops and going — maybe had to perform on a flatbed truck or they’d build a stage out of boards or it would be raining and they’d put a tarpaulin over the piano and stuff like that. It wasn’t…

104.t: What ENSA was, and why she joined rather than the women's army
104.s: They joke about ENSA meaning Every Night Something Awful; she says many players were second rate and she joined it in 1940 to avoid balloon-barrage service.
104.ch: Wartime entertaining: ENSA, USO and Jimmy
104.q: . . . a lot of the people in it were probably . . . what shall I say? . . . not first, not all first rate players. A lot of people that didn’t get much work anywhere else. I’m sure this happened a lot. In my own case, it was . . . we were . . . if I didn’t do that, then I would be forced to be a…

104.t: Moving from ENSA to the better-run USO in England
104.s: She found ENSA spartan, with bad pianos and broken-down buses; a friend, Zoni Dale, urged her to join the USO, which she did through its London office.
104.ch: Wartime entertaining: ENSA, USO and Jimmy
104.q: When I finally went with U.S.O. I realized everything was done on a much higher level than ENSA was. ENSA was really more . . . I guess it’s like I really found out about the American way. Everything is bigger and better. I enjoyed being with ENSA, but some of the conditions . . . It was the same…

104.t: The first USO show and landing in Normandy after D-Day
104.s: She performed with Cliff Hall and Sid Marion, listened to the invasion planes, and soon went to France with the first entertainers, playing for thousands of troops.
104.ch: Wartime entertaining: ENSA, USO and Jimmy
104.q: sure that . . . oh, you wouldn’t know the names, but I’ll mention them anyway. Cliff Hall and Sid Marion. Sid Marion, that was his last name. Did you ever hear of a show from years ago, Baron Munchhausen? You might have heard of it. Anyway, these people were known in the States years ago. Probably…

104.t: Turning to Jimmy McPartland, and USO guest stars in England
104.s: Williams asks about meeting Jimmy; she first recalls guest stars James Cagney, Edward G. Robinson and Dinah Shore joining USO shows.
104.ch: Wartime entertaining: ENSA, USO and Jimmy
104.q: U.S.O. I was well established in U.S.O. by that time, and we . . . There were different groups that would come and go. I guess I should backtrack a little bit. Some of the shows that we worked with in U.S.O. in England, they would bring over a famous guest star. One show that we had had James…

104.t: Normandy's ruined towns and the USO show with Willie Shaw
104.s: She describes the razed French towns and the troupe led by Don Rice, then Willie Shaw and his wife Julie, who knew Jimmy from Chicago.
104.ch: Wartime entertaining: ENSA, USO and Jimmy
104.q: God, I think he might have given up the ghost at this point. But anyway, when we arrived in Normandy Beach . . . I really hate myself for not having kept track or kept a diary . . . we would go through all these towns that were absolutely razed to the ground. They were just nothing but bricks and…

104.t: Marrying Jimmy in February 1945 and being separated
104.s: They married on February 4, 1945, were then sent back to separate units, and she begged rides on planes to visit him over a few months.
104.ch: Wartime entertaining: ENSA, USO and Jimmy
104.q: mind. Then to be in this hotel and enjoying playing every night. We’d do these concerts . . . We did some concerts in a local hall there. But then by this time we were talking about getting married. We did in fact get married. I think I always get the date wrong. February 4th, 1945. Then everything…

104.t: Learning repertoire from the BBC and records before meeting Jimmy
104.s: She learned most of her tunes from the BBC and records before she met Jimmy, and briefly retells how she moved from the Guildhall to vaudeville, ENSA, the USO and meeting Jimmy in Belgium.
104.q: Well I learned a lot of them before Jimmy. I knew them because all the tunes that were played in this country were played on the BBC. Big bands. Anything I heard on the BBC I could go to the piano and play. And then I had a lot of records that people brought to the house, of Duke and . . . I don’t…

104.t: Playing with Jimmy: learning to comp, not yet thinking of herself as a jazz player
104.s: She first played with a horn player when she met Jimmy, who told her to stop overplaying behind the soloist; she knew the repertoire but was mostly just in love and did not yet see herself as a jazz musician.
104.ch: Wartime entertaining: ENSA, USO and Jimmy
104.q: At that point that we were talking about, when I met Jimmy and started going out to play for the troops, I think I was still thinking of myself as a pianist . . . I must say that I knew all the tunes. I had no problem with repertoire. I could play all the tunes and anything that was being played…

104.t: Meeting Jimmy McPartland in Eupen and falling in love
104.s: Willie Shaw had Jimmy moved from a gun crew to Special Services; she sat in at his welcome party, they played for troops from Eupen, learned standards from him and decided to marry.
104.ch: Wartime entertaining: ENSA, USO and Jimmy
104.q: of extra rations and supplies and things that nobody was supposed to have, and he would always get them for us. He found out that Jimmy was in the area. I don’t know how this happened. He went to the commanding officer who was in charge of our U.S.O. group, and said, “This man shouldn’t be a G.I.…

104.t: How she found freelance work through Roma Clark and Dorothy Carless
104.s: She got jobs through contacts such as Roma Clark and Dorothy Carless, was in Felixstowe on a concert party when war broke out, and wrote no jazz tunes until the Hickory House.
104.ch: Jazz records, vaudeville and starting out
104.q: I was freelancing, and I guess I met a few . . . It’s funny. I’m really trying to think how this did happen, how I met this one woman that I worked with a lot, Roma Clark. I’m trying to think how I did meet her. It seems to me that . . . I’m trying to think what I belonged to, like an organization,…

105.t: Getting drafted while working with Lorenzo Flennoy
105.s: Working with Lorenzo Flennoy's band, Hamilton was drafted around the time of Pearl Harbor and sent with two others to Fort McClellan, Alabama.
105.q: Me, and Joe Comfort, and James Nelson, Hawk, Lorenzo, myself on drums and Doris Lathy on guitar. Anyway to make a long story short, I got drafted. There was only three of us. They sent us to Fort McLellan, Alabama. Me, Joe (Unintelligible), I forget this other guy’s name, but anyway they sent us…

105.t: Fort McClellan: mail orderly, bugler, and playing USO shows
105.s: In a segregated company he was made mail orderly and bugler instead of drummer, got hit by a rifle butt over mail, then was attached to the band to play shows and bond drives, meeting Forrest Tucker.
105.q: On this side of the mountain, Straw Mountain was the black troops, on that side of the mountain was the white troops. Well when I was in there the drummer with Claude Thornhill’s band -- damn, I can’t think of his name right now.

105.t: Southern favoritism and segregation in the army
105.s: He describes how good jobs went to southern boys, how noncoms were black but officers white, and how Jo Jones and Prez were barred from the band.
105.q: Well in the army, if you weren’t from the south forget it. All the good jobs, all the good things -- you know, if you’d been either from the east coast or west coast, you didn’t get them. No way, no shape, form or fashion. You know, you had to be good old southern boys.

105.s: He stayed in as a musician, rose to corporal, tried to get out, and was kept to play shows.
105.q: Yeah. I became a corporal. They didn’t want to give me a sergeant because they knew I was going to get -- I tried every day to get out, man. Some guys were just lucky and some guys -- I wasn’t that lucky.

105.t: Special Services tours and a Mississippi incident
105.s: He was in the army 1941 to 1945, never overseas, toured posts in Special Services, and tells of being near a lynching and his wife being taken for white on a train.
105.q: Well, no. All my brothers did, you know. All my brothers -- man, all four of us were in the service. It was combat down there, man.

105.t: Billy Exner, the army drummer who taught him to read
105.s: The Thornhill drummer is identified as William Exner, who met Hamilton in a field, taught him note values and drum music, and Hamilton already had his technique from Lee Young.
105.ch: Day two: LA youth and army revisited
105.q: Yeah, first of all man, he was a dynamite dude. I mean I can’t say enough accolades, good things about him. But as well as being a fantastic musician, he was fantastic drummer man and he could swing. And at that time man, the most important thing is -- you know, like from the beginning, if you…

105.t: Prez and Jo Jones in basic training
105.s: Fort McClellan was a basic training camp, and Prez and Jo Jones were made to carry rifles instead of being used as musicians.
105.ch: Day two: LA youth and army revisited
105.q: They were there for training. Basically Fort McClellan was a basic training camp and from there they shipped you out to -- as a matter of fact man, I had signed up for the Air Corps but they wouldn’t -­

105.t: Hospitalized in the psychiatric ward after seeing so many black soldiers
105.s: Culture shock from seeing so many black people landed him in the psychiatric ward for two or three weeks.
105.ch: Day two: LA youth and army revisited
105.q: Really. It affected me. And that probably sounds strange coming from, you know, a black dude but it was just -- that’s the affect. I’m being honest about it, you know. As a matter of fact I can talk about it.

105.t: Court-martialed for dragging his field drum
105.s: He refused an order on the field, dragged his drum across it, and was court-martialed and put on garbage detail.
105.ch: Day two: LA youth and army revisited
105.q: Yeah. Then they returned me back to duty. I got put in the stockade because I refused to -- we were on the field, we were practicing and the drum master, I forget his name, he was an fool. Anyway, to make a long story short, I refused to do something that I was ordered to do and I started dragging…

105.t: Sergeant Galloway and the marching band
105.s: A call about an old army friend recalls Sergeant Galloway, who later married Mahalia Jackson, and the marching band that shipped out troops.
105.ch: Day two: LA youth and army revisited
105.q: No. As a matter of fact, man, was it Sunday? Yeah, it was Sunday. I got a call from -- well my manager had called to ask me if I knew a McDonald and he says this guy from Gary, Indiana, had been calling me, wanted to know can you -- wanted my phone number. To make a long story short, Mac was…

105.t: Other musicians who passed through the army
105.s: Hamilton remembers Galloway and says most LA musicians went into the Navy.
105.ch: Bebop, band changes and the road
105.q: Yeah, well, there was Galloway. Let me see, none of the guys in the band that I was in, you know. Most of the guys -- fortunately most of the guys in LA, they all went to the navy. Gerald, and Jack, and Buddy, all of them were in the navy.

105.t: Learning the bugle and a story about a little drum
105.s: Asked how he learned bugle, Hamilton says it did not take long and tells a children's story of a drum aiming for Carnegie Hall.
105.q: Not long, I mean just practice; Carnegie Hall. I wrote a little story about a little drum, how a little drum became famous. And it ended with the Carnegie Hall thing. This little drum wanted to be played by a jazz musician. And he went around and he looked up a hundred -- and tried to be played by…

105.t: Jo Jones and Prez at McClellan; the Thornhill drummer teaches him to read
105.s: Jo and Prez were stationed there too, and a drummer from Claude Thornhill's band taught him to read drum music in the woods.
105.q: Jo Jones. Oh, let me tell you. The hippest thing that happened to me there, damn near had his name then, but anyway, the drummer that was with Claude Thornhill, I can’t think of his name right now but it will come to me. I’ll tell you tonight. But anyway we used to meet. We hooked up in the middle…

106.t: Straightening out the dates with the 369th
106.s: Briggs admits confusing his dates and clarifies he stayed with the 369th band until early 1919, after the war ended.
106.ch: Will Marion Cook and the Southern Syncopated Orchestra
106.q: I think there's a real mistake about dates. I think that I really messed up my dates. It was so long ago. I mean one year or two -- I was seventeen, eighteen, when I came up why I was eighteen.

106.t: Question about the Scrap Iron Jazz Band
106.s: Asked about a Scrap Iron Jazz Band, Briggs suggests it was one of the many groups formed by veterans of regimental brass bands who stayed in Europe.
106.ch: Chez Florence, the Hot Club and Django
106.q: during, after World War I, you had many members of the brass bands, who formed -- who stayed, different brass bands, I'm not just talking about Jim Europe's outfit.

106.t: Doc Cheatham's visit and Freddy's fate in wartime Holland
106.s: Doc Cheatham came to join Freddy just before the war and Briggs told him to go home; Freddy was trapped in Holland and forced by the Germans to care for his family.
106.q: he made a mistake, and the funniest thing is I told you yesterday, that Doc Cheatham, came over, three days before World War II was declared.

106.t: Arrested by the Germans on 7 December 1941
106.s: The Germans knew where all Allied nationals lived and picked up Briggs at 9 a.m. on the day Japan attacked the United States.
106.q: And, in the morning, we didn't even know that Japan had attacked the United States. We didn't know much. We found out when the Gerries came to pick us up.

106.t: Beethoven concert for General von Stulpnagel
106.s: The camp orchestra played Beethoven's Fifth for the Paris commander, who saluted Briggs, the only Black player, at the end.
106.q: But, by, (in a while) we had the Commandant of Paris, it came up and we gave a concert. It was more or less a Beethoven festival.

106.t: Camp life: tents, cold, cabbage soup and civilian status
106.s: Internees were treated as civilians, organised like a small city, and endured cold and worm-filled soup until the committee improved conditions during almost three years.
106.q: Yes, all together. All the Allies. Yes, all grouped together. And we're not considered as war prisoners, 'cause they couldn't force -- we would work if it was in the interest of our camp, to do things for our camp, we would work, but no one forced us to work, you see.

106.t: Liberation by Patton's army and his cousins' visit
106.s: The camp was liberated in August 1944 by Patton's troops; Briggs's two cousins in that army visited him in Paris that fall.
106.q: who were with him. I didn't see them, 'cause they were not in the group that liberated us, but I mean they were in the group that continued up to the Czechoslovakian border.

106.t: The Red Cross and the Gestapo
106.s: Briggs says the Red Cross inspections were useless because internees were locked in rooms and the Gestapo accompanied the largely German-Swiss inspectors.
