106.q: But, something I want to tell you that I hope the world will understand, one day is that the International Corps for Red Cross doesn't mean a thing.

106.t: Staying in shape in camp; Germans young and old
106.s: The daily orchestra rehearsals kept his chops fit, and Briggs jokes about the signature muted-trumpet note, and distinguishes decent older guards from young Hitler Youth recruits.
106.q: When I came out, I have to get myself in shape again, for resistance and everything, you see, endurance. Yes, I managed to keep up pretty nicely. But in our camp we used to have wonderful fun, 'cause at the end of our concerts, I would play with the -- with a muted trumpet. And, as soon as I hit…

106.t: No work under the Germans; the American consul says stay hidden
106.s: Briggs stopped playing, as French musicians were hostile, and the American consul Murphy told Americans to stay undercover.
106.q: That stopped, immediately. I had many propositions to work, but I did not work, because I knew that I would not be permitted to work. And the attitude of the French musicians didn't encourage me to try to work.

106.t: Aime Barelli returns defeated and receives Briggs's trumpet
106.s: The Nice trumpeter Aime Barelli, back from the army with only his mouthpiece, was taken in by Briggs, given a civilian outfit and his trumpet, and introduced to Charles Delaunay.
106.q: He came back as a beaten soldier, more or less. He had nothing and he had no where to go. He didn't know anybody in Paris, but he went to the local, and asked where he could find me. They gave him an address and he came up to see me.

106.t: Joining Lt. Fred Simpson's replacement band for the 369th
106.s: When Jim Europe's band went overseas, Lt. Fred Simpson auditioned the St. Marks band to form a replacement 369th regiment band.
106.ch: Will Marion Cook and the Southern Syncopated Orchestra
106.q: Yes, that is Lieutenant -- Mr. Simpson, Mr. Fred Simpson, was commissioned Lieutenant, to form this new group. The replacement group.

106.t: Interned at Compiegne and Creteil; bugler and orchestra
106.s: After a week at Compiegne he was transferred to a camp with a thirty-piece amateur orchestra and negotiated eating with the kitchen staff in return for blowing four daily bugle calls.
106.q: At Creteil. They first sent us to Compiegne. And I stayed at Compiegne, say about a week. Because, there was another Allied camp, where they had a group of about thirty amateur musicians, and as you know, the only type of music we could play then was light music and symphonies and things. That was…

92.t: Carter's Kelly's Stables bill; the draft notice and Carter's appeal
92.s: The Kelly's show with Carter, Nat Cole's trio, Tatum and Miss Rhapsody; later at the Apollo Collins was drafted and Carter appeared with him before the board.
92.ch: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
92.q: So I stayed in New York and went to work with Benny. And let's see now, who was on this bill? I think it was Benny Carter, and Nat, and his trio, Art Tatum, and we had a singer by the name of Miss Rhapsody. She didn't call herself Miss Raspody-- Rhapsody, it was Miss Raspody, you know. And I think…

92.t: Teaching Tiny Grimes for Tatum while in the army
92.s: On furlough in 1942 Collins taught Tiny Grimes chords and voicings for Tatum's trio, and says four army years kept him off the scene.
92.ch: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
92.q: But in the mean time Art had approached me about joining him with the trio, but you know, obviously I couldn't take the job because I had to go into the army, so I came back to New York on furlough and I went to see Art. He was working at this time at another club now, the Three Deuces, farther…

92.t: Teaching and Irving Ashby in the army
92.s: Collins always taught guitarists and showed chords to Irving Ashby in the army at Fort Huachuca, who then joined Nat Cole.
92.ch: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
92.q: Also, Pat, I know you're aware that I love to teach. And during that time I was doing some teaching also, as a matter of fact --

92.t: Into the army; great players outlasting changes of style
92.s: Collins went in as soon as war was declared and stayed four years; he notes great players like Roy remain great.
92.ch: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
92.q: I went in the service as soon as they declared war that year they said John. Got me right away. And I stayed in for four years, just about four years.

92.t: Army bands in South Carolina and Alabama
92.s: He served about four years, stuck in a weak South Carolina band that would not release him because he could read, before going to Oakland.
92.ch: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
92.q: So after -- I don't know what Prez did after that. I went in the army before Prez, I believe, and then Prez followed me in the army. And I stayed in the army for four

92.t: Oakland: recording with Billie Holiday and Vernon Alley; Marshall Royal's navy band
92.s: Stationed in Oakland around 1945, he recorded with Billie Holiday at the Fairmont, and played with Vernon Alley and Marshall Royal's navy band.
92.ch: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
92.q: Well, in Oakland all the musicians came through, and I got a chance to play all the clubs. As a matter of fact I recorded with Billie Holiday there, and she was at the Fairmont, I believe, or we recorded at the Fairmont. That was when she was married to Joe Guy. And Vernon Alley and I recorded with…

92.t: Recording with Tatum: 'Battery Bounce' and bad timing
92.s: Collins recorded with Tatum only once or twice, on unamplified guitar before the army, and missed a second chance when he left for Nat.
92.ch: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
92.q: I recorded with -- it's a funny thing. I only recorded with Art once. No, I didn't. Once or twice. It just so happened in Chicago during that time we weren't doing any recording when I started with him at the Duces. When I went to New York, this is when I recorded with him. But I left and went to…

92.t: Lester Young's court-martial and his changed playing after the army
92.s: Willard cites Blesh on Prez's court-martial over a pill; Collins found him burned out and not the same Lester after discharge.
92.ch: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
92.q: I don't think Lester ever recovered, really. You know, because the scene had changed so, and the army had probably demoralized Lester. I never could understand how they could keep a man of Lester's temperament in the army. You know, it probably -- I'm sure emotionally and otherwise it really took…

92.t: Why the army was wrong for Lester; Collins slipping away from training
92.s: Collins says regimentation and uncomprehending officers could destroy Prez, and describes dodging maneuvers until a master sergeant moved him into the band.
92.ch: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
92.q: Well, in the first place regimentation, you know, he couldn't go for that at all. This I knew. And he -- Lester was a very -- he was an introvert in a lot of ways, and a lot of people just wouldn't understand Lester. You know, they wouldn't understand him, and wouldn't know how to deal with him.…

92.t: Lester Young in Alabama: the guardhouse and the picture of his wife
92.s: Willard relates that Prez was jailed after a picture of his white wife was found; Collins knew only that he returned changed.
92.ch: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
92.q: Yeah, yeah. Oh, yeah, he was in Alabama. I knew where he was. He was not too far from where I was. I was in South Carolina. But fortunately I was with -- I was in a training camp, which means that we were there primarily to entertain the troops. We would march them in, entertain them while they're…

92.t: Meeting John Lewis through Kenny Clarke
92.s: After the war Collins heard John Lewis, whom Kenny Clarke had found in the army, and was impressed by the simplicity and depth of his playing.
92.ch: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
92.q: That's right. And I mean, this was just his way. It wasn't -- he wasn't capable of changing. Lester was very strong in his beliefs, and in his life style, you know. So they could destroy him. And something actually happened to him then, you know. So I played with him around New York a couple of…

92.t: Refusing to unload boxcars in the Oakland port company
92.s: Placed in a port company in Oakland, Collins refused boxcar duty, was made to wash a hundred windows on Thanksgiving, and was transferred to a band camp.
92.ch: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
92.q: didn't understand the type of company I was in, which didn't mean too much to me any way because I assumed that they had a band and that I would be in the band.

107.t: Army at Camp Roberts and Bop City: the Soldier Boy
107.s: Stationed near San Francisco, he found Bop City, played Cherokee with Dexter Gordon, became known as Soldier Boy, and Lester Young said he played too many notes.
107.q: Oh yes, I had to play lots in the service. Before going overseas, I was shipped to the Far East, where, after Basic Training, the Korean campaign was going on. But I was stationed at a camp that was halfway between San Francisco and Los Angeles, in the California foothills, and it was called Camp…

107.t: Segregation and playing in the Army in Japan and Korea
107.s: Basic training was in an all-black unit, but Japan and Korea were integrated; he joined the division band and avoided the front line.
107.q: Somewhat yes. I trained Basic Training in an all-black company that was part of an all- black battalion. But as soon as I got to Japan and Korea, it was all over, it was totally integrated. But I didn’t mention about how much I got to play while I was in Japan and Korea. I was in Japan for a very…

107.t: Going AWOL, the chaplain and the stockade
107.s: He went AWOL over Thanksgiving and Christmas, was told by the chaplain to give up jazz, did five days in the stockade and spent 13 months in Korea.
107.q: ‘52. In ‘51 I was drafted into the Army and most of ‘51 was spent in the California area, San Francisco. I went AWOL for over a month over Thanksgiving and Christmas because I was afraid that after I finished Basic Training, the idea of going, actually into the war as an infantry rifleman, you know…

107.t: The draft notice, induction and Fort Custer
107.s: Foster dodged draft notices between Cincinnati and Detroit, was inducted in March 1951, and met Buddy Montgomery at Fort Custer.
107.q: The draft notice came. The Korean War was in full swing. This is 1950, and a draft notice came to my parents home in Cincinnati. They sent it to me. I played musical cities with the Army for a few months, because I said, they’ll have to catch up with me in Detroit. My parents gave the draft board…

107.t: Playing sick to avoid Georgia; basic training at Camp Roberts
107.s: A white sergeant helped him fake illness and get California orders; he never touched a saxophone during 14 weeks of training.
107.q: He said, “You play sick, because you don’t want to go to Georgia. That’s the heart of the South. You don’t want to go down there.” So I actually for the first time in my life played sick. I was so convincing. He helped me along. He said, “Can’t you see he’s sick? He can’t be shipped out.” So they…

107.s: After Leadership School he overstayed a pass for 39 days over Christmas playing at Bop City, putting off Korea.
107.q: Just about. Not the first couple, but then after that. Then after that we went through a school, which is called Leadership School, during which time you couldn’t go anywhere. That was -- they gave us some kind of test, and I qualified. I figured this would keep me out of Korea a little longer, so…

107.t: Turning himself in and being sent to Japan
107.s: The chaplain told him to give up jazz; he got a 39-day sentence cut to five, then supply school in Japan, where he sold his horn.
107.q: Yeah, I went and turned myself in. I went to the chaplain. I explained that I was a musician and that I just got carried away, didn’t want --

107.t: Korea: supply work, the division band and Pepper Adams
107.s: He worked supply, auditioned for the 7th Division band, and met Pepper Adams, Bernie Peacock and slide-saxophonist Snub Mosley.
107.q: I was in a supply company of an infantry regiment working supply. I did that for a couple of months. Then I went to audition with the division band. I hiked about ten miles down a Korean road just to audition for this band. I passed the audition, and I was transferred from this supply company to…

107.t: The army band's jazz combo and the records they heard
107.s: His combo with William Boone played for the troops, and the men heard Monk, Bird, Diz and Miles records.
107.q: There were good musicians, yeah. We had a jazz combo in the army band, in the 7th Division Band. We had the marching band, we had about a 14- to 15-piece dance band, and we had a jazz combo. In this jazz combo there was pianist named William Boone, who was a native of Brooklyn. If it hadn’t been…

107.t: War, marijuana and boredom in Korea
107.s: He saw no combat but heard gunfire nightly, disliked the army, and recalls smoking marijuana grown in the fields.
107.q: It didn’t feel good at all. I did not like it. I did not like the Korean countryside. I hated the army experience of getting up early in the morning and having a long day, a long hard day, and finally getting to bed at night and getting -- we’d get a pass to go into a local village. All you could…

107.t: Weekends at Jimbo's Bop City, and sitting in with Dexter Gordon
107.s: He rode to San Francisco on weekend passes, sat in with Dexter on Cherokee, and was known as 'Soldier Boy' and written up by Ralph Gleason.
107.q: California was most interesting, because I was wondering, whenever we got a weekend pass, should I go to LA? Should I go to San Francisco? Because I know most of these metropolises should have a jazz scene, but I didn’t know which way I should go. I figured if I go to one, that will be it. It so…

108.t: Moving to New York and Marine Corps service at Montford Point
108.s: He has lived in New York since 1947; in the Marines he was Assistant Bandmaster at Montford Point, then returned to Hampton briefly and left for Lunceford.
108.q: I guess yes I have as a matter of fact, since 1947. I was born in Colwyn, Pennsylvania though. And I went into the Marine Corps for three years and when I came out I went back with Lionel Hampton and I stayed there a short time and I wasn’t very happy and I left that band and went with Jimmy…

108.t: Drafted into the Marines and playing in the band
108.s: Wilder was drafted in 1943 and chose the newly recruiting Marine Corps; Bobby Troup got him into the band, where he became assistant bandmaster and played for Chesty Puller and at dances.
108.q: That’s one of the reasons I went into the Marine Corps. I had a choice of going into the Army, the Navy or the Marine Corps, which had just begun to recruit black marines. This was the first time. I was not in the initial group, but the platoon that I was in brought the number of black marines to…

108.t: Rough start for black Marines in the South
108.s: Integration of the Marines was hard, with only white officers in authority and Southern racial conditions made harsher by the military.
108.q: Yeah, it was rough in the beginning. It was a pretty rough situation because there were no black officers and there were only a few black non-commissioned officers, corporals and maybe a couple of buck sergeants. But that came later actually. So that all the personnel with any authority were white,…

108.s: After dodging the draft by transferring boards, he is classified 1-A and chooses the newly opened black Marines.
108.ch: Marine Corps and family at war
108.q: Oh yeah. I was 1-A. The only thing about that was, after I was classified 1-A, I had been trying to avoid going in, period, by transferring the draft board from Philadelphia to California. We were in California. So they let me transfer it out there. But then, when I didn’t go in out there, and we…

108.t: Father and brothers in service; assistant bandmaster at Montford Point
108.s: His father joins the Navy and two brothers the Army; Wilder becomes assistant bandmaster at Montford Point.
108.ch: Marine Corps and family at war
108.q: Yeah. My father was in the Navy. My father had been in World War I by putting his age up, saying he was older than he was. He was 17 years old. Then he was in 1-A at the time of World War II, and having been in the Navy before, he said, rather than wait for them to draft him, he would sign up,…

108.t: Leading the marching band and ruffles and flourishes
108.s: As technical sergeant he runs the marching band and must know the ruffles and flourishes for each rank.
108.ch: Marine Corps and family at war
108.q: We had a dance band, in which I was not in charge of that. There was another sergeant in charge of that. I was a tech sergeant. I was in charge of the marching band.

108.t: Segregation and abuse of the first black Marines
108.s: Black Marines at Montford Point face insults, police harassment in Jacksonville and unequal treatment.
108.ch: Marine Corps and family at war
108.q: Oh yeah. That was the beginning. They were just beginning to enlist black Marines. My platoon brought the number of black Marines at Montford Point to ten hundred, the first thousand, which sounds like a big deal, but there were other guys who were the first 40. They’re the ones that really caught…

108.t: Bobby Troup and the officers who fought discrimination
108.s: Officers including Bobby Troup press for fairness and are punished; black athletes' teams are broken up.
108.ch: Marine Corps and family at war
108.q: But the conditions were really rough. We had some fellows who went, for instance, to Ohio, and met the same thing. They were – we were all proud. We were in a Marine uniform. Go home, you have the uniform on, and they were challenged by Army MPs. “What the so-and-so are you doing with that Marine…

108.t: Getting moved from combat training into the band
108.s: Troup helps get him transferred; the band was good with players from southern black colleges and he never went overseas.
108.ch: Marine Corps and family at war
108.q: It was a while. When I first went in, I was in special weapons. We were all taking combat training at that time. Then, actually, it was Bobby Troup who began putting pressure. He said, “You got a guy here who’s played with” this band and that

108.t: Father's and brothers' wartime service and his brother Curtis
108.s: His father in Navy bands, his brothers in combat in Europe, and his close relation to bassist brother Curtis.
108.ch: Marine Corps and family at war
108.q: My brother? Oh yeah. He was a – he played with Damita Jo, the singer. He was with her. He used to sing with her too. And he played with some other trios. But he died many years ago.

108.t: Music as morale during the war
108.s: Bands traveled if they played free for bases.
108.q: It was quite important, morale-wise, especially with the big bands. They were given permission – I know, when I was with Lionel Hampton before I went into the service, we could travel all over the country only as long as they promised, when they were close to a military base, that they would give a…

109.t: Frank Stouffer's Japan offer and the fate of the band
109.s: He turned down a contract to Japan in 1935; trumpeter Jimmy Brown died in an internment camp and Jimmy Allen returned in 1938.
109.q: Frank Stouffer his name is. And while we were working with them right along there, you know. It wasn't a very hard job. So they got a contract to go to Japan, in 1935.

109.t: Called up: family situation and brother's war work
109.s: Unmarried, with his stepfather dead and his brother exempt as a welder building Liberty ships, he reported for the draft without dodging.
109.q: Yeah. Well I decided, you know -- I said, "Well, my career has been interrupted, so what else is there?" You know. So I just -- I didn't try to dodge my obligations. I just went and said, "Here I am. Do whatever you want to do with me, but --,"

109.t: Camp Upton, segregation, training in Alabama, declining warrant officer
109.s: Drafted with Ralph Watkins and separated by race at Camp Upton; trained at Camp Siebert, and turned down a warrant-officer path.
109.q: Yeah. So when we got through the line, and they said, 'All the colored here and all the white here,' and that was it. And I didn't see him until --

109.t: Choosing overseas; the chaplain keeps him off D-Day
109.s: Offered Jackson, Mississippi or overseas, he chose overseas; in Liverpool and the marshalling area a priest kept him from the D-Day landings to play hymns, and he reached Le Havre in the autumn.
109.q: Because they sent the band I was playing with there to Jackson, Mississippi. So they asked me, "You have a choice, Kenny, you either go to Jackson, Mississippi or overseas." So I chose to go overseas, you know, because I figured that --

109.s: At the Lichfield camp Black soldiers who crossed the street could be shot; the colonel was court-martialed.
109.q: He was at a very -- it was a very bad camp and we had a lot of incidents and things like that, so he stayed there and tried to keep order, you know. What was the name of that? Litchfield.

109.t: 13th Special Service: music department and the soldiers' chorale
109.s: Trained in chemical warfare, he drifted into music, helped found the 13th Special Service as head of music, and led a 12-voice chorale that toured the front and played Paris's Madeleine Theatre.
109.q: But little by little I began to form little groups and they began to sing and then played in the church, and finally they made a company, the 13th Special Service, and I was head of the music department. And they elected a colored Lieutenant, Lieutenant Chaney (PHONETIC). So they put him over the…

109.t: Instrumentalists in the unit; teaching a drummer so he could play trombone
109.s: The unit had a small band; Clarke played trombone and trained a big soldier to play drums so he would not have to carry the drum kit.
109.q: So I couldn't cope with the drums and teaching everybody and directing the chorale, and all that, so --

109.t: Rouen, prisoners, the Ardennes search and Germany
109.s: Stationed in Rouen guarding German prisoners, then searching the Ardennes for missing soldiers after the Battle of the Bulge, and later posted near Heidelberg and Mannheim with the German Youth Association unit.
109.q: Where we made our landing. And we were guarding prisoners, German prisoners, there. We arrived in October, we stayed through Christmas. I remember because I remember German soldiers singing Christmas carols, and singing with our group along with them. And then it went up into the

109.t: Captain Arthur Taylor gets him sent home
109.s: A Sergeant called him AWOL after a trip taking a Major to Brussels, but old Pittsburgh schoolmate Captain Arthur Taylor checked his points and sent him and his friends home.
109.q: And there was a Captain who was assigned to our company whom I had went to school with in Pittsburgh, Captain Taylor, Arthur Taylor.

109.t: Demobilisation at Fort Dix; contacting Dizzy
109.s: At Fort Dix he met James Moody and Joe Gales and wrote to Dizzy, then went to see his brother.
109.q: Well, while we were in Fort Dix I met James Moody, because they were all being demobilized also. Joe Gale, a tenor player. And we became buddies, you know. We would play around in the camp, because it took us about -- about 10 days to be demobilized.

109.t: Back with Dizzy's band; meeting John Lewis in the 92nd Division
109.s: At rehearsal he found Moody and Gales in Dizzy's band; John Lewis phoned from Albuquerque, and Clarke explains they met in 1944 in remnants of the 92nd Division.
109.q: Yeah. Well, I showed up at rehearsal, as I was telling you, when I came home, and at rehearsal I looked at the fellows in the band, and there sat James Moody and Joe Gales.

96.t: Playing 'Blue Bells of Scotland' from the troop ship
96.s: Arriving at Greenock, he plays the song his mother taught him, bagpipes answer and the colonel restores his sergeant's stripes; he plays it again.
96.ch: Army cornet and Bix's Bach horn
96.q: And she taught me how to play 'Blue Bells of Scotland' and so I figured I'll blow the thing. And I did, I played 'Blue Bells of Scotland' the first chorus real straight and pretty and then I jazzed it up in the second chorus.

96.s: On transfer to Special Service he first hears Marian play Honeysuckle Rose and is won over by her ballads.
96.q: got a call one morning after I came off this patrol. I just came off the patrol and the colonel wanted to see me. I had put in before that that I wanted to go into Special Service and play the cornet again.

96.t: Playing with her show behind the lines; the first date
96.s: They play with a USO show near the front, and on their first date she pays for lunch.
96.q: where we would play. We go out in the Ardennes Forest and play for these guys. I give those gals a lot of credit, they were right up there. Oh, I invited her out. I know, the first, we had a day off I invited her to go to Spa in Belgium. I said, we have a day off, do you want to go? Sure.

96.t: Eupen, the Capitol Theater and requisitioning a grand piano
96.s: At the Eupen rest area he requisitions a collaborator's grand piano for Marian's show.
96.q: Then we went to, things were quiet there just before the Battle of the Bulge deal. So we left that area in the Ardennes Forest and went to a town called EUPEN. They pronounce it over there YOU-PEN. We pronounce it (OY-PEN). EUPEN. And they set us up in hotels and everything. And it was a rest area…

96.t: The Battle of the Bulge: Marian returns through paratroopers
96.s: Civilians are evacuated; Marian returns through paratroopers to take musicians for a Christmas show.
96.q: get married in Belgium because I didn't have any divorce papers. So the only way we could get married was in Germany.. And so the chaplain was getting things set up but everybody tried to talk her out of it and talk me out of it. But no, no, no. And then the Bulge came along. The Battle of the…

96.t: Strafed on Christmas Day; firing a 50-caliber gun
96.s: During dinner German planes strafe them and he helps man a 50-caliber at a German fighter.
96.q: And during that Christmas Day by the way, a rather interesting thing happened. I knew how to work a 50-caliber machine gun and while we were having dinner we started to get strafed. These 109s started to strafe us and everybody hit the floor you know. And I ran outside and I was down on the ground…

96.s: The chaplain sets things up, Marlene Dietrich's show arrives, and they marry on 3 February 1945 with a week's honeymoon in Brussels.
96.q: So, that's true. And so she set the thing up. But in the mean time they didn't send me up to the front lines, they kept me there in Upon and we stayed there. And then the break through of the Bulge was over and a man came back with another show with Marlena Deitrich as a matter of fact, Marlena…

96.t: ENSA, and leading General Huebner's orchestra
96.s: Marian was on loan from ENSA; he became the general's orchestra leader and flew to Paris to see her.
96.q: Yes. She was on lend from the British ENSA which is the equivalent of our USO. She was transferred over. They needed piano players who could play accordian and so on and so forth. She could do anything on those things.

96.t: USO camp show with Celeste Holm; Nuremberg
96.s: After discharge he leads the orchestra for a six-month show; an accident ends it.
96.q: Anyway, when we got, oh I don't suppose you want to hear more about this. I got my discharge in Paris and went with one of the USO camp shows for a six month period. And Celeste Holm was our star and I was the orchestra leader and Marian was the manager of the show. And we went to the Nuremberg…

96.s: He takes currency control books from an officer and sends money orders home at three to one.
96.q: Some little lieutenant in Remes, France. I get in and this guy had just come from America and hadn't seen any action or anything. A young guy and a smart alec and he was selling money orders to me, a lieutenant!. An officer, selling me money orders. He wanted to sell me money orders. Three hundred…

96.t: Army service from Normandy, and the cornet carried through the war
96.s: He served in anti-aircraft, hit Normandy D plus 4, lost his patriotism and tried to get into a band, carrying the Benge cornet.
96.ch: Army cornet and Bix's Bach horn
96.q: : Well I called myself a drunken patriot. Because I used to drink a lot and I guess that's where I got my courage but man, I wasn't drinking when I hit Normandy and oh, oh, Lord. So I lost my patriotism fast and tried to get back in a band. It took me from June 10th until around October something.…

110.t: Hearing about Pearl Harbor on his 21st birthday
110.s: He was visiting his brother Howard in Concord when the news came at a service station.
110.ch: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
110.q: For my birthday I went to Concord to visit Howard, who was teaching at Mt. Diablo High School, where my mother had created that high school [ ] from there, and now he’s teaching. He had graduated from San Francisco State Teacher’s College. At this

110.t: Postwar plans: working nightclubs and joints
110.s: He had planned to keep playing nightclubs, especially jazz places with African-American audiences, and says he would have been happy with that.
110.ch: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
110.q: I was working at this point in my senior year. Many jobs were six nights a week in nightclubs. So I knew I could make – I was always getting union scale then, and you could live on that. So I wasn’t worried. I had a fairly good reputation that I could work. So that’s what I planned to do, was just…

110.t: Marrying Iola on a three-day Army pass
110.s: He arranged a quick wedding in Carson City with no family present, then drove back to camp near Riverside.
110.ch: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
110.q: Below Riverside, California, so it wouldn’t have been too far, to go over the border. I decided, “If I can get a three-day pass, I’ll go back home and go to Carson City, Nevada, get married and see your parents and see my parents.” Nobody came to our wedding. [ ] To this day, when I think of the…

110.t: Trying to join black Army and Navy bands at Fort Meade and Washington
110.s: Prompted by Gloyd, he tells how he sat in with a black Army band and with Bud Harr's Navy band but was barred from joining either.
110.ch: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
110.q: Oh yeah. I’ll tell that story. After the band broke up at Camp Haan – there were three full-size 28-piece bands. We were told there would be one band left. That means two bands got to go. Some of us went in to the infantry. Some guys went to another camp as a band, but broken up from Camp Haan.…

110.t: Troop ship to Europe, Verdun and forming a band
110.s: He crosses on the George Washington, reaches the mud at Verdun, plays for a Red Cross truck show and is kept from the front to lead a band of wounded men.
110.ch: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years

110.t: Pearlman, Studs Terkel's The Good War and the Cronkite recording
110.s: The man who built the truck changed his name to Waxman and appears in Terkel's book; Brubeck also recorded Private Brubeck Remembers with Walter Cronkite.
110.ch: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
110.q: Pearlman changed his name to Waxman. If you want to check up on him, Studs Terkel’s book The Good War has an interview with him, and Waxman starts talking about me.

110.t: Choosing Mills College to study with Milhaud
110.s: His brother Howard's studies led him to Milhaud, who told him before the war to come study with him afterward.
110.q: My brother was studying with [Darius] Milhaud. He and Pete Rugolo went from San Francisco State [College] to Mills to get their masters degrees. They would be some of the first males to attend Mills. They allowed it on masters degree programs. It was through Howard that I heard about Milhaud. While…

110.t: First meeting with Paul Desmond at the Presidio audition
110.s: Before going overseas he auditioned for a Presidio band where Desmond called his changes wigsville.
110.ch: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
110.q: I was on my way overseas in the infantry. Dave Van Kreidt, who had come to live in the bomb shelter at the College of Pacific – unannounced one day, I came back from school and there in the cellar was Dave Van Kreidt on one of the rusty old beds. He’d moved in without asking anybody. What he did…

110.t: The jazz beat in the room and catatonic patients responding to live music
110.s: The room warmed to the beat, which recalls an Army hospital where live jazz drew responses from catatonic patients.
110.q: It was surrounded by apartment houses and a lot of sentries and everybody watching everything, but you still felt that there could be sniper, maybe up, and that’s why they had sealed this room off. So we’re going to play in this room. You just feel a little nervous tension. When we started playing…

110.t: The son of the army pianist who took his place
110.s: Years later a piano tuner turns out to be the son of the pianist whose job Brubeck took, and Brubeck tells him his father played better than he did.
110.ch: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
110.q: The son of that pianist. I’ve got his name written down, because I always forgot. His father’s name was a hard name for me to remember. He tuned my piano before a concert, the son, and he said . . .

111.t: Enlisting in 1946; Fort Dix and Fort Lee band school
111.s: He enlisted wanting an Army or Air Corps band, trained at Fort Dix, then the military band school at Fort Lee where he taught.
111.q: No. I used to see this recruiting station and I said, “well what am I doing I’m tired of working in this laundry [business]”. I said. “Ill join the Army” so that’s what I did.

111.t: Transfer to the 766th Army Air Corps band
111.s: He was transferred to the Air Corps band in Columbus, Ohio, after teaching drum cadences at Fort Lee, and says he loved Army life.
111.q: Yes, exactly. And the Army Air Core was the same, it wasn’t any different at that time. Before I got out they designated it as the Air Force, and they took it out of the Army jurisdiction.

111.t: Segregated units and bandleader Mr. Bryce
111.s: He recalls integrated band school but a segregated Columbus unit, with a bandleader who reminded him of Weist.
111.q: Yes. But you know the only difference was that in the band training school it wasn’t segregated. And this was in Camp Lee! So they had people from all over the Army white black anybody else. So it was just, “You’re here to study you learn to march in the Army and how to play these marches”. I…

111.t: Marimba with Ragland and playing bass drum
111.s: Besides duty he studied marimba with a Columbus Symphony percussionist and chose the bass drum for its role in the cadence.
111.q: I played all of the percussion instruments. I played the bass drum because nobody had the will to do it. I was the one that said, “I don’t mind playing the bass drum” because I like to listen to the cadence and the bass drum is essential to the cadence. If you don’t hear that the cadence isn’t…

111.t: Special Services show and working as a stagehand
111.s: He explains the Special Services unit that formed a touring stage show, where he was stagehand rather than a band member.
111.q: I did! What eventually happened was the Special Services men came through. Some guy from Washington [D.C.] he came through and he organized a unit that could play at all of the Air Force [Formerly Air Core] bases throughout the United States and in the world and whatever, and create a stage show.…

111.t: Operation Happiness and subbing for Perry Reed
111.s: He organized the show Operation Happiness, learned big-band playing from drummer Perry Reed, and took his place; he was discharged as T/5.
111.q: Well I started organizing this show called Operation Happiness. We took that show to – we had transport planes and we’d load up the planes and go to Texas and go to California and all over the United States and we’d do these shows. I enjoyed that. I listened to—there was this drummer called Perry…

111.t: Playing drum set in the Air Force; Perry Reed again
111.s: He confirms he never played other service bands, that his stagehand job let him learn the show, and he subbed on the drum set.
111.ch: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
111.q: No I never did cause the guys they had these small groups. And I really wasn’t interested in that at that point. We played the NCO Club, t Officers’ Club to make some extra money and stuff like that. But I never got interested in that.

111.t: Racism, Black GIs in Japan and his father's draft refusal
111.s: The talk moves to race, Black troops in Japan, and Elvin's father walking to Jackson to refuse the World War I draft.
111.q: She was in Fukuoka they had an air base down there and the Korean war was on and they were sending people back and forth from Korea.

111.t: What the Army gave him: self-discipline
111.s: He says the Army gave him self-discipline.
111.q: Well it gave me a certain understanding of self-discipline. We all have to have that if we intend to grow up and mature as a man or as a person. You know, here you got a horn you say, “Do you know how to play it? I see you got a horn but do you know how to play it?” (Laughs) Somebody has to be…like…

111.t: Going home for his father's illness
111.s: He explains the Red Cross furlough, his short stay in Pontiac and the bus trips back to base.
111.ch: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
111.q: Yes well I got a compassionate furlough from the Red Cross. I didn’t now my father was ill it was just one of my brothers or my sisters must have called my base or the Red Cross. Next thing I know they’re saying, “You gotta go home. Your father is sick” so that’s how that came about.

112.t: Working out his age at the draft
112.s: A long exchange in which Albertson and Wooding try to reconcile his 1895 birth, voting at twenty, and being drafted before turning twenty-one.
112.q: No, I couldn't be. What, see, I'll tell you why I couldn't. When I registered, I had no right to register for the draft. Because, the reason I had no right to register for the draft was, I had been voting, from 1916 I had been voting. And posing as a man. Then, when I went up to, when I was called…

112.t: What the draft and Army taught him
112.s: He says being drafted was the best thing for him because he learned discipline and manhood.
112.ch: Charley Johnson and the Army band
112.q: I learned how to deal with other people. I learnt how to obey the authorities, and how to respect those that are over you and how to know how to get out of those under you. Those are the things I learnt. I learnt manhood, I learnt to be a man and how to be a man. Which a lot of people don't know…

112.t: Army band and Lieutenant Bill Vodery
112.s: Wooding says he was a second-class musician in the band led by Bill Vodery, Ziegfeld's arranger.
112.ch: Charley Johnson and the Army band
112.q: and ended up as a Second Class musician. I played in the band. But, I wasn't any kind of non-commissioned officer for the simple reason why, every day I was in the Y.M.C.A. practicing, playing. And I was also watching my friend I took so much off of. Old Bill Vodey. Old Bill Vodey was the rage for…

112.t: Sailing for France and the band's members
112.s: He names bandmates, says it took three tries to join the last non-labor-battalion Black band, and that he played baritone horn.
112.ch: Charley Johnson and the Army band
112.q: Yeah, we went to war. We went to, we landed in St. Nazare. We was -- when we came back to St. Nazare, we were deloused there. But it was a wonderful experience. When we came to America from there, we came in at Hampton Road, and the guys actually cried on each other's shoulders. We had some great…

112.t: Bugle Blues copied from the Fifteenth Regiment
112.s: The band played Sousa marches and tried to copy Jim Europe's Fifteenth Regiment band's Bugle Blues.
112.ch: Charley Johnson and the Army band
112.q: : Oh yeah, Sousa marches, and then they started -- we tried to imitate, one thing that we tried to imitate was Jim Europe, at the Fifteenth, they had a fellow named Fats. And Fats played -- from Chicago -- and he played this "Bugle Blues." That's the first time I heard the Bugle Blues, and

112.t: Sousa played straight; Army shaped character not music
112.s: The band played Sousa straight, and the Army taught him discipline and appreciation of home.
112.ch: Charley Johnson and the Army band
112.q: : Oh yeah, because it was necessary. It would have been a crime to take a Sousa march, like "Stars and Stripes", or one of those other marches and mess with it.

112.t: Length of service and war's end
112.s: He served about fourteen months from early 1918 to 1919 and first heard 'fini la guerre' in the Meuse-Argonne.
112.ch: Charley Johnson and the Army band
112.q: Then we were mustered out in 1919, and we come back.

112.t: Willy Lewis and Johnny Mitchell stranded in Europe
112.s: Some band members, like Willy Lewis and Johnny Mitchell, stayed and were caught in Germany during the war.
112.ch: Second European tour and the crash
112.q: Well, he, they got caught over there. Johnny Mitchell was caught in there, too. And they couldn't get out. Johnny Mitchell and, I think that's the reason why Freddie Johnson is dead today. Because they had to -- they were caught and put there to entertain the German officers and everything. They…

112.t: Army band repertoire and French audiences
112.s: He confirms the Bugle Blues is the Bugle Call Rag, says the band played ragtime and marches, and played for French townspeople.
112.ch: Charley Johnson and the Army band
112.q: No, no, there wasn't no jazz. Cause they didn't have any jazz, then. Not those boys. They were -- we had some of them there, and some of them are still living around here. But what they had, they called Ragtime.

112.t: Army anecdotes: saltpetre, Meuse-Argonne and the German plane
112.s: He tells comic stories of the saltpetre prank and shell shock joke and of a German pilot waving at the band.
112.ch: Charley Johnson and the Army band
112.q: So one fellow, he tells a funny case. He was making it across to the latrine, as we called them, and as he got half way across there, the pain struck him. And he couldn't go no farther, so he was trying to hold himself, and he raised one leg. And there was two nurses and an officer that came by,…

113.t: Drafted at Leavenworth while playing in Kansas City
113.s: After dodging his induction papers on tour, officers pulled him off the bandstand in Kansas City; George Salsbury finished the gig and he was inducted.
113.ch: Army and return to Kansas City
113.q: Yeah I fooled around and got delinquent you know. What I wanted to do I figured I says while we’re on the road traveling, so I’ll either go in when we get back to New York I’ll go in from New York, or either go in when we get to coast, the west coast. And so I had wrote them and told them to send…

113.t: Back in Kansas City: Dave Dexter's session and losing the band book
113.s: On returning from service he joined Dave Dexter's recording session, and the band's book of arrangements was lost, forcing a restart.
113.ch: Army and return to Kansas City
113.q: Well the day that I got back to Kansas City it was Dave Dexter was recording so it was, he was in Kansas City recording and I got in on that.

113.t: GAC bookings, Clyde Bernhardt and 90 straight one-nighters
113.s: He went into the Army in May 1944 after GAC booked solidly; trombonist Clyde Bernhardt joined and complained that 90 straight one-nighters was too much.
113.ch: Army service and after the war
113.q: He was with the band then. He played with Louis Russell's band, and he came up with this other band that -- I don't know if it was the band that he came up the river with.

113.t: Taken off the bandstand for the draft at Kansas City
113.s: Booked a year ahead, he kept missing draft papers until two men arrived at the Kansas City auditorium and took him to Leavenworth.
113.ch: Army service and after the war
113.q: Oh, yes, well, you see, we were booked. By the time I went in the service, we were booked pretty good. I think about almost a year in advance.

113.t: The band's music book stolen after he went in
113.s: Pianist George Salsbury finished the night; McShann told John Tomino to take the music home but it was stolen from the stand, so the band could not carry on.
113.ch: Army service and after the war
113.q: I said, 'well, wait a minute, I'll find somebody to play in my place.' I found Salsbury, so he told me he'd finish the night on piano.

113.s: He was put in anti-aircraft training, was refused Special Service because of his papers, and was released after almost a year.
113.ch: Army service and after the war
113.q: So I got down there, I was down there in anti-aircraft, and so come to find out there was no way I could get into Special Service. The way they had this thing fixed up. Well, they were angry at me, see. Just like the guy told me that night. He say, I'll show you. Now, on your papers, they got two…

113.t: Playing the officers' club to avoid bivouac
113.s: At Camp Stewart, Georgia, he never joined the band, playing the officers' club and slipping out of rough exercises.
113.ch: Army service and after the war
113.q: No, never was transferred. Now, the only thing that I did while I was in the service was this. I was in A Company, and I knew that I didn't want to -- I knew my feet was flat and I knew how long I would last out there.

113.t: Flat feet, the doctor's note and the bayonet
113.s: A doctor was astonished by his flat feet and gave him a note; when a corporal tried to tip his bed he came out with a bayonet.
113.ch: Army service and after the war
113.q: So, anyway, I went up to the doctor's one day, the doctor -- I did have allergy -- you know those woolen blankets? Caused my nose to run and I'd sneeze and all that stuff. So I went up there with that. So the doctor looked at me, and he says, Private, why don't you fasten your shoes? So I told him,…

113.t: How he finally got out: furlough, hospital and discharge
113.s: A sudden 14-day furlough, a hemorrhoid operation and a review of his record led to discharge at the Sheraton near Chicago.
113.ch: Army service and after the war
113.q: Well, I'll tell you what. All of a sudden, they decided to give me 14 days furlough. So I told the sergeant, I says, I was over there at the officers club, I says, they're giving me 14 days for nothing. I haven't done anything. What would they be giving me 14 days for? He says, well, the Army don't…

114.t: Drafted into the Air Force and sent for his horn
114.s: Drafted straight out of high school, he told the Air Force he had a horn and was put in a segregated band at Greensboro.
114.q: They said, yeah, I said, "I have." They said, "Send for it." And I sent for the horn because they said, "We want to form a -- a band, you know, a -- a band." 'Cause I was stationed in Greensboro, North Carolina and it was segregated. Three-quarters of the base was Caucasian, and the other,…

114.t: Arriving at Greensboro; German prisoners of war and racism
114.s: At 18 he traveled south to Basic Training Center 10 and saw German prisoners eat where he could not, then reflects on ignorance and race.
114.q: I was 18. Yeah. Uh-huh. [affirmative] 18 years old and -- but, you know, when I look back, the Lord was working things out for me, you know, because I got -- went down there and this was the thing I was telling you. I was from Newark, New Jersey, supposedly to be up North. When we went down, we…

114.t: Service years 1943-46, the Big Top and first meeting Dizzy Gillespie
114.s: Southern attitudes, hearing Gillespie's band at the Big Top, being invited to try out, and playing Lloyd's Manor in Newark for $7 a night.
114.q: Well, they did, I think, to a lot of people because at the time, they needed every -- every -- every person they could get, I guess.

114.t: The Negro Air Force band and its lessons
114.s: Authorized Air Force band musicians gave lessons; the band had arrangers like Dave Burns and Clinton Garner and drew visitors from the white band.
114.q: Yeah, because what they did was -- what they did was they had -- the Air Force band, the authorized Air Force band, they had the people, the trumpet player, the saxophone, come over and give us lessons, see? So that's how we -- you know, like, we started learning. We had a band.

114.t: Second-class in town while prisoners had more rights
114.s: He could only go into the Negro section of Greensboro while a German prisoner had more rights.
114.q: Oh, yeah, could go into town, but go in the town, but you go in the Negro section of town. And, Lida, I'm telling you, it was so stupid, you know, when you stop and think about it, like here I am, I'm in the Air Force, I'm supposed to be an American soldier, right? And there's a prisoner of war and…

114.t: Duties of the band; the colonel and the KP meeting
114.s: Playing reveille, parades and a funeral march for soldiers with venereal disease, and his run-in with the colonel over prisoners doing KP.
114.q: Yeah, I was in the band. Yes, though we would play, like, we would get up and play reville, you know. We would play for parades. We would play for, like, if people got sick for the wrong thing. Like, I have to say this.

114.t: Armed services still segregated when he left
114.s: Armed forces were not integrated until Truman's presidency.
114.q: Oh, no, listen, I was discharged, I mean, they didn't become integrated for a few years. Not till Truman was president.

114.t: Drafted into the segregated Air Force band in Greensboro
114.s: He is drafted, sends for his horn, and joins a Negro band at Greensboro, where racism affected life off base.
114.ch: Early life and the Air Force
114.q: said no I like that better than the others. Then I heard Coleman Hawkins, and Prez. Now when I heard Hawk, he didn’t knock me out like Lester Young did. But when I got older, I realized that Hawk was playing the changes better than Lester Young. But Lester Young had that beat and that sound, you…

114.t: Playing dances at the Big Top and meeting Lou Donaldson
114.s: The band played dances mostly under the Big Top, where he met Lou Donaldson of A&T College.
114.q: Oh, we played dances, yeah. Uh-huh. [affirmative] Yeah, but they all -- all -- always. Did we ever play? I think we did, yeah. We even played some of the Caucasian dances, too. But -- but we played mostly, you know, over there under the Big Top. You know, that they called it. You know. And, like,…

68.t: Recognition, his own band, and Lester Young drafted
68.s: Tate is satisfied with his career; he tells how Lester was tricked by a policeman, drafted, and jailed in Alabama until Norman Granz got him out.
68.q: Well I don’t know. I don’t have too many, I don’t have too many gripes really. I’m kind of satisfied with the way I’ve done. Because see when I got my, after I got my, when I organized my band, I was the leader and I paid the salaries. You know for 21 years I was on the job, you know, one job. So I…

68.s: Tate says the Army changed Lester, and names his best later records.
68.ch: Lester Young and the early Basie years
68.q: Yeah, yeah. He was. They kind of changed him a bit. You know, actually, to me, his best recording, the two best recordings after the Army were the one he made, that 'D.B. Blues' he and Vic, and he and Buddy Rich and Nat King Cole.

68.t: An FBI agent in a zoot suit catches Lester Young and Jo Jones
68.s: Young and Jones dodge the draft until an undercover agent in Los Angeles arrests them.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: Well, he and Jo Jones -- what actually happened, they draftdodged for like a year. A lot of musicians were doing that because when they'd get their papers that come to the house, "Come down to the induction center on," you know, "examination --" something like that, they would say, "Well, I didn't…

68.t: Artie Shaw and Buddy Rich fill in for Lester and Jo Jones
68.s: With Prez and Jo in the Army, Shaw plays Lester's parts on clarinet and Buddy Rich sits in on drums; a V-disc results.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: came to town. I said, "Basie, don't worry." By this time, Prez was drinking like a quart of Granddad a day. I says, "Man, they don't want Prez. His health won't allow it." I says, "I don't think he's healthy enough for the Army." I says, "And you know they don't want Jo because he's crazy." That's…

68.t: Ten years with Basie and how the band changed
68.s: Tate was in the band 1939 to about 1950, as the Army took players such as Buck Clayton and Illinois Jacquet came in.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: I left -- actually left about 1950, I would say about ten years. Of course, if you're speaking of the years like down in Little Rock and a couple of times like that, I would say 11 or 12, you know, in and out, you know, but about --

68.s: A friend on the draft board kept postponing his induction until he was classified 4-F.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: Yeah. Well, look, I had a Jewish friend that was up to -- my draft center was right around 146th Street, see? And there was a box actually about as long as from here to over there. And he used to tell me all the time, he said, "You know, it would be a shame for them to put you in the Army," he…

68.t: Basie got out of the Army too; Tate offers money and is refused
68.s: Tate says Basie also avoided service, and the sympathetic draft officer refused any payment.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: it was going to cost me a couple grand or something like that and I didn't give a damn. So man, when I went in and offered this cat some money, you know, he says, "No, no, no," he says, "no, no, no, you've done enough." He says, "You just keep playing your sounds and things. You've done enough. I…

68.t: Musicians' draft tricks: Don Byas, Billy Eckstine and Sweets Edison
68.s: Musicians faked heart trouble with benzedrine or acted effeminate to be rejected.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: Don Byas went down and they were taking the -- he stayed up all night and he was taking benzedrines. Benzedrines would be like an inhaler that --

68.t: Why the Army wanted Lester Young and Jo Jones, and how they passed
68.s: Draft officials wanted to make an example of the pair; Prez's hip talk amused the examiners.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: I don't know how Basie beat the Army. Let me see, how did he beat the Army? I think he had spinal meningitis or something one time and --

63.t: Pearl Harbor news in Providence and enlisting in the Navy
63.s: Shaw heard the Pearl Harbor news backstage, announced it to the theater, gave notice to the band and enlisted in the Navy.
63.ch: Breakup, the 1940 band and the Navy
63.q: Oh yeah. When the war broke out, that was . . . I was in Providence when that happened. We were playing on a stage, and I forget what happened. Oh, I went backstage. I went off into the wings after announcing a dance act. You’d have acts with you. The band was playing for the dance act, and I went…

63.t: Minesweepers, then leading an awful Navy band at Newport
63.s: He was put on minesweepers on Staten Island, then in charge of a poor band at Newport playing officers' dances, which he hated.
63.ch: Breakup, the 1940 band and the Navy
63.q: In the Navy? Hell, no. I was out on minesweepers. They decided I should do that. They put me in charge of a band. It was awful. They put me in charge of a Navy band. Worst experience I’ve had in my life. Terrible band. Half of them were Navy men, and some had some dance band training. So here you…

63.t: Going AWOL to see Forrestal and getting orders to form a band
63.s: After a second boot camp, Shaw went AWOL to Washington, saw Forrestal, and was authorized to recruit musicians for a Pacific band.
63.ch: Breakup, the 1940 band and the Navy
63.q: Red Mike [Shaw imitates a growling voice] is a guy who’s face gets red when he says this: “Stand up and salute, sailor.” I went to see him. I had no idea. I just asked if I

63.t: Navy Band 501, Davey Tough, and refusing to risk the instruments
63.s: Nobody knew what to do with Band 501; Shaw got Davey Tough in, refused an admiral's order to send music and instruments, and became a chief petty officer.
63.ch: Breakup, the 1940 band and the Navy
63.q: I can’t. I really can’t. I can’t tell you about that. It was the worst experience I’ve ever had in my life. I was in the Navy in a totally anomalous position. Nobody knew what to do with that band. Nobody knew what to do with me. I didn’t know what to do. In effect I had my own little platoon in…

63.t: The Nimitz note, a reprimand, Guadalcanal and Halsey
63.s: Shaw tells how a note to Admiral Nimitz led to a reprimand, then shipping out; he lost hearing in his left ear at Guadalcanal and had a breakdown.
63.ch: Breakup, the 1940 band and the Navy
63.q: Chief petty officer. Equivalent of a sergeant. I didn’t want to be an officer, because I was playing for enlisted men. I refused officers’ dances. I wouldn’t do that. I played for large numbers of enlisted men. Whenever anyone asked me, ordered me to do something, I’d ask them to put it in writing,…

63.t: Wartime audiences, war zones and a quiet New Zealand hospital
63.s: Troops reacted wildly, the band played where the USO could not, and an NZ hospital audience's silence turned out to be rapt attention.
63.ch: Breakup, the 1940 band and the Navy
63.q: Oh, the audiences were just bloody remarkable. Never saw anything like it. Never. You’d hit two notes of a piece and there would be a roar. That music meant tremendous

63.t: The Navy band never recorded; rehearsing at Treasure Island
63.s: No recording was possible in the jungle clearings; the band was shaped up at Pier 92 in New York and Treasure Island.
63.ch: Breakup, the 1940 band and the Navy
63.q: Before we went away the band was nothing. We rehearsed it in Pearl Harbor. I mean, not in Pearl Harbor, but in Treasure Island. That’s where I really got it in shape. Or in Pier 92 in New York, which was a hellhole. By the time we were through with that, we were embarked on a train, and it took us…

63.t: Resuming the war story: the band beaten up, Sam Donahue takes over, Miller's fate
63.s: Shaw dislikes talking about the Navy, says the band was spent, Donahue kept it going in Britain with a different philosophy, and comments on Glenn Miller.
63.ch: Breakup, the 1940 band and the Navy
63.q: It’s hard for me to do that. As I say, for me it was such a . . . You know Charlie Parker . . . not Charlie Parker. Lester [Young] never got over his Army experience. It killed him. Finished him. When he got through with that, he was done. There are people who don’t belong in that, and I didn’t. I…

63.t: Day two: square radio players and making the Navy band sound like a band
63.s: Shaw recalls studio orchestras of non-jazz readers, then fixing the Navy band by having the dance players play square, and Guy Lombardo, and the wartime Rudy Tanza lead alto.
63.ch: Jazz, its audience and the 1953 records
63.q: . . . at CBS for example, Bunny Berigan was in the band, and one of the other trumpet players was what we used to call a “square.”

115.t: Drafted: the letter and the induction in Chicago
115.s: Gus stayed with McShann until the Army; the induction letter followed him, and John Tumino told him in Chicago he must report to Fort Sheridan.
115.q: He went in later. Bob Maybane went in first. He was the first one in the band to go to the Army. That's the tenor player.

115.t: Failing to get into the Navy; the spinal tap
115.s: He lied to try for the Navy, claimed to have syphilis, and was sent to the Army anyway after a painful spinal tap proved it false.
115.q: But I knew it right there in Chicago. So I wanted to get in the Navy, see, because I had a friend that played in the Navy. Clarence Trance, he was a trumpet player.

115.s: Pills meant to make the heart flutter only gave him a strong heart; he took a 15-day furlough, then returned to Fort Sheridan.
115.q: But some guy gave me some pills that they -- before then, they called them Geronimos. It's supposed to make your heart flutter, keep you from going in the Army. All right, I took about three of these pills. And I went before the doctor, taking this exam. He put the scopes on and listening. He said,…

115.s: Gus is inducted at Fort Sheridan and sent to Camp Rucker, Alabama, where he joins the 215th Army Band and arrives at night.
115.q: But when I got to Alabama that night, they met me at the station, and I was the only one to get off the train about 3:00 in the morning, and one of the sergeants that picked me up was grumping because he had to get up and drive all the way into Ozarks, it was. To meet the train, to pick me up.

115.t: Integrating the Army band; Joe Comfort
115.s: He says he integrated the band; his first sergeant was bassist Joe Comfort.
115.q: And my first sergeant was Joe Comfort. Maybe you know him. The bass player, he used to play with

115.s: They discuss McShann's flat feet and his work in Special Services playing for officers.
115.q: Special services. I don't even see why they took MacShann because he had such flat feet.

115.t: Raising the price of band gigs for the noncoms
115.s: Gus charged a sergeant $8 a man and overtime for a dance, forcing the Army to pay better and making band gigs desirable.
115.q: Because -- only thing that got me was, I found out that when you play for the officers or noncom in the Army, you wouldn't get anymore than about two dollars for playing. And so I said, 'Well, I'm going to break this up if I can.' Which I did.

115.s: He was in about a year and a half and got out on migraines; he describes marrying in Chicago, his second marriage.
115.q: and a half, something like that. I would have been in longer, but then they told me I couldn't get out. Said this camp was one of the camps that you just couldn't get out of the Army like that.

115.t: Strict mother; parents separate as father goes to the Army
115.s: His mother was very strict; his parents separated when his father went into the Army in World War I, and Gus remembers the troop train passing the house.
115.ch: Childhood in Tyler, Beaumont and Houston
115.q: Yeah, yeah. I can remember when he passed by -- we lived right by the track, see. The train passed right by the house, just like this couch there.

116.t: Dillard group, trip to Los Angeles, and joining the Marines
116.s: After Dillard he played with Edward Blackwell and the Batistes, drove to Los Angeles, came home when his father was ill, was drafted and volunteered for two years in the Marines.
116.q: It wasn’t so much a decision, you see the military was still conscripting at that time. So when I finished from Dillard I had been playing locally with Edward Blackwell, Harold Batiste, Alvin Batiste, who was a clarinet player; and Peter Badie was the bass player, or Richard Payne who was also a…

116.t: Marine Corps training and the Corps Four at El Toro
116.s: Boot camp in San Diego, the Marine band at El Toro, then the Corps Four quartet on a TV show and later a radio show.
116.q: And well I went into the Marine Corps, you know I went through the boot camp and the infantry training and all of that stuff. So when I was assigned I remember the recruiter, once I’d decided that I would join, he says, “Yeah, man, well you can go to Parris Island,” I said whoa, stop right there. I…

116.t: Recording with Battiste and joining the Marine Corps
116.s: He records original music, then accepts a Marine two-year program and trains in San Diego.
116.ch: Ornette, Los Angeles and the Marines
116.q: Yeah. Harold Battiste, we went in a studio and made a recording with Blackwell and – who was on it? maybe Richard. I almost forgot – but we were recording music that everybody wrote. Harold wrote. I wrote. Alvin wrote. Not long after that was when I went in, in January of ’57. The reason why I…

116.t: Why the Marines did not commission musicians
116.s: Brown asks why he never went to officer school; the Marines did not commission music majors.
116.q: Oh yeah, everybody. You got to go past the shrink when you get in the military. He said, “Why didn’t you apply for OC?” I say, “The Marine Corps don’t commission music majors,” for whatever reason, not that I was looking to be a Marine officer anyway.

116.t: World War II museum and Black soldiers
116.s: The museum shows only one Black serviceman, and Marsalis comments.
116.ch: Katrina, race and New Orleans culture
116.q: I don’t know how much of that is the fault of Nick Mueller. Nick and I were on the faculty together at UNO. He was largely responsible, along with Stephen Ambrose for getting that going. There’s a level of responsibility for which has been turned over to the dominant culture. One thing that I know…

116.t: Rank, military duties and the Lebanon alert
116.s: He left as a corporal; he recalls the 1958 Lebanon alert while taping a show.
116.ch: Ornette, Los Angeles and the Marines
116.q: When I went in, it was after Korea and before Vietnam. So even had I not been doing music, there wasn’t much else going on. But it fairly close in Lebanon. I remember we were in the studio in Los Angeles, at CBS, and getting ready to tape a show. The lieutenant got a message. The message was all…

116.t: Driving to Los Angeles and the draft notice
116.s: He goes to California with Blackwell and Battiste after Ornette sends a ticket, then is drafted.
116.ch: Ornette, Los Angeles and the Marines
116.q: I was in California, Harold, Edward Blackwell, and myself. We drove up to Los Angeles, because Ornette Coleman had sent a ticket for Edward to come up to Los Angeles, and I had just finished from school. I wasn’t doing nothing. So I told my ma. I said, “Look. I’m going out to California.” Harold…

116.t: Returning home: G.I. Bill, marriage and scarce gigs
116.s: He doesn't use the G.I. Bill, marries and hustles for scarce gigs.
116.q: I didn’t use that. It was interesting about that. I didn’t use it. I didn’t understand the military too well, because I got married not long after I came back, and I didn’t even understand that I could go to that – what do you call it? – the PX or whatever.

117.s: Doler faked a swollen leg and cracked wise to the Army psychiatrist but was still taken and spent four years playing golf in a Florida band.
117.q: Well, Bill was -- we were now not getting ready to go in the Army and Bill got a -- we used to call it greetings from Uncle Sam, meaning we'd like you to come down and see us, he got his before I got mine and he went down and he was interviewed and Bill did everything -- oh, yes, when we were…

117.t: Army service fronting a band in the Aleutians
117.s: Freeman went into the Army and spent 22 months in the Aleutians fronting a band, touring islands in the show Take A Break, bored but safe.
117.q: But they took Bill into the Army anyway, and he ended up with a wonderful deal. He was in Florida for four years in the Army playing in a band where he played golf every day and he was worried about me. He said, 'Bud, as neurotic as you are, you'd better do something because if you go in the Army…

117.s: Freeman recalls Hammett as a buck sergeant editing the camp paper, lecturing on China and Russia, and politely rebuffing a general.
117.q: Oh yes, we had all the lovely conveniences, but there were no women there, which of course, is the first horrible thing to happen, and so Dashiell Hammett, the great detective story writer had the paper called the Adakian, which he edited, it was his paper, and he and I were very good friends and…

117.t: Freeman's Army years and Hammett's visit to Condon's
117.s: Freeman was 36 when he entered, spent 28 months in, and recalls Hammett and Lillian Hellman visiting Condon's in 1945.
117.q: Well, I was 36 when I went into the Army and so I think -- let's see, I went to -- I was in the Army 28 months, I came out when I was 39 and I was in the

117.s: Freeman never saw Hammett do an unkind act; he politely edited staff writers on the Adakian.
117.q: the people who worked on the paper for him and if a man wrote something he didn't approve of, he was so polite and said, 'Well, don't you think it ought to be this way,' and it was a most interesting paper. It talked about books and it talked about --

117.t: Discharge: news of the bomb and three days at Fort Dix
117.s: Freeman hears of Hiroshima on furlough, then is discharged because he was 39, after three wild days at Fort Dix.
117.q: Well, anyway, I could be wrong about his name because as I said earlier, I have always been that way about names, having the uncle with my same name, I forgot his name.

117.s: Freeman says Hammett refused to name names and went to jail for six months, dying not long after.
117.q: business, he just refused to give names who were involved and so he went to jail for six months and he didn't have to but there he was, he was a good friend and didn't want to give names to people and --

117.t: Art Tatum's champagne and putting aside the uniform
117.s: On his first night out of the Army Freeman hears Art Tatum on 52nd Street, who pours champagne with him, and then takes a month to give up his uniform.
117.q: Yes, very, very lucky and I will never forget what a thrilling thing that was. I went home that night and I was married at that time to Escaleda and we looked in the paper and Art Tatum was playing at the, I think, the Three Deuces or the Downbeat on 52nd Street and we went down of course, to hear…

31.t: Drafted in 1918 and the Camp Dix band singer Opal Cooper
31.s: Whaley is inducted while working at Suntaug Lake Inn, gets sent off with a party, and at Camp Dix plays piano for the singer Opal Cooper.
31.ch: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
31.q: I was playing down at this place, Suntaug Lake Inn and one Monday I went to work and there was greetings for me. United States Army has inducted me.

31.t: Troopship to France, the torpedo scare and the wet camp
31.s: He describes the convoy, being seasick when the ship was thought torpedoed, meeting shell-shocked soldiers and marching in rainy France.
31.ch: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
31.q: We went over and we had a convoy see and we got about a couple days out, the convoy left us and the -- you could hear the water slushing against the outside of the ship and one day the lights went out. Now we're six decks down and I was seasick and the smell of the ship made me seasick and I was in…

31.t: Transferring into the Pioneer regiment band under Will Vodery
31.s: He gets from headquarters company into the band because he can read, under Will Vodery, and recalls clean-up duty and a 14-piece orchestra.
31.ch: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
31.q: See, I could read music, and this guy he was a singer, see, and I was in headquarters company, see when I went there, they put me in headquarters company and I could play the piano and this guy could sing, so then I went to the man and says, hey I want to get in the band, so they transferred me to…

31.t: The 807th Pioneer band, Junkman Rag and not Jim Europe's 369th
31.s: They play Lucky Roberts's 'Junkman Rag' for the president of France; Whaley clarifies he was in the 807th Pioneer regiment, not Jim Europe's 369th, and mentions a captain who resigned.
31.ch: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
31.q: we went to entertain President ______, he was the president at the time and when he got off the train the band played the 'Junkman Rag,' Lucky Roberts' 'Junkman Rag.'

31.t: Armistice, Brest delousing, Newport News and discharge
31.s: He recalls the armistice shooting, six months waiting at Brest, a Newport News lecture and Chicken Richards's arrest, and discharge at Dix.
31.ch: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
31.q: Yes, it was in 1918 and when we got ready to come home, we went to Brest, and now Brest is way up on a hill and we went to - delousedus and they give us summer underwear.

31.t: Meeting Eubie Blake in Boston and confusion over Army bands
31.s: Whaley met Eubie Blake in Boston in 1918, and they sort out Jim Europe's 369th, Mikell's and his own 807th band.
31.ch: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
31.q: Eubie I met in Boston. They came up there with a show and I was playing down in Leminster and they bought the show into Worchester and they got stranded. That was way back in 1918, I think.

31.t: Will Vodery as bandmaster, and Whaley playing flute and piccolo
31.s: He met Vodery as Army bandmaster in 1918 and learned flute and piccolo from a Frenchman to fill a gap.
31.ch: Will Vodery and the road shows
31.q: Yeah, I took up every instrument. They had enough but they didn't have no flute player, no piccolo player. So I had a French man there, and he taught me the flute.

31.t: Learn to read, white musicians in Boston, and Caruso directing at a Reading roadhouse
31.s: He says Boston jobs were all colored until the 1918 war, and describes a 1912 Sunday job where Caruso directed overtures and tipped $200 to the band.
31.ch: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
31.q: Oh, yeah, when I came to New York I used to tell everybody learn how to read. If you can't read, you can't read because up until the war in 1918 the white musicians weren't known in Boston, everything was colored. Colored musicians had all the jobs and then after the world war there was a -- the…

75.t: Eight days through the mined Channel with refugees
75.s: The ship took eight days to clear the Channel, carried refugees hiding gold, and passed U-boat convoys.
75.q: We left that one Saturday night at 11 o'clock. It took us eight days to get through the English Channel, because it was heavily mined. Eight days to get out of the Channel.

75.t: USO unit, Kenneth Spencer and Cafe Society acts
75.s: He was in the first all-Black USO unit, was meant for Russia with Kenneth Spencer, played Cafe Society acts, and recalls singer Aubrey Pankey.
75.ch: The war years: Barnet, Hot Lips Page, Newton and Kirby
75.q: Now, I don't want to go into this, it isn't my area, but I was also in Cuba during the War. I represented the first all so-called Black unit of the USO, the first experimental... Primarily I was in... I was also in Cafe

75.t: Touring Caribbean bases for the USO
75.s: The unit toured Guantanamo, British and Dutch Guiana and Trinidad by helicopter and plane, entertaining troops across the British-owned Caribbean.
75.ch: The war years: Barnet, Hot Lips Page, Newton and Kirby
75.q: : We toured by helicopter and everything else. Due to the War... We had bauxite mines all the way down to South America, and we had bases naturally down there. We stayed up at Guantanamo. Guantanamo is in Cuba, and that was our headquarters. We'd go to St. Julien and (?) and (?) if I have to name…

75.t: Who was on the USO tour; War Bond shows
75.s: The unit comprised Spencer, Willie Bryant, Julia Gardner, Betty Logan and Ramirez as sole accompanist, and sold War Bonds across the islands.
75.ch: The war years: Barnet, Hot Lips Page, Newton and Kirby
75.q: Yeah. And not only that. We did entertainment in public places where they could sell War Bonds. They would buy the Bonds to see us, and after we'd leave they would just give them back! The Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and all through there, Jamaica... All of them down to South America.

75.t: Following Clyde Hart in Kirby's band
75.s: Billy Kyle was in the Army, and Ramirez followed Clyde Hart in John Kirby's group.
75.ch: The war years: Barnet, Hot Lips Page, Newton and Kirby
75.q: was... I was with him before he had that band. That was with the Palmer Brothers and Kirby.

75.s: The sextet: Procope in the Army, George Johnson on alto, Buster Bailey, Bill Beeson on drums.
75.ch: The war years: Barnet, Hot Lips Page, Newton and Kirby
75.q: Procope was in Fort Washuka(?). He was in the Army.

75.t: Jimmy Davis, the Army and Lady Sings the Blues
75.s: Jimmy Davis was drafted and pitched Billie Holiday; she wrote of him in her book, implying Ramirez did not write the song.
75.ch: Lover Man and the postwar years
75.q: Now, when Jimmy got in the Army, we me... And we were conscientious objectors. They took us back and forth, back and forth, you know. They came to the time that they didn't ask you "Do you believe in war?" They just took you. But Jimmy had to go in, and I went into Special Service, USO, you know.…

75.t: Tribute to the first all-Black USO troupe
75.s: On 13 May they are to receive a tribute at the 369th Regiment Armory; only he and Julia Gardner survive from the troupe.
75.ch: Closing: recent career, family and travel
75.q: Dick Campbell of the sickle cell organization. There will be a lot of people there. I'll tell you much more about it before you leave. We are the only two living people from the original first all-Black USO troupe. You must remember, during the time that they sent colored acts over there for the…

118.t: Army band in Manila and Okinawa
118.s: Drafted in 1941, Williams formed a small band in the service, played around Manila and Okinawa, and built the camp himself.
118.ch: Army service and GI Bill school
118.q: Oh yeah, I mean I do my own singing. Do any singing. Do any singing? Oh. Then I wired them down that way up. Well I went to the service in 41. I came back out when I started a little band in the service. Yeah, and I played all around Manala, Okinawa, you know, around. You were over in the 70 band.…

118.t: Mitchell and Simon Frazier, Steve Lewis, and missing the older players
118.s: They discuss Frazier cousins and Steve Lewis, and Williams says being drafted at 19 or 20 made him miss many older pianists.
118.q: Yeah, he made that band jump. And during that time now they had some other old piano players like I just mentioned a while back, like Mitchell Frazier. Oh yes, I never heard anything about him.

118.t: Playing the H&J with Brother Cornbread
118.s: He played with Cornbread at 16 and again during the war; he formed a band at his Ordnance company after going in late 1941.
118.q: Well, I was quite a young man. Well, I tell you, when I first played with Brother Cornbread, I probably would have been about 16 years old, but I mean at the H&J, I played with him during the wartime, like uh, like, like, you know, early fotties.

118.t: Service band in Manila and basic training
118.s: He toured the Philippines with a service band, trained at Camp Livingston and played blues on the ship crossing.
118.q: I got my basic training, you know, right here in Cape Livingston, Louisiana. How about that? Yeah, right out there, 17 miles on the other side of Alexander, Louisiana.

118.t: Service travel to the Philippines and Japan
118.s: He went to Manila and Japan with his own band, with army transportation.
118.q: Yeah, I went, uh, I think I didn't go to Europe, no, but I've been to Japan, I've been to the Philippine island, I've been to Japan, I've been to the Red Land. Yeah.

118.s: A five-week USO-style tour from Saigon, two gigs a day by plane and helicopter, in danger and amid the dead.
118.q: That's the way it was, you know. A frog had a few heart attacks about it. It hurted him. Contra pretty frightened himself.
