118.t: Years in the Army and discharge
118.s: Clarifying Cornbread dates; he entered in February 1942, left in 1946 disgusted with promotions, in Army ammunition ordnance.
118.q: Yeah, I mean, after I come out, I played with cornbread at the age of 16, but after that, I must have been in my, way in my 20s, after I come out of the service, and I played with my 8 and J. Truthfully, I did the play with him by 8 and J. after I come out, when I came out, I'd come out of the…

119.t: Induction into the Air Force and segregation on the way
119.s: At 16-17 he enlists on his uncle's advice and meets segregation at a Miami lunch stop and in Alabama on the train to San Antonio.
119.q: Yeah I had to earn some money. So I went to the man that was raising me at the time, my uncle, and I said, “what would you do now that you’re graduated from—” now that I’m graduated from high school. He says, “I’d go in the Army.” You know at that time it was an option. And I found myself walking…

119.t: Tuba audition and posting to Great Falls, Montana
119.s: As a tuba player he is given six months by Warrant Officer Proctor to improve his reading, then is sent to Montana, where he sees snow for the first time.
119.q: Not at that time, no. Not at that time. So we went through the training and all of that. And by the way, I was a tuba player.

119.t: Tuba duty, a staff sergeant, and hearing about Schillinger House
119.s: He served about three years as a tuba player, has an odd run-in with a drunken sergeant, and pianist Oscar Tunnard tells him about the Schillinger House (Berklee).
119.q: Yeah, sousaphone, yeah. And I did that for about, that hitch for about three years. And I learned a lot from other musicians and the method books and observing what they were doing and so on. But I’ll tell you another experience I had one day in the latrine. We had to go through Basic again because…

119.t: Roswell and Shreveport: Iceland refused, segregation
119.s: He cannot be posted to Iceland because he is black, chooses Shreveport, and describes segregated towns near bases in Roswell, Montana and Louisiana.
119.q: I says, “yeah, sign me up.” I wanted to get out of Roswell, New Mexico. That’s where we were. We were in Roswell, New Mexico.

119.t: Shreveport: officers, spiritual meeting in the balcony
119.s: On base in Shreveport there is no segregation among musicians and officers, but he sits in the balcony at a spiritual conference.
119.q: I think ’58, ’59, ’58. But on the air base everything was fine. There were quite a few officers that played instruments that had love for the music. And because I had my little prestige thing going they all wanted to come over and play with me. So we had that kind of relationship. There was no…

119.t: Newfoundland and practicing eight to ten hours a day
119.s: Posted to Ernest Harmon Air Force Base in Newfoundland, snowed in, he practices relentlessly and reflects that individuals were mostly kind despite the laws.
119.q: Newfoundland. Ernest Harmon Air Force Base. That’s where all the military planes used to go through — not all of them but a great deal of them — used to go through during the days when they had props, these four-engine jobs. Elvis Presley came through there and stopped over.

119.t: Hitting bottom and rejoining the Air Force
119.s: After work dries up in Philadelphia and Atlantic City he re-enlists and resolves to become the world's greatest bass player.
119.q: Yeah. Well no, that’s another story. That’s another story. A week in Philadelphia and then I went to Atlantic City for a while, and then there was no more work. I says now what’s happening. I began to assess myself and I said well what’s happening. I says you do have a skill, you can play the tuba,…

65.t: World War II draft takes his musicians
65.s: The draft took band members; Pin Madera left first and was replaced by the Filipino Amado Punzalan.
65.ch: War years, Decca records and La Conga
65.q: Yes, ahh, Amado Punzalan, a Phillipino.

65.t: Draft notice and induction at Camp Upton
65.s: He worked fifteen days after the March notice, then reported to Whitehall Street and Camp Upton.
65.ch: War years, Decca records and La Conga
65.q: In March. It was a big envelope and I was acquainted with the envelope already because Pin Madera received one, you know, so I said to myself, well, they got me. They give me fifteen days, so I worked the fifteen days because I need the money for my family; so that particular morning, Sunday…

65.t: Plans for Marcelino Guerra and Varona's unreliability
65.s: From the army Machito said to put Guerra in his place; Mario formed Guerra's group, called the Second Afro-Cubans.
65.ch: War years, Decca records and La Conga
65.q: Well, in that particular time, I was in the Army. When Mario told me that Marcelino Guerra was coming to New York, I said: put Marcelino in my place because I have a

65.t: Why the Second Afro-Cubans was formed
65.s: Mario wanted to give the talented Guerra a band for the off days, and Machito sang with him to help him get known.
65.ch: War years, Decca records and La Conga
65.q: Well, Marcelino is so talented and Mario love talent and he payed respect or tribute or he considers himself obligated to help a person that have talent. Marcelino had the language barrier. He don't want to Marcelino waste all his talent, so Mario says: "Let's organize a band for Marcelino", and he…

65.t: Back from the army: Jose Curbelo starts his band at La Conga
65.s: On discharge Machito returned to La Conga, where Curbelo had become a bandleader with a similar instrumentation but a different style.
65.ch: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
65.q: Well, I come back to La Conga at the - Jose Curbelo a new manager, a manager and he sold the name that he acquired, La Conga, because La Conga was like a show-case of the Latin music, so he went to Miami, went to different places in New York because there was an opening. The Cuban music was crazy,…

65.t: Chino Pozo and Tito Puente leave with Jack Cole
65.s: Both left with dancer Jack Cole for $200 a week; Puente returned and was later drafted, while Chino Pozo went with Graciela.
65.ch: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
65.q: Oh, he went with - him and Tito Puente left with a dancer, a very popular dancer and choreographer. They went to Chicago and from Chicago they went to California to make some kind of a show out there at the - one of the finest hotels.

65.t: The voyage on the SS Oriente
65.s: A hurricane stretched the trip to six days; he made friends among the merchant marines.
65.q: I met a lot of people that I am - then - they became my friends, people working, you know, merchant marines. They helped me tremendously and we became friends and when I got here in New York, I had friends already.

120.t: Playing in the Katherine Dunham show
120.s: His group plays the Dunham revue in two theaters; he records transcriptions with Brad Gowans and buys a house in Dumont, New Jersey.
120.ch: New York, Nick's and the Army
120.q: Yes. Well, we were a great success with the Katherine Dunham Show and when that show closed, we went from there to another theater; see, her contract ran out in that theater and, then, we went to the--- another theater that was on - was it 48th or 49th-- I can't just remember the theater----

120.t: Drafted into the Army after an all-night Commodore session
120.s: He cuts some of his best Commodore sides the night before reporting to Fort Dix in December 1943; Dunham promises him a job after the war.
120.ch: New York, Nick's and the Army
120.q: day or the night I was to go in the Army the following day and I went into Fort Dix and, uh, I had made some of the best sides that I have ever made for Commodore on that particular one. Of course, I came back from the Army and made some more Commodores - different times --

120.t: The Pick magazine article and his miserable basic training
120.s: A Pick magazine story on his Commodore sessions gets pinned up at camp, earning him every dirty job; he calls himself the world's worst soldier.
120.ch: New York, Nick's and the Army
120.q: --who had covered that record session for PICK MAGAZINE - he wrote for PICK and, uh, the unfortunate thing is I got the picture story - all about Wild Bill and all the pictures and all the things and the Commodore records and all the things -- and the story broke at a very bad time for me, because…

120.t: The Army-authorized Dixieland band at Asheville and Fud Livingston's arrangements
120.s: Because men kept being reassigned he got the Army to pay for arrangements, many by Fud Livingston, and his band played officers' clubs.
120.ch: New York, Nick's and the Army
120.q: Well, I guess it was the only one I know of and the reason for it was that I needed--- they were changing men on me all the time; there was a point of redistribution and I would be losing guys; they'd be sending

120.t: Joe Barufaldi and other bandsmen who went on or left music
120.s: Barufaldi is still playing; a great pianist in the band took the GI Bill to Harvard and became a lawyer; Davison would like to forget the Army.
120.ch: New York, Nick's and the Army
120.q: Oh, sure. And, then he goes down with Billy Maxted in Florida - quite often, but I got him back; I got him out of -- he lived at Plymouth, Rhode Island - or is it Plymouth--

120.t: Discharge, the Howdy Club delay, and a job with Art Hodes
120.s: Discharged when the bomb dropped, he sells his house, waits for Condon's club to open after killings at the Howdy Club site, and plays a Village club with Art Hodes.
120.q: So, when-- one of the times I went back Condon told me about his club. He said - now, don't forget, as quick as you get back, let me know you're in town. So, I did get out when the bomb went off; I was automatically discharged and I went back to my house in New Jersey and realized that how real…

120.t: Leaves in New York and Condon's plan for a club
120.s: On leaves he plays Town Hall with Condon, who says he is opening a club; soldiers crowd round Davison's car radio to hear Condon's broadcasts.
120.ch: New York, Nick's and the Army
120.q: Well, on a leave--- everytime I had a leave, I wound up doing Town Hall with Condon and all this stuff - and this is when we cooked up the (inaudible). He said, now you know, I'm opening a joint - you know, I'm opening up Eddie Condon's Club and I want you in the thing and the minute you get out of…

121.s: A country boy arrives in Chicago in a zoot suit without an overcoat; punishments in boot training and liberty in Boston.
121.ch: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
121.q: Yeah, well, I don't know if you remember the Cab Calloway thing. It was the big hat with the feather in it and the long coat with the chad and the tight-legged pants. Well, I had a gray suit suit when I went in there. And I got to Chicago, and it was cold. And I didn't have no overcoat, because we…

121.s: After leave they made shells at a depot for about eighteen months; he was seaman first class.
121.ch: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
121.q: Oh, well, I was seamen first class. You know, really we were sailors, but we were like, more or less like Seabees.

121.t: Logistics support company and the white company sent first to Okinawa
121.s: His all-black unit trained three months but a white company with less training was sent first and nearly wiped out.
121.ch: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
121.q: And, you know, when we left Camp Perry, when we finished our training, you see they changed, they changed our uniform. And then we went to the uniform. Our work uniform went from dungarees to green, fatigue green. Yeah. So, we had the green uniform, kind of like the Marine, with the helmet and…

121.s: Protecting supplies from the Japanese, shooting at people, and turning back from a sniper hunt on Sugar Hill.
121.ch: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
121.q: Everybody hit the ground. And, you know, I was like, no, on day. And so what we had to do was get the supplies off the ship, protect them. Because they were, well, we did, we had skirmishes with the Japanese who were trying to come in to get the food or whatever, and we had to protect them from…

121.t: End of the war and discharge in December 1945
121.s: Eleven months on Okinawa, the false and real surrender, discharge on the lakefront, and meeting Emerette on the way home.
121.ch: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
121.q: 11 months. 11 months. Because we secured the island completely. And then they started rebuilding. You see, and I was on Okinawa when World War II ended. And I don't know if you remember reading about the first, the false alarm, when they said the war was over, it was a false alarm. And boy, we…

121.t: What the Navy did for him
121.s: He credits service with teaching him to take orders and grow as a person.
121.ch: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
121.q: and how did it change your life? Well, okay, yeah. The Navy, to me, the Navy was a big asset in me being who I am today. Because, like I said, I went in the day I made seventeen. I was a little kid with a child of mine and all this. And going into the service, then, I had three years on my own, you…

122.t: Navy Chief recruits black musicians for shore duty
122.s: At 22 and 1A, he jumps at the Navy offer to avoid the infantry; he was still a raw musician.
122.q: I was 22, yeah 22 years old. Let’s see around June or July, the Navy sent a Chief Musician out to our union meetings. See we used to have separate union meetings. A black union, we would meet in Oakland at the Elks building there. They had a building with a bar upstairs and there was quite a…

122.t: Train to Great Lakes; Clark Terry's bunk; Camp Robert Smalls
122.s: The band rides to Great Lakes in a private car, sleeps in Clark Terry's bunk, and hears of the ship's company band.
122.q: three years at St. Mary’s College. See we went in, when they called us we were all put on temporary leave when they first recruited us. Then when they told us okay it’s time, then we got on the train and this was in 1945 [sic] around October, maybe the first of October, yeah, got on the train, the…

122.t: Great Lakes happy hours: Lunceford, Eddie Peabody, raiding the band
122.s: Entertainment at Great Lakes includes the Lunceford band; the Chief gets the band out before it is raided and returns to California.
122.q: Yeah. And so they would have happy hours. And when they would have happy hours you would have the entertainment that would come in. One happy hour they had the Jimmy Lunceford Orchestra.

122.t: Pay, living off base and playing at St. Mary's; OWI recordings
122.s: Navy pay and allowances, lessons with Herb Sanford, weekly dances for cadets and weekly recordings for the Office of War Information.
122.q: Well they added to it with quarters and subsistence I think it amounted to around oh I think around $87 or $92 a month or something like that. But see in 1942 for crying out loud, what was the rent? People were paying — oh heck they weren’t paying very much rent. Because you had price and wage…

122.t: Wartime dance-band boom: Hampton and Cab Calloway at Oakland Auditorium
122.s: The Navy band is rated top in the Twelfth Naval District; Oakland draws huge crowds for Hampton and Calloway.
122.ch: Big bands in the Bay Area
122.q: Well they had bands all over the place you know. So they picked our band. Now I don’t know why. I found out in later years that the Captain of our station, he was somehow related to somebody, one of the Admirals here in the Twelfth Naval District so I don’t know whether he had the pull or what, but…

122.t: Personnel of the Naval Pre-Flight band
122.s: He lists Marshall and Ernie Royal, Vernon Alley, Baranco, Curtis Lowe, Jerome Richardson, Jackie Kelso and Buddy Collette's second band.
122.q: lead alto players in the country. His brother, Ernie Royal, outstanding trumpet player who ended up in New York doing studio work, but they all were with the original Lionel Hampton band, the band that made “Flying Home.” Vernon Alley of course, Mister Music, he was in the band, Wilbert Baranco,…

123.t: His mother's work, the 1944 draft and discovering Randolph Street
123.s: His mother works for the Navy department; he is drafted into the Army Air Corps in 1944 and, stationed in Illinois, discovers Chicago's Randolph Street clubs.
123.q: Oh she worked wherever she could. She was a switchboard operator; you know what they used to have for telephones before they had all these gimmicks. She worked for the Navy department for many, many years. I don’t know what she was doing, but that was during the war when I was away. I was drafted…

123.t: Weekend passes to Chicago, Elmer's and Jimmy Rainey
123.s: He explains his idle Champaign duty, and recalls first hearing jazz at Elmer's with guitarist Jimmy Rainey, plus Jimmy Gourley and Ronny Singer.
123.q: There were three of us that would run a mimeograph machine to run off special orders, it didn’t take but one. But every other week two of us took a pass and went wherever we wanted. So I came into Chicago about every other week.

123.t: Settling in Chicago, the Sherman Hotel and the GI Bill at Roosevelt
123.s: After discharge he works at the Sherman Hotel, hears the bands, and registers at Roosevelt under the GI Bill around early 1947.
123.q: I had a friend of mine I met there, when I met Jimmy Rainey. He said, “come to Chicago, and I’ll get you a job taking tickets at the Aragon.” It ended up that I got this guy a job hanging coats in the basement of the Sherman Hotel by the... what do you call that room... the Panther Room, where all…

123.t: Jewish neighborhood, Dobbins Vocational and a missed chance to meet Bechet
123.s: He describes his neighborhood and trade school across from Shibe Park, and walking away from a club where Sidney Bechet was playing.
123.q: They wanted me to go to a trade school, which was ok. So I went to Dobbins Vocational, which happened to be across the street from Connie Mack Stadium, Shibe Park, the home of the Philadelphia Athletics.

123.t: Goofing off in the Army and no famous musicians
123.s: He explains his failed radio training, a one-performance try at an entertainment MOS, and that Billy Byers was the most famous musician he met.
123.q: What do they call it when you goof off? I forget the term, anyhow. I spent one year, eleven months, and what was it, twelve days or something trying to get out as soon as I got in. Gold brick or something. I was supposed to learn radio and aircraft radio repair, and I was foolish enough to fluff it…

123.t: Boot camp in Texas and Jack Teagarden at the camps
123.s: He recalls Texas basic training with a Dixieland band, and hearing Jack Teagarden's band and meeting Billy Byers and Harry Biss.
123.q: No no. The first one was in Texas, in the panhandle near all the Oklahoma oil fields. And the only water we could drink was mineral water, which had to be ice cold. Otherwise you couldn’t drink it, it was filled with oil. So we ended up putting booze in our canteens when we went on our marches. And…

19.t: Leaving the Crystal Caverns and rehearsing Trummy's band
19.s: Osie Johnson goes into the Navy, Malachi hands his arrangements and band to Phil Phillips, and they rehearse Lunceford-style charts.
19.ch: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy
19.q: In the meantime, a month or so before that, Osie Johnson had been called into the Navy. So that kind of put a dent in our band -- although we got a very good drummer, a guy named Charlie Buck. But it wasn't the same thing. The idea had kind of fallen. So I decided that I would take this thing on.

19.t: Draft notice after the Apollo week and his reluctance to serve
19.s: Called up just after the band plays the Apollo, he explains why he felt he had no place in anybody's army.
19.ch: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy
19.q: We stayed down there until about June, I believe. Then we went in and we did a week in the Apollo Theatre. I think right after that was when I got a message from home with some greetings that Uncle Sam had called me to go into the Armed Services. Which broke my heart! Because I was the last person…

19.t: Great Lakes: the Navy band of Willie Smith, Clark Terry and the Royals
19.s: At Great Lakes he finds an all-star Navy band that invites him to join but he is unwilling.
19.ch: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy
19.q: Anyway, I went home and went for induction, passed it with flying colors, and they put me in the Navy and sent me to Great Lakes. I went up to Great Lakes, and this where Osie Johnson and Willie Smith, Clark Terry, the brothers... The first alto saxophone player with Basie and his brother.

19.t: First night in the barracks and the officer's 'you colored boys' speech
19.s: After jokes about Jody, a small officer threatens the Black recruits, and Malachi prays to get out.
19.ch: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy
19.q: Plus, the first night that we went in the Navy, after we went through some kind of cleaning inspection -- that's what you go through when you first enter there... Then that night, we were in these barracks, and the barracks were all Black guys in there. And an incident happened that just made me…

19.t: Telling the Navy examiners he has used drugs
19.s: A board questions him after another musician's arrest, and he answers as if he knows heroin to win a discharge.
19.ch: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy
19.q: Anyway, the next day... For that week... You're in boot camp for a week. They take you through all kinds of inspections. They inspect you for everything from crabs to venereal disease, to all...you know, they go in... One guy looks in... Two doctors, one looks in one ear and the other one looks in…

19.t: Discharged after eight days and sent home
19.s: The Navy decides he serves better as a civilian, and he surprises his wife by returning.
19.ch: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy
19.q: Finally, after a question-and-answer period of about 35 minutes, they told me to go back to my barracks, and they would contact me later. I went back to the barracks, and in a couple of days I was summoned to go back to this (?) place. They said, "Well, John, we've made a decision. We feel that

124.t: Army and Navy base shows as Armstrong's music director
124.s: Airlifted to bases for two concerts a day, the band played a secret B-29 plant in Arizona without leaving the vehicle.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: Like, when I was with -- I'll give you a good incident what the straw boss -- the best thing -- Like, when you're working with a guy like Louie Armstrong, who don't want no responsibility of nothing.

124.t: Draft status, USO plans and the recording ban
124.s: McRae was a family man and cannot recall how he avoided the draft; his brothers went on the USO and Shaw's Navy band, and Lunceford made no records.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: During the war. Let's back up a bit. You were -- when they started drafting -- well I guess you were about thirty-three years old so, were you considered too old to be drafted or because -- Because I think they were drafting what they call "able bodied men" up to thirty-five, but you had a family…

124.s: Edgar Sampson wrote on the road while the band worked nearly every night, with Army and Navy hospital shows and transcriptions.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: nights we had off was maybe Sunday night. Would be one night. We had one night off a week, and we were booked, for like, three months solid.

124.t: Wartime shortage of musicians and the decline of big bands
124.s: Many musicians joined the armed forces; McRae's brother Bob led a Navy band; travel limits and rising small bands undermined big bands.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: Remember I was telling you that Artie was in Hawaii or somewhere? And my brother, Bob, went in the Navy -- lieutenant or something, you know.

124.t: Air bases, Fort Huachuca and secret security
124.s: Armed services flew the band to Arizona bases, where security kept them from seeing anything, and Jimmy Mundy wrote at Fort Huachuca.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: Yeah, armed services. We were in California and went out to the airport, and they flew us to Tucson, Arizona -- from California. They flew us out to Tucson to do -- Then we had -- we had two dances. We had

124.t: Playing for wounded soldiers at Walter Reed
124.s: McRae calls the hospital show one of the hardest dates of his life, as hundreds of amputees lined the aisle.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: When we walked in there -- I wanna tell you this. When we walked in there, they had all these soldiers, and lot of them had lost their limbs and legs, and everything.

77.t: Where she was when World War II broke out; Palladium with Teddy Hill
77.s: She first thinks she saw trenches in Hyde Park and played the Palladium for six weeks with Teddy Hill's band, then recalls hearing of Pearl Harbor on a bus in New York.
77.q: World War II broke out. I was in Europe. I was in Europe because I know -- I saw them digging the trenches in Hyde Park, and I was working in one of the -- someplace in London -- in -- either in the provinces or someplace in England.

77.t: Taking the first USO unit, Rhythm and the Blues, overseas
77.s: Dick Campbell sent her with the first Black USO unit to China, Burma and India, and later on European and American tours; Snub Mosley came later, and she was the only woman.
77.q: Yes, that's right. I was right here in New York, but I was getting ready to go back to Europe. So in the meantime Dick Campbell called me and asked me to take the first USO show.

77.t: Command performance for Eisenhower and Zhukov in Hamburg
77.s: From Nancy, France, she was taken to Hamburg to entertain Eisenhower and Marshal Zhukov at the command headquarters.
77.q: See, because I was -- I had my troop in Nancy, France. And they -- they wired the publicity man, whoever it was, and told him to get me, because there were a lot of USO shows in different vicinities around then, but they wanted me, wanted my show.

77.t: The USO show that wrecked camps around the world
77.s: With a guitarist, pianist, bass player and drummer she toured World War II theaters; the soldiers wrote ahead to other camps and thousands crowded around.
77.q: theater, played the whole part of it, all through it, see? Took the first Negro unit called Rhythm and the Blues, and what a group I had! I had a guitar player, a piano player and a drummer, and they -- and a bass man -- and talk about masters.

77.t: The first USO units: CBI, Three Rhythm Rascals, ETO and Eisenhower
77.s: Dick Campbell sent her first to China, Burma and India with the Three Rhythm Rascals, then to Europe where she performed for Eisenhower, Zhukov and Montgomery; she earned ribbons for danger.
77.ch: Gangsters, records, women musicians and the blues
77.q: India. Yeah. China, Burma, India. That was my first tour for USO. And Dick Campbell sent me. He was the one that -- you know, the getting together of the talent for USO, you know, the colored talent.

77.t: Twelve years with the USO and thin dresses with Snub Mosley
77.s: From World War II through Korea she was the only woman with Snub Mosley's 17 men, dressed in slinky dresses in the cold, and played stateside including Riker's Island.
77.ch: Gangsters, records, women musicians and the blues
77.q: Even in that cold weather. So they told me in later years I was going to feel it. Walter Winchell wrote a beautiful article and so did Dorothy Kilgallen, about me working in those thin dresses, and no coat or anything around me. And the men with their gloves and things on. And I didn't even catch…

125.t: Company clerk in the CCC camp
125.s: He started his professional life in the CCC, sending money home, and became company clerk under Captain Clark of the 48th Infantry.
125.ch: Moving, Columbia Missouri and leaving home
125.q: Well, that's where I think my career would begin as really a professional musician, ironically. I went in the army not knowing what I was going to do, or how I was going to do it. All I knew was that there was some sort of security in my mind, in joining the army. Not only was it an avenue of…

125.t: Army discipline as a school for manhood
125.s: Thompson says the army teaches immaculateness and manhood to people who cannot go to school.
125.ch: Moving, Columbia Missouri and leaving home
125.q: In the army. They won't tolerate it. You have to lie down and make your bed, just like they say in the boy scouts, you have to learn how to be a man, and be immaculate. In the army you have to make your bed every day. This is why the army is a good place for a lot of people who aren't able to go to…

125.t: The camp men loved him: food saved for the pianist and manly affection
125.s: Playing piano won him affection, saved food from the cooks and a lifted spirit; he explains the hand-slap greeting as brotherhood.
125.ch: Moving, Columbia Missouri and leaving home
125.q: That was one of the main reasons, yes. It had to be first, and naturally my talent to play piano made people feel good. Well, it was a combination of two things to me, because see, if someone's complimenting you, that makes you smile and feel good, so you automatically give to them.

125.t: Ten months in the army and signing paychecks for illiterate men
125.s: He stayed ten months, joking about staying 40 like Jack Benny, and signed an X on payrolls for men who could not write.
125.ch: Moving, Columbia Missouri and leaving home
125.q: Very humorous. But I stayed in the army for 10 months to be exact, you know, and while I was in the army I would go into town on my leave. You know, every-

125.t: CCC work, playing piano in the mess hall
125.s: The company cleared land, Thompson was thrown off a work truck, and the men loved him for playing piano in the mess hall.
125.ch: Moving, Columbia Missouri and leaving home
125.q: I don't remember, there could have been 500. And we were dealing in conservation of land, you know, clearing wooded lands. I think now perhaps this is how the present freeways started, by the clearing of those swamp lands. And I -- at one time I got so disgusted I wanted to get out with the boys, I…

125.t: Captain Clark stands up to the townspeople at Delta, Missouri
125.s: Locals near Cape Girardeau and Delta, Missouri objected to the black company; the captain armed his men, showing Thompson that not all whites hung blacks.
125.ch: Moving, Columbia Missouri and leaving home
125.q: And I never will forget this. As I said it's significant, just as I had left Columbia, Missouri where a man, a black man had been lynched, the people in this area where we were sent, which was in the vicinity of Cape Jurado,

32.t: Arrested without his draft card in Missouri and sent to Camp Funston
32.s: White tells of being jailed for lacking his registration card and being sent on to camp.
32.q: Yeah, it's in Kansas, but it's not in central Kansas. You're almost over to the mountainous side. You're almost around to the Colorado corner.

32.t: Arrival at Camp Funston, the sergeant's slap and the typing test
32.s: White describes the slap at the gate, reporting to the major, and being picked out for office work and then for musicians.
32.ch: Army service and the 816th Pioneer Infantry Band
32.q: New Mexico. But anyhow, it's cold up around there. Well, I finally reached Camp Funston on one of these old slow trains, but it looked like they didn't care how you traveled in those days, you see, army movements. I reached Camp Funston along about two o'clock in the afternoon. Maybe it might have…

32.t: Winning the bandmaster's job of the 816th Pioneer Infantry Band
32.s: In an elimination contest White impressed the lieutenant and was made bandmaster; the band toured by train on Liberty drives to Camp Upton.
32.ch: Army service and the 816th Pioneer Infantry Band
32.q: Oh, they were fine. We dated them down in Clovis, New Mexico one time. But that's either here or there. Anyhow, this fellow was already in his first lieutenant's uniform. And they had sent him to take charge of the 816th Pioneer Infantry Band. He held a rehearsal with we twenty-four fellas. And he…

32.t: Verdun, Harry Truman, Pershing and the return from Le Havre
32.s: White tells of concerts at Verdun, serenading Truman, the Montfaucon cemetery with General Pershing, his status as bandmaster, and the wait in Le Havre.
32.ch: Army service and the 816th Pioneer Infantry Band
32.q: Well, then began the history of the 816th Band. Well, the history of the 816th Band measures up very creditably. In that while we were stationed in Verdun, every afternoon except Saturday and Sundays, we had to play a concert in Chevert Square in Verdun. Aside from other planes that we did around…

32.t: Honorable service record and later invitations to rejoin Army bands
32.s: White cites his citation letter and offers to have joined regular Army bands, including one at Fort Huachuca.
32.ch: Corrections and views on early Black music
32.q: I never had a committed an offense except not having my card with me. Card with me, yeah. And that's been claimed by the War Department and the United States Army even while I was in the service.

126.t: Washington Artillery on the Mexican border
126.s: In 1916 his National Guard battery went to the Mexican border, where five string players kept playing and were popular in the battery.
126.q: Well, I belonged to a Washington artillery, which was the National Guard out there, and in 1916, the National Guard out there was assembled and sent to the Mexican border. And, uh, in this battery sea, which I belonged to, were five string music players. So, we continued out playing music while we…

126.t: Back in service in 1917 and music stops
126.s: They were mustered out in February 1917 and back in on April 7th; the group scattered and there was no music until 1919.
126.q: Well, we left the Mexican border in February of 1917. We came back to New Orleans and were mustered out within ten days. But on April the 7th, if you recall, we were mustered right back into the service for World War Number One. And then the thing really broke up. All points of the compass these…

126.t: Aerial observer in World War I
126.s: Hardy trained as an artillery officer, became an aerial observer, describes the work, flew over the lines about 42 hours and finished in France.
126.q: And our work was to contact the ground troops and let them know what position our line was with reference to any kind of an advance that they would want to make. We were also required to take photographs of various sections of the front lines. We were also required to strafe the enemy at times,…

126.s: He met no musicians to collaborate with in the war; only a Rainbow Division comedy show and military bands.
126.q: I can't remember. Except the Rainbow Division put on a big show right after the war in France. That's the 42nd Division of New York. They had a lot of semi-actors from off of Broadway and so forth that put on a show, you know, for all the troops. But it wasn't instrument music. It was sort of a…

126.t: Time in New York and returning home in 1919
126.s: He was in New York from May 5 to 22, 1919, eager to get home after three years away.
126.q: No, not too much, no. Um... I was anxious to get home, too. I'd been away from home, you might say, for three years, because I was only out of the service about two and a half weeks in New Orleans before I was mustered right back in again.

127.t: Army service: bugler, brass band and dance orchestra
127.s: Miller became the unit's bugler by blowing back a sergeant's call, taught others, and played in the brass, string and jazz bands; Chiff's background discussed.
127.ch: Army and arrival in New Orleans
127.q: Yeah, I was bugle. I played in the brass band and I played in the dance orchestra. Didn't I tell you about it? I used to go along and watch a fella named Chiff and the brass band parade, watch his fingers. I was fast enough to make the same thing he'd be making, but he told me that wasn't no good.…

127.t: Army band at camp: size, parades and bugle duty
127.s: Punch describes the roughly 65-piece Army band where he learned music, and its daily parades.
127.ch: Army band and the Waifs' Home
127.q: Oh, that's where I learned my music at in that band. Let me tell you, I played in the big brass band, I played in the dance band, then I was bugle car. I was right on it. Head voice, drink voice, did everything in front.

127.t: How he got into the Army brass band by playing bugle
127.s: Punch walked out of line to play a bugle call, was placed in the brass band and studied there; he knew only blues when he went in.
127.ch: Army band and the Waifs' Home
127.q: No. I'm going to tell you how that happened. I couldn't play nothing but the blues or anything, but I'll tell you what happened. I was like, how you, uh, the, uh, the, uh, carpool, bugle carpool, had four bugles on his side, four hanging on his side. And he's making an arm, and he said, anybody got…

127.t: Earliest music memories and Army songs
127.s: He heard mostly blues before the Army, then Army songs and standards such as High Society.
127.q: Well, I'll tell you, before I went to the Army I didn't hear nothing but blues and things like that. When I went to the Army I liked them Army songs, like Over There, you know, Alexander's Ragtime Bay and all them kind of songs. But before I went to the Army I didn't remember a lot of blues and…

127.t: New Orleans musicians in his Army unit: Clowns Todd, Chiff, Paul Ben
127.s: Fellow Army musicians including pianist Clowns Todd, trumpeter Chiff and trombonist Paul Ben.
127.ch: Army and arrival in New Orleans
127.q: Well, just Oscar Shields. There was about the three of us, oh no, what is I'm talking about? Clowns Todd, Chiff, there's a triumphant player named Ben. Ben, Ben something, he from off the river to a real Creole fellow. Ben, he named Ben, I can't think of his first name.

128.t: Learning trombone in the army band in France
128.s: Jim tells how an officer, Lieutenant Lion, took him on and taught him trombone, and the band played around France.
128.ch: Army service in World War I
128.q: Yeah. on his hands, came on with the band, was a good position. And William Foster, you know, all the people, you know. And William Foster said, Bob, you called me Bob, he said, he said, let's come and get the band with us, with the lines. And they brought all them boys, put them on nice, put them…

128.t: Landing at Newport News and the camp commander story
128.s: Jim recalls landing at Newport News and a colored camp commander being made to dig trenches.
128.ch: Army service in World War I
128.q: I left Newport News, but in the land, in North of Virginia. Newport News, Newport News, in North, across, they built a terminal there, you see? Yeah, yeah. Answer it? We went business, we built a terminal there, I built to, is that right? I built to that. Listen, and the, the land is over there,…

128.t: Drafted into the Army band in France, learning trombone
128.s: Drafted and sent to France, he talked his way into the band, learned trombone with help from Willie Foster, and played for troops for 18 months.
128.q: No, they drafted. They drafted. Yeah. Yeah. So how did they come pick up trombone? Which the lieutenant was, he wanted the band, you know, for the company. And so he asked them, any fellas had an idea they wanted to take apart in music. Well I knew I could play guitar, but I didn't put no trombone.…

128.s: Robinson took up trombone in the army in 1917, put it down after the war and returned to it near Economy Hall.
128.ch: Country bands, trombone and city life
128.q: yeah I played in your time, that was my first time and I picked up the trombone in 19...19...19...1917 in World War II, the trombone and after the war was over I came back home and I put it down for a year and I couldn't prove it and after I took it up again I picked up the last time I was born and…

128.t: Chewing tobacco from army days and a doctor's advice
128.s: They discuss chewing tobacco as a habit begun in the service, and a doctor telling Robinson to smoke fewer cigarettes.
128.q: You couldn't, put, you couldn't put in your mouth when you're, when you're on a hike like that, you see? But if you, if you, if you're the lion standing for, for any kind of inspection of, you've treated, any kind of thing you have to, you couldn't put it in your mouth. After you're off duty, you…

129.t: Early band experience, the butterfly-bomb death of a drummer, and VE Day
129.s: He had learned from a drummer in an Artie Shaw type band; a cinema drummer was killed by a butterfly bomb. He remembers dancing in the street on VE Day.
129.q: Yes. I studied with a drummer who used to let me sit next to him when he was playing with an Artie Shaw type big band. So this was great, great, a great opportunity for me. And occasionally he would take off himself. Eventually he retired I think, and I got the job. Prior to that I was working in a…

129.t: Mr. Blakey's tiny vibraphone, and the secret of his being a British spy
129.s: Appleyard bought a two-octave vibraphone from a man who played aerodromes during the war, and learned years later he was a spy using the instrument as cover.
129.ch: Vibes, Bermuda and arriving in Canada
129.q: there at the time. I remember once I went in and there was a brand new set of Slingerland drums with big cymbals. I couldn’t believe it. I thought jeez, I’ve got to get to America, I’ve really got to get to America. Anyway, this night we were playing this aerodrome — and it was a very large…

129.t: Compass-adjuster apprentice who joins Felix Mendelssohn's Hawaiian Serenaders
129.s: While fetching Admiralty charts he tapped drumsticks in a record shop and was recruited to audition for a vaudeville band, where he earned far more than as an apprentice.
129.q: Yeah. We would take a ship out into the River Humber, which was about three miles wide, and we’d take a bearing, and say that was true north, and in those days the compass was not magnetic, they worked with magnets, and adjust accordingly the magnets and what have you, to bring it truthfully into…

129.t: Royal Air Force band service and the wing commander story
129.s: Kept as a drummer in a military band, he refused the warrant officer's offer to sign on, and decades later shared a dressing room with the wing commander of the RAF bands.
129.q: Well once they found out I was a musician they sent me home to get my drums, which was great, because I wanted to see that lovely girl. And I had a weekend’s leave and brought it back. And it was a military band. And when it came time for me to be demobilized — I had to do 18 months — everyone, it…

129.t: Growing up in Cleethorpes: air raids, evacuation and butterfly bombs
129.s: Born in Grimsby and raised in Cleethorpes, Appleyard recalls sleeping in an air raid shelter, evacuation to Wales, and the butterfly bombs, then leaving school at 13.
129.q: Yes. I was born in a place called Grimsby, on the east coast of England. It was the largest commercial fishing port in England. And I was born there on a Tuesday and I didn’t like it. They moved me on a Wednesday down to a place called Cleethorpes, which is a place adjacent to it, a seaside resort.

130.t: Leading the 410th Air Corps Band at Douglas, Arizona
130.s: As band leader of a big Air Corps band training P-38 pilots at Douglas, Arizona.
130.q: Right. In ’43 or whatever, ’42, ’43. I was a band leader in Douglas, Arizona in the Air Corps and I was up in L.A. picking up some dance band equipment which the government, it wasn’t G.I. equipment obviously. And I picked up some mutes and derbies and some dance band stands for my jazz band,…

130.t: Winged Victory show with Dave Rose, and a lobby chat about Bill Berry
130.s: Assistant conductor to Dave Rose on Winged Victory; Rowe digresses on Bill Berry and jazz clubs.
130.q: Yeah, well I was over on the Marianas and when I was at Douglas I ran into Dave Rose, who was the musician director for a new show which was going to be called “Winged Victory,” that Morris Hart wrote, and Swifty Lazar the agent, he was a captain in the show in the Air Corps. And I was delighted to…

130.t: Guam with Joe Anderson and Ernie Anderson memories
130.s: Ran into Joe Anderson on Guam, stayed in his tent, talked of Ernie Anderson and the Condon TV shows, and later played at Hamilton for Joe.
130.q: Well we wound up on Iwo Jima and then Saipan-Tinian and then the war was still on and I was in Guam and they ran out of cots for the boys and we were sleeping on the ground in a tent on a G.I. blanket. And I was walking down the road and I ran into Joe Anderson, who was involved with Hamilton…

130.t: War's end on Guam: Peter Lind Hayes show, Tyrone Power, Bobby Troup, Tinian
130.s: Touring island shows, hitching a flight with Tyrone Power, meeting Bobby Troup, and the Enola Gay unit on Tinian.
130.q: Oh I was on Guam actually, and there were six or seven of us, Peter Lind Hayes and a few other guys who were involved in the Winged Victory show. Because when David Rose left Winged Victory I became musical director and I was conducting every night. When the show broke up we all wound up — well not…

130.t: Surrender false alarm and Radio Tokyo piano program
130.s: Celebrating the war's end, a false alarm, the emperor's announcement, and Bushkin's piano program at Radio Tokyo.
130.q: Yeah it was quite a surprise because we were in the trans and flyers barracks and the M.P.’s drove up around three or four in the morning and said “hey guys, the war is over.” And I had stashed a half a gallon of pure alcohol, which I got from an aircraft carrier, which you could mix with the…

131.s: He tries everything to fail his physical at his father's urging and is passed anyway.
131.q: Well the night that I — I took my pre-induction physical in Jacksonville, Florida. We were playing at the Cape Colony Inn which was owned, it was in Coco Beach, Florida, which was owned by the astronauts. And a trumpet player, Paul Squire drove me up there. My father said, “I’ve never wished you…

131.t: Draft board, the Army band audition and enlisting
131.s: The draft board warns him; recruiters push him to audition for an Army band, and his unusual rudiment earns a 97 and a place in the New York Army Band.
131.q: the final table with the guys with the stamp. And I said I had to have failed, you know. He takes this stamp, I thought he was going to break the table. Bang! Fully qualified for military service. I said, “oh my God.” Here we go man. I mean even my eyes. I mean I used to wear glasses. I had 20/200…

131.t: New York Army Band and lessons with Sonny Igoe
131.s: He plays concert and stage band at Governor's Island and studies the Bellson/Breines book with Sonny Igoe on a government lesson plan.
131.q: No — yes, this was a concert band. We played parades up and down Fifth Avenue, you know, the whole bit. But then there’d be the symphonic band, I mean the concert band, and I was good a tympani because that’s what I played in high school, because of my ear, and I could tune and play the tympani and…

131.t: Governor's Island memories and Jim and Andy's
131.s: The band's move to Staten Island, a final ceremony at Governor's Island, and going to Jim and Andy's with Igoe to meet Jake Hanna and Joe Jones.
131.q: But I played the final ceremony there, and then I took that picture, and now in the bookshop and when you get off you see the whole history of Governor’s Island, but I’m

131.t: Transfer to Korea, the Seventh Infantry Division Band and Korean life
131.s: A levy sends him to Korea instead of Saigon; he plays with saxophonist Carter Jefferson and shares Charlie Parker records.
131.q: I showed you how I got in and all this and that. So now we’re over on Staten Island with the New York Army Band and a levy comes down from Washington. Man, I was the drummer with the stage band. And everybody figured well D’Imperio’s never going to get transferred out of here because there’s nobody…

132.t: Drifting through college, then submarines and law school
132.s: He did not play at Hamilton, was interrupted by the war, then went to law school and never practised or played again.
132.q: Monk, I don’t know that I really ever thought about it to tell you the truth. In those days I went off to college and in college here I didn’t play. We had occasional visits from Eddie Condon, Ernie Anderson, Joe’s brother, was his manager, and he came up here several times and other big bands and…

132.s: He chose submarines from midshipman school and was oddly selected despite failing the engineering questions.
132.q: Well I don’t know. I was in the midshipman’s school at Columbia. And there were I think 1,200 of us. And they put up lists, what did you want to do. And I got to thinking about the fact that most all the guys who were basically civilians like me got to do landing craft. And I thought that was a…

132.t: Overseas in the Pacific and a close call
132.s: He declines to discuss Australia exploits but praises the service and mentions a near-death time.
132.q: No, but it was a wonderful experience, wonderful people. I never met a single person I didn’t like in the service, in the submarine service. It was a great experience.

132.s: He thinks a short universal draft would be good for citizens and notes the Marines are fully staffed.
132.q: That’s right. Well just going through boot camp, today you don’t have to go to war. If you can handle boot camp, say a Marine boot camp, you’re a better man, and you’re a better citizen too.

132.t: Music and movies aboard the submarine
132.s: They played electrical transcriptions and watched Destination Tokyo hundreds of times.
132.q: Oh sure. And we got — I’ll never forget — we got a lot of the electrical transcriptions that the guys did, and boy there’s some wonderful jazz on those things. And it’s too bad they ended up the way they did but we’d get those, I used to play those all the time.

133.t: Drafted: Fort Dix basic training and cavalry wireman duty
133.s: He was drafted, went through basic training at Fort Dix, and was a cavalry wireman until Special Services took him; a lieutenant kicked his helmet to wake him.
133.q: Yeah, then I went to a place called Fort Dix down in New Jersey for basic training, which lasts six months. And then uh, read my orders to, to, uh, go, uh, by ship to Germany and stayed there a year and a half.

133.t: Special Services in Stuttgart, Jazz One and fellow musicians
133.s: Walton played in Special Services shows then led the Army band Jazz One in Stuttgart, with Eddie Harris, Leo Wright, Houston Person and Lex Humphries in the orbit.
133.q: Yeah, yeah. Those were my duties. But some time we did, first we did a few variety shows which included the son of Bing Crosby, a guy named Gary Crosby, for inst… as an example. Uh, and uh, various and sundry musicians who had applied to this Special Service Unit. And uh, that's where uh, uh, my,…

133.t: Race in the Army: integrated on paper, separated socially
133.s: The Army was formally integrated by 1955-56 but soldiers drank in separate bars, and a show tour was chased out of a redneck bar by thrown bottles.
133.q: Oh, uh, it was totally, it was totally integrated uh, by uh, by the time I got in there – '55, '56. I think Truman had done that, as far as I remember. Uh you know, I mean uh, in terms of doing something uh, uh, gettin' it uh, uh, uh a law passed or something. Word has it that Harry Truman did…

133.t: Sitting in with German jazz musicians in Stuttgart
133.s: Off-base he sought out German musicians at the Atlantic Bar in Stuttgart, dodging the MPs.
133.q: Ah yeah, yeah. Yeah, they were, they were fine. Uh I can't remember a lot of the names uh, but uh, they certainly uh were uh, uh, you know, competent musicians. We sought them out and uh set in with them. They were glad to see us coming, you know. Especially in downtown Stuttgart, the Atlantic Bar;…

133.t: Declining to re-enlist and using the Army to shed
133.s: He refused officer training because he wanted to return to New York, and used the Army time to practice and write, though none of the music was reused.
133.q: [laughs] No. Not at all. In fact I could have become an officer. They came through with the uh – what do you call it? – the uh, uh aptitude tests and uh … but I, I didn't uh, I didn't want to be any part of the military after my required time. I wanted to get back to the city. And uh, explore ……

134.t: Wilson Junior College and his brothers Bruz and George
134.s: After DuSable he spent a year at Wilson before being inducted; he describes his brothers' late starts on drums and guitar.
134.q: Oh yeah. Bruz was – because Bruz came to me one time and asked me. I think he was 27. He said, “Am I too old to play music?” I said, “Oh no, man, you can always.” He said, “I mean, I want to play as well as you play.” “Well now, that’s another story.” Because Bruz – I looked up. Bruz was with Sarah…

134.t: Drafted into the Navy band at Great Lakes
134.s: Freeman describes boot camp, Dyett's note getting him into the Navy band, and the draft pulling in the stars.
134.q: That had a lot of effect, because they drafted just about all of the able musicians. They got me when I was 18, up at Great Lakes. I was trying – Captain Walter Dyett, again, he got me in that band, because see, after I went through boot camp – and I’ve always been an ex-boxer and all that stuff.

134.t: Who was drafted and who escaped
134.s: They discuss the 18-to-45 draft, his flat feet, and why Bird, Dizzy and Sun Ra did or did not serve.
134.q: And they didn’t ask you, did you want to go? I told them my feet were flat. They said that makes no difference. Say, “March, brother.”

134.t: Navy bands at Great Lakes and the Pacific
134.s: He describes the A, B and C bands, being shipped to Hawaii with the Hellcats, and air raid alerts.
134.q: Oh yeah. We went on. They were still bombing. The war was pretty thick in ’42. With the men, they just put us on the E deck – that’s A B C D E – and then turned the lock. I said, boy. And then they have these alerts when you were in the E deck.

134.t: Playing Body and Soul in the Navy band; duties
134.s: Osie Johnson writes a background for Freeman's Hawkins feature, and he describes a band's duties playing for officers.
134.q: When I got passed that stage, I stopped. When I got in my teens, I stopped, until I got in the service, and guess what my feature was? Coleman Hawkins’s Body and Soul.

135.t: Rejected as 4F, then drafted and sent to aviation cadet training in 1943
135.s: Heath tried to volunteer as an aircraft mechanic, was classed 4F for being underweight, then was classed 1A when drafted and qualified for aviation cadet training.
135.q: Anyhow, this background, I’m a little naïve, 18 year old, and the war started in ‘41, and I said, “Oh let me go down here and volunteer to be an aircraft mechanic with my mechanical knowledge.” I went to the courthouse there in Philadelphia, went through the whole process, signing up, taking the…

135.t: Keesler Field in Biloxi: tents, tests and calling cadence
135.s: Heath describes six months of testing and humiliating conditions at Keesler Field, being outspoken, and his earlier high school years in Wilmington.
135.q: graduate. Most of the cadets were college graduates or people who had been flying before, some kind of aviation background. And they let us in there, but they let so many in and they didn’t have anywhere for us to go…

135.t: Tuskegee: college detachment, primary flight training and the air base
135.s: Heath describes learning wind vectors, flying small trainers and a Stearman, and moving to Tuskegee Army Air Field for the segregated training program.
135.q: Well there is one thing I must tell you before that. When we did go to Tuskegee, the institute, I was sent to what they called “college training detachment,” for about four or five months to learn some geometry, little advanced about wind vectors and things like that, that I didn’t know about. In…

135.t: General B.O. Davis, the Tuskegee Airmen film and bracing upperclassmen
135.s: Heath comments on the accuracy of the Tuskegee Airmen movie, the hazing, soloing the AT-6 and receiving his commission and wings in January 1945.
135.q: B.O., Jr. was a commanding officer through that air base and they had gone overseas by the time I got there. That movie about the airmen…

135.t: Walterboro: P-40s, P-47s and no combat
135.s: Heath describes transition training in South Carolina, mock dogfights with Marine pilots, and his unit's cancelled deployment as the war ended.
135.q: No, I didn’t have to go kill anybody. I was pretty fortunate. But in May of ’45, we had gone through the transition into P40, which is War Hawk, like the Flying Tigers are famed for. And we used to say that we got some of the planes backward, the teeth painted out on them. They gave us inferior…

136.t: The Shinagawa quartermaster depot club and where the camps were
136.s: Brown pins down the Shinagawa location and the unknown camps; she recalls that the club's audience was mostly black soldiers.
136.q: Shinagawa. And there was a … today Shinagawa … today, it‟s the east side, which is the ocean side, there was nothing there. Today it is the most hip place. Even Dean & Deluca has a store [there]. It‟s like a really upscale, and uh, [as] famous here as the Oyster Bar in the station, [Grand] Central…

136.t: The dangerous trip home to Ryoyo past Russian troops
136.s: Students were sent home in secret; she describes the journey, cropped hair and Russian soldiers stripping the family house.
136.ch: War's end and the return to Japan
136.q: Then, after that it was very difficult. Uh, what I understand is this may not be all the gossip, it could be very true. Because when you start thinking about how the Japanese military runs, what I understand was the ones who decided, they had a meeting, they thought maybe … you know, we were about…

136.t: Occupation of the house, leaving Manchuria and DDT at the port
136.s: Soviet, Communist and Nationalist soldiers occupied the house; the family lost everything, left in 1946 and was dusted with DDT at Ujina.
136.ch: War's end and the return to Japan
136.q: Oh, just, we were fine, I was the only one who wasn‟t together [with them], except my oldest sister was married to a military man, so they were in China, they weren‟t there. Um … this was, as I said, it was 1946, uh…1945, excuse me, summer, and „til 1946 we were permitted, we left there, the first…

136.t: First impressions of Japan and settling in Beppu
136.s: The small trains of Japan and the family's settling in Beppu, her parents' home region.
136.ch: War's end and the return to Japan
136.q: No, I had been several times with my mother, because my mother often visited, and because I was the youngest, so she always took me along, so many times. But [sighs], first, I tell you, first my impression from Ujina port back to where my parents came from—we settled in Beppu city—and the train, to…

136.t: The last school year, nurse training and the war's end
136.s: She never finished high school, trained four months as a volunteer nurse, and the war ended before the training did.
136.ch: War's end and the return to Japan
136.q: No. No. Before I finished high school [the] war was ended. So I was an “honorary graduate,” just like anybody else in my class. So, that‟s the year I was supposed to graduate, the following year in March. Here, everything [begins] is September, but in Japan it was March, the [school year] starts…

137.t: Declining a captain's rating when Miller went overseas
137.s: Miller's offer of a captain's rating and training did not suit him; he stayed about a year and a half and did not go overseas.
137.ch: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
137.q: Yeah, they offered me captain's rating. They wanted me to take three months training to protect myself, and here was a girl -- Mazie, wasn't it? Mazie, and in the field he was going to give me a captain's rating, and I didn't want to go. I didn't want to go overseas. I didn't want to travel…

137.t: Taking over the International Sweethearts of Rhythm
137.s: He left because his bands kept being drafted, rehearsed the Sweethearts in Washington, and had them stun musicians at the Apollo.
137.ch: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
137.q: Every time I would get a good band together, they'd draft the guys. And I just said, -- and so, the girls played the Apollo in Buchanan. I wasn't with them. They said, if you get over to a fellow named Eddie Durham, -- and when they got in touch with me again, that's when I went to Washington, D.…

137.t: How his birth year got moved
137.s: His brother gave wrong birth years to the draft board because his mother was too ill to testify.
137.q: Yeah, that's how ________ got involved. He set the records up, just himself.

137.t: Tenth Cavalry exhibitions and Joe teaching him to shoot
137.s: In Kansas City in 1927 he saw old Tenth Cavalry soldiers put on shooting exhibitions, hitting targets while falling; Joe taught him to use a rifle.
137.q: When I was at Kansas City in the 27 -- 1927, I didn't tell him -- I went out to see the old soldiers that my brother used to be with.

137.t: Brother Joe's army service and musical training
137.s: Joe served with the Tenth Cavalry, learned music in the army, and taught Durham on visits to his camp from about age eight.
137.q: Somewhere around in there. Yeah, he was young when he got (inaudible) Army and he stayed in until that last war. He was in that last war.

71.t: Japanese soldiers in Shanghai and getting out before the war
71.s: He saw Japanese troops drilling in the streets, advised the band to leave, and the war broke out two weeks later, leaving Reginald Jones in a camp.
71.ch: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
71.q: Yes, there were American bands in the hotels. So, one morning after I came out, it must have been about 8 o'clock and we would ride the rik.shas, you know these .................... That's the first thing we did when we got to China was to get in a rik.sha and ride. These little guys pull them like…

71.t: Lost draft card and being called up
71.s: He and Freddie Greene lost their cards; writing for a new one got him drafted, the first in Basie's band to go.
71.q: Yes. Until 1943. We had made a picture in California and I had lost my, my card. I don't know what, you know, your rating card, whatever your number is. And Freddie Greene had lost his out in California when we were making a movie. And he was walking down Hollywood Boulevard looking at some men's…

71.t: Army camps, gaining weight and the rifle that hit his lip
71.s: He took the Army as a rest, was in Upton and Shanks, put on thirty pounds, and was kept off the rifle range after a kick hit his mouth.
71.q: I didn't have to do one-nighters. I could sleep and eat good food. And eventually I got to like it. I kind of liked it because a lot of times all the soldiers would break their necks getting out of there on a Friday knowing they don't have to be back until Monday.

71.t: Hard treatment as Basie's 'Jody' and avoiding being shipped overseas
71.s: Clifton Glover pulled him out of the induction line, sergeants rode him, and he kept being scratched from shipping lists until Sy Oliver requested him.
71.q: Yes, yes. But I was really supposed to have been shipped overseas so many times. When I went up into the Reception Center up in Camp Upton I asked where, Clifton Glover was up there before me and he was one of the leaders up there. He met all the recruits coming in. And one day he said he was…

71.t: Army band duty: shows, piers, retreat parade and discharge
71.s: At Camp Kilmer the band played radio shows and sent off troop ships on freezing piers; he was among the last out in 1946 after a one-trumpet retreat parade.
71.q: Yes. He was the main arranger and we played on the radio. We had one show once a week where soldiers would come from all different camps. Sy would make arrangements and other people would make arrangements. And we rehearsed and then we'd do this big show every week That was one thing we did.…

74.t: Photographs from Korea: Pruitt and Bernie Peacock
74.s: Describing a 1952 Korea photo and trouble with Carl Pruitt and Bernie Peacock.
74.ch: Leading his own band in New York
74.q: The funny thing about him was I remember meeting him that time he sent me a record, he moved back to Detroit, it's where his home is.

74.t: USO camp shows from Fort Lewis to Boston
74.s: His first USO tour runs from Fort Lewis through Salt Lake and the Boston harbor ports.
74.ch: Queens Terrace, Decca records and Amen
74.q: The first time I played. I went down to Fort Lewis, and came back Salt Lake City; all the way back up to Boston, played all those ports on the harbor of Boston and came back to New York and New Jersey.

74.t: Korea photographs, Pruitt and Bernie Peacock
74.s: Details of a Korea photo and two difficult sidemen.
74.ch: Hollywood, Ken Murray and the Penguin years
74.q: I don't know; he was recommended to me, and I was so sorry. I had to send him back. Everybody had trouble with him. Benny Goodman had him too for a while

74.t: USO tour continued: Germany, Korea and Japan
74.s: After France and Germany, Korea with Budd Johnson, Pruitt and Peacock.
74.ch: Package shows, Miami and the USO
74.q: We spent all of August in France, in Germany September--part of September anyway and then we came back and played New York for a couple of weeks and I did a few gigs that

74.t: Bette Davis and the Hollywood Canteen
74.s: Bette Davis asks him to play the Canteen and insists Black soldiers may dance with white hostesses.
74.ch: Hollywood, Ken Murray and the Penguin years
74.q: One of the nicest things that happened to me there was my favorite move star called up and left a message--I wasn't there, that afternoon she called up, Bette Davis, and asked me if

138.t: Taking over the military band as major, Spanish-American War era
138.s: Laine tells how Major Violet asked him to lead a 35-man military band, which he enlarged with piccolos and drilled for street marches until they were to ship out.
138.q: Yeah. That ain't too long ago. Oh, it's about. Oh, yes. That was in the Times-Picayune. Yeah. You were 66 then and he's 85 now. Yeah.

138.t: Kentucky Days and the kid band that won over a military band
138.s: At Biloxi, soldiers joke about a kindergarten band, then applaud Laine's boys' playing of Kentucky Days.
138.q: That was my favorite. Is that right? I'll tell you a little instance that's happened about Kentucky Days. Now, this is a queer thing with our boy, Alfred. I've got three bands in Biloxi. Understand me? Uh-huh. I've got a band for West End Junior, band for West End Fire Company, number three, and a…

138.t: Camp Beauregard band in World War I
138.s: Laine was sent for to organize an Army band at Camp Beauregard, stayed about seven weeks, then quit music.
138.q: Yes. Yes, exactly. This bugbearer played. Exactly. I said, look here. I said, that ain't my stuff. Nothing in the world is. Same stuff to that thing. Now, I quit playing music right after War I, first war. Not some of them, most of them were drafted. One of them died in the Army. Well, they took…

138.t: Spanish-American War drum and bugle corps photo
138.s: Laine describes his fifteen-piece bugle and drum band at the time of the Spanish-American War and the photo of six players.
138.ch: Early drums, photos and the Laine home
138.q: That's right, yeah. Now, when they were getting ready to go across, Armistice again, stopped us from going. They had a beautiful band. Bugle, piccoloos, and drums.

139.t: Army engineers: playing for officers and showing movies
139.s: Drafted in 1942 into the engineers, he played piano at the officers' club, collecting money in his canteen, and sang and ran movies.
139.q: See, my canteen was my kidney cup. My canteen, where I used to drink out, was my kidney cup. Them guys started drinking that 7% beer down there. And I come home, my cup full of money, every night. Then I go to the PX and get that old 7% beer. But you had to be from the home to me to drink with you.…

139.t: Stateside postings and diesel mechanics school
139.s: He served three years, sixteen months in the States around Florida, diesel school in Illinois, and departure for overseas.
139.q: Down in Florida. All over Florida. Fort Myles, Sarasota, Tallahassee, Ole'Anna, St. Petersburg, Pensacola, Miami, then all over Florida. And then... Fort Chapel.

139.t: Overseas in Sicily and Italy, avoiding K.P.
139.s: He spent twelve months overseas, did little work, avoided peeling potatoes, and showed a couple of movies a week.
139.q: First place, they had me on, what do you call it? Peer them potatoes. I wasn't going to peel no potatoes.

139.t: Diesel training and discrimination in civilian jobs
139.s: Back home he could not work as a diesel mechanic because Negroes were not allowed, and he got a movie projector job when someone died.
139.q: Neither one of them did help me because when I came back here, movement, had a gang of movement pitching machines operating at that time and I applied for a job and couldn't get a job nowhere. The man told me to put my name on the roster as a move projector operator. And I had to wiggle my name and…

140.t: Spending money; mother signs Ali into the Army
140.s: Ali made no spending money; his mother signed him into the Army to get him off the street.
140.q: No. And you know my mom and dad was giving me money. Until I went into the service. I went into the service when I was — I had to put up my age to get into the service because I was getting a little rambunctious and mom wanted me off the street. So she took me to the Army and signed me in.

140.t: Second Army Band and Special Service
140.s: Ali stayed three years; the band got him out of regular Army duty and playing in town at night.
140.q: Right, right, right. And I stayed there for three years in the service. And when I came out I had my head a little screwed on a little better, because I got into the Army and really got into the music thing because that was one way of ducking the regular Army stuff. You know like the digging the…

140.t: Witnessing Army integration at Camp Pickett
140.s: Ali recalls the Army desegregating overnight, the fights that followed, equal pay, and the band staying calm.
140.q: No. I was in the Army when they integrated. I was there. You know, I mean, you know they integrated the whole Army in 24 hours.

140.s: Ali's mother felt she had risked him in Korea, but he served in Germany and learned drumming in the drum corps.
140.q: Yeah. You know that was the only mistake that my mom felt that she had made is to get me in harm’s way, because she insisted I go into the service because I was getting pretty stupid in the street. I had quit school, I didn’t want to go to school, I didn’t want to do anything other than hang out in…

141.s: He did basic training at Fort McClellan and disliked the small town.
141.q: Oh, yeah. Well, I didn’t know about Lester Young at that time. But I spent basic training at Fort McClellan. It was a small town, and I didn’t like it there.

141.t: Army band in Colorado Springs with Tommy Turk
141.s: He played piano in trombonist Tommy Turk's band at officers' clubs and came home in a zoot suit, now a musician.
141.q: Yes. Tommy Turk was a great trombonist, and I used to play with him... I was playing piano in his band, and we used to play at officers’ clubs and around. He was a great player. I knew it at the time, but I later met him when he was with Jazz at the Philharmonic...

141.t: How the Army changed him; Sartre and Camus
141.s: Allison has little to say about the Army's effect, but Audre recalls him pressing existentialist books on her.
141.q: Well, I remember that when I met you, you wanted me to read Jean-Paul Sartre, Camus, Aldous Huxley, all those writers. I remember, I had to run to the library and get all those books.

141.t: Back at Ole Miss as an economics major, zoot suits and long hair
141.s: Home from the Army he studied economics for his father, wore a DA haircut and bought zoot suits in Memphis.
141.q: I took economics because of my father. He wanted me to take economics.

61.t: End of the series; scouring New Haven for cheap records
61.s: Wartime shellac shortage ended the series; he and Jerry King bought records for pennies from a jukebox man named Max.
61.ch: Army years and return to Columbia
61.q: undeserved, because he had absolutely nothing to do with them, and four that had the huge John Hammond paraphrased liner notes. At that point, the series stopped, because World War II was rolling along. The Japanese captured Singapore, which was the great port for the outlet of Malaysian shellac,…

61.t: New Haven radio show, the draft and friends' wartime paths
61.s: He ran a half-hour jazz show using Ellington's Reminiscing in Tempo; then he was drafted, while King and Fuller served.
61.ch: Army years and return to Columbia
61.q: He was kind of a goofy guy, but that’s all right. We got a lot of good records from him. During that time, the Hot Jazz Classics faded away. I was still writing for Tempo, and I had my own radio program, which the David Dean Smith Music Shop let me do for half an hour over a New Haven station. I…

61.t: Army service: Leyte landing, Mindanao and New Guinea
61.s: He landed at Leyte on the second day, avoided a minefield, and served in the rear infantry through to the end of the war.
61.ch: Army years and return to Columbia
61.q: Leyte, yeah, the first landing. I was in on the second day, which was very fortunate, because the first day was very tough. The second day was cloudy, and the Japanese air force didn’t show up. So we got ashore without being disturbed. On the third day they bombed the beach and we were already…

61.t: Grand Canyon, the outbreak of war and the train home
61.s: At the Grand Canyon he heard of the bombing of Warsaw; Stearns went on to Hawaii and Avakian returned by train with his aunt.
61.ch: Yale, Stearns and the big bands
61.q: Oh yeah, we got there all right and stopped off at the Grand Canyon on the way, by the way, which was an incredible experience. I met a nice young girl about my age on the one evening that we spent there. The two of us parked under the stars in Marshall’s car while Marshall was in bed already, I…

142.t: Drafted into the army and discharged early
142.s: He left high school at 15-16 for the army, served about two and a half years, and was released early thanks to a commander who liked to compose.
142.ch: Army, politics and jazz in Cuba
142.q: Almost three years, two years and a half. It was supposed to be three years, but I get rid of it because of the integration of the commander who liked to compose music. The

142.t: Race among Cuban musicians and in the army
142.s: He says race was not a factor among musicians, since the best were Black, though in the army and party most officers and conductors were white.
142.ch: Army, politics and jazz in Cuba
142.q: Not really. The best musicians on that island were the Black people. Well, not only,because Ernesto Lecuona was white and was the representative of the Afro-Cuban composers was a white guy, was Ernesto Lecuona and nobody denied that. And I never feel that in that sense. It’s very simple, if you…

142.t: Repertoire and purpose of the officially formed big band
142.s: The orchestra played music banned months earlier, such as Route 66 and Mancini, on imported instruments; Paquito believes it was formed to counter the image that the revolution blocked jazz, and it got him out of the army.
142.q: I am almost sure that this orchestra was formed in order to improve or to deny the impression that the revolution was blocking Jazz music.

142.t: Army band and finishing the conservatory in uniform
142.s: In the army concert band with strong young players, he continued clarinet studies and gave his graduation recital dressed as a soldier.
142.ch: Army, politics and jazz in Cuba
142.q: Yes because in the army, I was in the marching band. They have a concert band, in the army. Pretty good, pretty good, because they have many of the young musicians in the streets, in the cabarets and in the symphony and all that, and they put it together a pretty good concert band.

143.t: Great Lakes band: A, B and C bands and jam sessions
143.s: Panken lists notable Navy musicians; Donaldson was in the young C band and sneaked into jam sessions with the older players.
143.q: these guys you’re talking about were a little older than me. They played in a band they called the A-band. Then they had another band. The guys were a little older. The B band. I was in the C band, because I was 18, and most of the guys in the band where I was were 18 years old. We were young…

143.t: Back at A&T and the Mombassa Club
143.s: Discharged after eleven months, he finished coursework and began playing commercially at the Mombassa Club with Billy Tolles and Nipsey Russell as emcee.
143.q: No, not at that point. When I went back, it was the middle of the semester, and I didn’t stay on the campus. I had to get me a room out in the town. I was still making up some courses that I had lost during those 11 months. After I got the courses made up, I started actually to play a little…

143.t: Playing bebop with the Army base band in Greensboro
143.s: Players from the Overseas Replacement Depot band, including Moody and Dave Burns, were surprised by his bebop and he played with them.
143.q: Oh, yeah. When I came back from the Navy, they had an Army base in Greensboro, the O.R.D., Overseas Replacement Depot. I was back at the cottage, and the guys from the Army band used to come over and play with the other band. They hadn’t seen me. Then I came back, and I’m playing bebop. I’m not…

143.t: Drafted into the Navy and the Great Lakes audition
143.s: He bluffed his way into the Great Lakes band by playing clarinet for the bandmaster, then learned saxophone in two weeks.
143.q: Well, it’s a funny story. In 1945 I was drafted into the U.S. Navy. I didn’t volunteer. I was drafted. And I went to Great Lakes. When you go to Great Lakes, you have a pool, say, of about 200 musicians. Anybody who says they’re a musician, they put them in the pool. A lot of them wasn’t that good.…

144.t: Army band at Fort Knox with Cannonball Adderley and Junior Mance
144.s: Fuller dates his service to 1953-55 and describes the last all-black Army band at Fort Knox, with Cannonball as director without rank, Junior Mance as clerk, and Mel Wanzo.
144.q: Junior Mance was the company clerk because he was the piano player. He had to play the glockenspiel, or whatever that thing is.

144.t: Tank Corps classification and friends killed in Korea
144.s: He was classed for Tank Commander School and later learned men from his outfit were killed in Korea while he was playing with Yusef Lateef.
144.q: an application and I don’t know shit about a tank! (Laughs) You know, the ones you had to fill out? Tank Commander School, which doesn’t mean you’re going to command the thing, you’d be in the turret rather than loading and doing stuff like that, and putting tracks on the tank. You could be one of…

144.t: Integrating the Louisville white orchestra, missing from records
144.s: Fuller says he and Mel Wanzo integrated a white orchestra in Louisville in 1955; a military history now lacks any record of it.
144.ch: After the Army: school, race, politics
