144.q: It’s a natural thing to do! I didn’t know that until—I’m sorry my hand was busted, but last year I was supposed to play with…I really got upset. I was mad about my hand being messed up. I fell on ice and before my wife died, I couldn’t use this left hand. I worked at the Kennedy Center, anyways.…

144.t: Chronology: job, draft, Cannonball, the band, then Wayne State
144.s: Brower clarifies the sequence from the factory job to being drafted at 19, Cannonball, the Army band, and Wayne State.
144.ch: After the Army: school, race, politics
144.q: I didn’t know I was going to go into the Army. I was sucked up! “You’re 19! How did you miss this! They started drafting at 18! Get in that service”

145.t: Leading the Navy band and the Bombadiers at St. Mary's

163.t: Basic training in Texas and the timely flu
163.s: Drafted, he went to Texas basic training; flu delayed him until his transfer to California came through.
163.q: Yeah, any physically able guy, I mean in a certain age limit, sure. And well I didn’t tell the whole story, but anyhow I was drafted and they sent me to Texas for Basic Training, which was out of the — whatever they call it — Vallejo is in a certain region there, whatever they call it. And Texas is…

163.t: Segregation in the Army bands; Latin musicians in Texas
163.s: Service bands were segregated; at Camp Hood Latin band members were barred from bars by a white line.
163.q: No. It’s funny, I don’t remember it ever coming up. We had Latin guys in that, except when we went to Texas it was a problem for the Latin guys. Remember we were really reminiscing. We eventually left Vallejo and we were transferred to a couple of different places and we ended up at Fort Hood. It…

164.t: Army band, infantry and Special Service in Germany
164.s: Drafted into an excellent Army band, then infantry and MP duty at Heilbronn, before moving to Special Service shows at Seckenheim and two-piano gigs in Heidelberg.
164.q: drafted, and I mean luckily I got into an Army band. We had Ziggy Elman, Charlie Teagarden, and a bunch of the studio guys, the lead alto, Blake Reynolds from Paramount, lead alto from Fox, Russ Cheever, a couple of the guys, Red Ballard and Bruce Squires who were the two trombones in Benny’s band,…

164.t: Meeting Tony Bennett as Joe Bari
164.s: Smith met a soldier called Joe Bari who was Tony Bennett, using the name to avoid anti-Italian prejudice.
164.q: Not an awful lot. We dated a few German gals at the time. But there was a guy named Joe Bari in the outfit with us in Seckenheim, and Barry is the grandfather’s name with Tony Bennett, I mean that was Tony. He was in the Army. And I said, “why did you go in the Army under the name of Joe Bari?”…

164.t: Guarding SS men at the Heilbronn prison camp
164.s: He describes the huge camp, going in unarmed to find SS men, and child soldiers at the war's end.
164.q: We didn’t deal too much with the population. I mean other than Patton set up this prison camp in Heilbronn and we had a half a million prisoners in there, not all Germans, some Hungarians and what have you. And periodically we had to go in there and find the SS men that were amongst them that had…

16.t: Writing for the Camp Smalls Navy band
16.s: He describes being pulled from Ellington's band into the segregated Navy and the large jazz and symphonic bands he wrote for, including the Blue Jacket Choir with Harry Belafonte.
16.q: Okay, where shall I start. Well I'll just talk and you tell me when you get enough. First of all, my experience with the U.S. Navy Band was two things: wonderful and terrible. All right? First of all, terrible because I had just been hired by Duke Ellington to write music for his band which was the…

16.t: Denied promotion in the Navy and his protest
16.s: Black sailors were not advanced in rating; he refused to arrange, signed in and out, and the ratings came only two weeks before discharge. He also was on the arranging staff at the Naval School of Music.
16.q: would write it. If he didn't like it, he'd just throw it. Same way with me. I would write whatever I wanted to write and comes Friday and have rehearsal, if you didn't like it, you'd just tear it up, throw it away. And if they didn't like it, your employers, they could fire you and that was okay…

16.t: Tape change and a note about living with Mercer's mother in Washington
16.s: Billie reminds him that he roomed with Mercer's mother in Washington during Navy school; tape is changed.
16.q: Billie's reminding me … put this on tape too because a lot of people don't know that I lived with, had a room with Mercer's mother when I was in Washington, D.C. at the school of music. The Navy School of Music.

165.t: Segregated army and race fights in Britain
165.s: Hendricks recalls his army service, being sent as a segregated unit to fight Nazism, and fighting white American soldiers over relationships with British women.
165.q: No, I hadn’t started playing – I didn’t start playing drums until after I came back from World War II, which really was World War II. Whoo, what an experience that was. Good Lord. I couldn’t believe what was going on. In the first place, I couldn’t

165.t: USO shows in England and high school productions
165.s: He produced USO shows in England, drawing on writing and directing Scott's a Poppin' at Scott High School.
165.q: Yes. In England I put on shows for the USO. I had directed shows in my high school. They had a yearly show called Scott’s a Poppin’. I used to write, produce, and direct that, so I put that on my resume in the army. So they picked me to do the same thing. When they would send USO shows to England,…

165.t: Disarming a white soldier at a USO canteen near the front
165.s: At a USO near the front, a young white soldier said he did not like blacks; Hendricks replied agreeably and they talked.
165.ch: Vocalese and Lambert, Hendricks and Ross
165.q: Absolutely. It always works. When I was in the Army, we were 18 miles from the front – I’ve got to go back to the Army now.

64.t: Avoiding the draft, 4F status and a War Department job
64.s: Declared 4F with exhaustion and a lung spot, he rested and worked at the War Department in Washington instead of entering the Army.
64.q: Because I was in school. If you were in school they didn’t draft you. When I got out of school, you know I was vulnerable. So consequently as soon as I got out of school I didn’t some to New York because I didn’t want to come to New York and have to leave. So I said I will wait until I am drafted…

64.t: How the war changed Washington's music scene
64.s: With good musicians drafted, itinerants and amateurs filled the scene, hotels opened to Black players, and Southwest clubs were run down.
64.q: Almost everybody who was a good musician was drafted so the music scene was filled with women and people who were itinerate. I remember guys like Fats Wright a very fine pianist from Philadelphia who influenced Bud Pal and a lot of other folks, came down. Fats Wright was there for a while. Ernie,…

64.t: Black patriotism and treatment of returning soldiers
64.s: Taylor describes the patriotism of Black communities and the irony of soldiers returning to segregation while German prisoners were served.
64.q: Well everyone in Washington, and I can only speak for Washington and the communities that I grew up in, in Petersburg and in Washington we were, America was our country. You were as patriotic as anyone perhaps more patriotic because you

88.t: Lester's army trouble and his white wife Mary
88.s: Lee says Lester's commanding officer was right that the wife in the locker photo was white, and that Lester could not adjust to orders.
88.q: Well, the commanding officer was right. She was a white woman. You know, she was not a light skinned black woman; she was a white woman. Her name was Mary, and they'd been married for several years ... several years, and I heard the story, but you also have to remember about Lester, as I told you,…

88.t: Lee's view of Lester's induction and the army's posting of black soldiers
88.s: Lee thinks Lester should have gone to a band like Great Lakes, recalls him jumping the wall at Fort MacArthur, and says black soldiers were shipped south.
88.q: if I had not been rejected, I was on my way to Great Lakes. But when I was to be examined, I had requested that that was the band I wanted to go in, because that was Snooky Young, and there was Gerald Wilson, and there was Willie Smith, you know, and Jimmy the trumpet player ... good trumpet…

88.s: Lee rejects the view that the army permanently broke Lester, saying the effect lasted a year or two.
88.q: No, I don't really think that's true. No. I don't really think that's true. He wasn't a person that I found was really vindictive; he didn't carry hate around with him, and if he did -- if he did, his music wouldn't be the way it came out. I don't think that you can play so beautifully and then…

166.t: Lester Young: his humor, Prez and Lady Day, and how the Army changed him
166.s: Lester was funny without trying; the Army and gin left him nervous and paranoid.
166.ch: Clarifications and portraits: Lester Young, Byas, Blanton, Ben Webster
166.q: No, just him. Like he -- during he and Billie Holiday's association on records, she named him Prez and he named her Lady Day. And he didn't know how, he wasn't aggressive enough to get a girl. So Billie Holiday would have to go out and get a girl for him, you know. But later on he came out of that…

166.t: Jo Jones's idiosyncrasies and the Army
166.s: Jo Jones had been in mental institutions and came out of the service rattled.
166.ch: Clarifications and portraits: Lester Young, Byas, Blanton, Ben Webster
166.q: Well, he came out -- he come out rattled. He was real nervous. But Jo Jones, like, I don't know that people was aware of this. But the first time that I saw him, I couldn't stand him because he was with -- this was the night that I left home -- hoboed out here. I saw him that night. He would lift…

166.t: Macon: the Krupa trumpeter beaten by military police for speaking to Simmons and Sid
166.s: A white soldier-trumpeter coming to see Simmons and Sid was beaten by police and MPs; years later he explains how it ended.
166.ch: With Benny Goodman and Louis Armstrong
166.q: All right, we had a -- I hate this, why can't you just say people, instead of Caucasian or white or colored or black? We had an audience in the balcony and it was a black dance, so you know who the audience was, right? But if it

167.t: The group breaks up and the draft board turns him away
167.s: The Spirits broke up out west, and the Army gave him an induction physical but never inducted him.
167.ch: Moving to California and the war years
167.q: Uh-uh. They had me -- you know, had me sell all my clothes and get ready for it, but they never called

167.t: Leading the Teddy Bunn Group; Leonard Feather
167.s: During the war years he had his own group, and Leonard Feather looked him up for pickup record dates.
167.ch: Moving to California and the war years
167.q: Well, He is. Because if he knew me when I was over there in Europe, you know, and he'd been collecting my records by that time, you know he's old.

167.t: Rejected by the draft; bebop musicians dodging; working for Red Callender
167.s: He was called, tested and rejected by letter; they discuss bebop musicians feigning craziness, and he worked with bassist Red Callender in L.A. toward the war's end.
167.q: Yeah, they called me, but I got out of it. I went down and took my test and everything else. That morning I had to go down to report, to get my suit on. I got a letter that morning. Rejection. So --

90.s: After a party at Al McKibbon's he is examined for the draft and rejected because of his broken arm; also luck at dice.
90.ch: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
90.q: But I want to tell you something that happened before that. I was drafted also. I had turned eighteen, and the draft was on. And I was drafted... So the night that I had to go to the induction center for my examination, the night before rather, they had a big party for me, a going-away party up at…

90.t: Leading a band in Alexandria, Louisiana
90.s: After the funeral he joins a group playing Alexandria near Camp Polk, is voted leader, and meets Lips Rose again.
90.ch: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
90.q: : So anyway, I got back to gigging around Detroit. And before long, my grandmother passed, and I went back to the funeral. And while I was there, some friends of mine that I had played with, one in particular that I didn't mention, who had played with the Doc Palmer Orchestra, the first orchestra I…

90.s: On the night of Pearl Harbor he was playing a female-impersonator floor show at Enrico's, and he also did taxi dances.
90.q: I'll never forget December the seventh, the night that the Japanese had bombed Pearl Harbor. I was working at a place called Enrico's over on Rivard(?) and Watson. And people came running in the place, shouting 'We're at war! We're at war! We're at war!' I never thought of anything like that, you…

168.t: Slim drafted; Stewart joins Art Tatum in late 1941
168.s: After Slim was inducted, Stewart, passed over by the draft, joined Art Tatum in Los Angeles in late 1941, staying on and off for several years.
168.ch: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
168.q: I met him out there. I had met him first in New York, but then that's where I joined Art Tatum.

168.t: Irony of Black musicians being drafted for a segregated country
168.s: Crouch asks about the irony of Black musicians fighting without full rights; Stewart says it was seldom discussed and calls the war sad.
168.ch: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
168.q: Well, not offhand. Of course, my buddy Slim, he mentioned it a few times after he came out of the service, you know. But I might say that on the other hand, the guys didn't talk too much about it, you know. It's just one of those things that they had to do and that was about it. It was a sad thing,…

168.t: The war years: 52nd Street and musicians talking about the war
168.s: Stewart remembers 52nd Street and the whole country hungry for jazz in 1941-45; musicians discussed the war and Slim was drafted.
168.ch: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
168.q: '41 and '45. Well, like, if I remember, I spent a lot of time on 52nd Street and somehow, well, 52nd Street was the most prominent thing in my memory. The activity in music was terrific, you know. 52nd Street was really jumping; and, of course, when I traveled with my own group and with Art Tatum…

169.s: Called up while with Barnet at the Capitol Theatre, he tells the draft psychiatrist he would not fight and is rejected.
169.ch: Hampton, Andy Kirk and Charlie Barnet
169.q: : Yeah, '41, '42, it was pretty rough. Like, we were at here the Capitol Theatre, I think at one time, and they called me up for the induction meeting to the Army and shit, and I told them, "I ain't fighting for nobody. Are you kidding me? I must be crazy." But they told me, "Well, either you fight…

169.t: The USO tour band and the trip to Japan
169.s: Oscar Pettiford organizes a six-piece USO band with J.J. Johnson, Skeeter Best and Rudy Williams; they play radar camps and travel to Japan then Korea.
169.q: : Yeah. Well, Oscar had met this doctor from Orange, New Jersey or somewhere, and they had talked him into getting a six-piece group together so that we could play the USO camps -- which he did. We all got together. First we had Budd Johnson on tenor, and then we switched over and got Rudy…

169.t: Korea: bad food and a narrow escape from K-5
169.s: They play near the front; the camp they left is wiped out the next day.
169.q: First we went to Tokyo, and we stayed there until we got our shots and so forth. Then we went to Taegu, and we stayed there for two or three days, and played for the bases there, all the different setups they had there. So we played for that. Then we went up North to Korea, which was horrible. Boy,…

170.t: Marriage, Grand Rapids and a WPA band
170.s: Ware marries, stays in Grand Rapids, and plays in a WPA band at Fort Custer until the draft breaks it up.
170.ch: Flip Benson, Grand Rapids and the Army
170.q: Well, we were playing -- this is 1941 -- the war had broken out, and so I got married, and Flip was going out to the west coast, and I didn't want to leave my wife, so some musicians around Grand Rapids said, "Well, maybe we can get you in one of the WPA bands here" -- so I put in for it, and they…

170.t: Jimmy Baker's band and the nine-month job in Port Huron
170.s: Ware plays a monotonous nine-month job with Jimmy Baker and Emmett Spicer until his draft papers arrive.
170.ch: Flip Benson, Grand Rapids and the Army
170.q: I ran in to another fellow -- at least there was a fellow who come through there looking for me; they had heard about me - Jimmy Baker. He had a 6 piece band. And this was in '42. We went up to Mirinit and Minominee, Wisconsin, for a summer job, and it was a tenor, trumpet, bass, drums and piano,…

170.t: Army Air Force service and first meeting with bebop
170.s: Ware serves as a combat engineer from 1943 to 1946, avoids the base band, goes to the Pacific, and meets musicians who play the new music.
170.ch: Flip Benson, Grand Rapids and the Army
170.q: Well, when we went through our basic, we had 45 musicians and I didn't read, so I wasn't even apt to get in the army band or the post band or anything like that. But all these musicians -- they were just making up battalions; like I said, we were in the Army Air Force, and they made us engineers;…

73.t: Earl Warren's absence and the new trumpets
73.s: They trace Earl Warren, Snooky Young, J. J. Johnson and others, and wonder when the draft ended.
73.q: Yeah. No. He didn't work for anybody else.

73.t: Jo Jones and Lester Young drafted
73.s: They recall that Jo and Lester went into the Army, which hurt the band; Shadow Wilson took over.
73.q: Yeah. But, the only one I could think of after Jo, would be Shadow.

73.t: When Lester left and whether he returned
73.s: They sort out dates for Lester's leaving, the Kansas City Five records and his Army service.
73.q: Right. Right. That's what happened. That's why Paul was there. Because Lester left -- it was a quick thing. But, as far as Lester coming back --

171.t: McShann's induction and the Amarillo dance
171.s: McShann played one night at the Plantation Club before the Army; Ramey took the band back, giving their own dance in Amarillo.
171.ch: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
171.q: was something like that. Anyway, there was no case of -- Johnny had to pay $25 each for them. But we got to Los Angeles and it was there that McShann joined us. And we played the Plantation Club and then McShann had to go back to the Army. Now, he's inducted into the Army.

171.t: The band collapses after McShann is drafted
171.s: When Ramey refused the Brown plan, the band folded; Gus Johnson entered service in November 1943.
171.ch: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
171.q: Well, I understand six men got to Cincinnati, no music or nothing, you know. And that's the last I -- that you can say that happened to that band. But by that time McShann didn't hardly -- they only had Schoolboy and John Jackson of the -- of the what's his name in -- Kansas City musicians in the…

171.t: Lester Young's army abuse and its effect on his playing
171.s: Prez told Ramey that guards used his head for target practice in the disciplinary barracks, which changed his style and led to 'D.B. Blues'.
171.ch: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
171.q: know, he was married to a white girl. Her name was Mary. And when they put him in the service, I guess it just -- the desire to see her or something. They put him down in some Southern town. I think it was Alabama somewhere. And he sent for her.

172.t: Baby Dodds tape, Ridgley's brothers and Celestin's age
172.s: A Baby Dodds tape is mentioned, Ridgley's brothers were Spanish-American War musicians, and Celestin turns out to be older than Ridgley.
172.q: No, no. No, no. No, no. I never did. Was Celestan as old as you or not? Well, you know, in the beginning I thought he was, but when he died he wasn't. I see.

172.t: His brothers who played in the Spanish-American War bands
172.s: Two older brothers played baritone and alto in the U.S. band.
172.q: One, Manier Richley, that's my brother, and my other was U-S-A-M, U-S-A-M. I like my daddy. See? He played baritone. He was pretty good baritone. But there wasn't nothing in it much for dancing. They didn't make that. So they didn't.

173.t: When he stopped playing and World War I send-offs
173.s: He quit playing before 1920, and no band sent off soldiers to the war.
173.q: No. They used to load them on ships. You understand? Yes. But they never made nothing of it because I don't think there was enough of New Orleans boys would go on that ship. You understand? I guess if there was a thousand or maybe five hundred boys from New Orleans was going on that ship to go…

173.t: Flag raisings after the Spanish-American War
173.s: Barber Johnny Hummel hires him and others to play at a flag raising. The craze spreads and they play free for friends.
173.q: There was, one woman see the other with her hair cut off, she's gonna get her damn hair cut off, and that's the way it was with that flag raisin then.

20.t: Few Clothes' place, the draft, and joining Jack Carey's band
20.s: Working in the district, Lee is chased out for lacking a draft registration card and joins Jack Carey's band with Edmund Hall.
20.q: George Few Clothes Place. So Buddy Petit had joined the tuxedo band with Celestan, then went out to the suburban garden. So I goes out to George Few Clothes in the district and work for, and work where Buddy Petit was playing with Jimmy Noon and that bunch. So, that time, there was coming drafting…

20.t: Buddy Petit, the Decatur Street job, Sidney Arodin and wartime
20.s: Lee praises Buddy Petit's playing, describes a mixed band on Decatur Street with Sidney Arodin and Lazy River, and why he avoided shipyard work in the war.
20.q: I couldn't tell the difference between him and Buddy, him and Bunk. Buddy Petit was the corner player that really knocked me out. He really, he really, none of our comments playing like between Buddy and Bunk. Buddy Petit was the corner player that had a great big tune and a beautiful soul. And he…

174.t: Claiborne Williams band and George Williams, a Navy bandmate
174.s: He praises George Williams, a first-class musician now teaching in Baton Rouge whom he saw at a parade, and mentions other Navy colleagues.
174.q: Very, very first class musician. And he's back in, up in Baton Rouge. He's teaching, yeah. My wife teaches school. I think he's teaching music at some school, I think. I'm not sure, but I don't know. He's also selling instruments and everything. Yeah. We played, he was standing on the corner of…

174.t: Three years in the Navy band and the Army band afterward
174.s: Dejan served three years and three months in the Navy, then joined an Army band at Camp Plauche; he compares it unfavorably to the Navy band, and tells of the first Christmas Eve party.
174.q: Well, I was in there for three years and three months. Three years and three months. Right across there. We stayed in boot camp for 16 weeks, but we can't have the rest of the time.

175.t: Lessons for a quarter and the post office band
175.s: Lessons cost 25 cents; he played in the post office brass band, rehearsed twice a week, and mentions service years.
175.q: That's right. But under Professor Chalini I enjoyed my music very much. As a matter of fact I didn't get as much out of it as I should have or I could have because at that particular time, being the youngster you know you always come home from school, throw your books on the couch or the machine…

175.t: Regrets about quitting music after the Army
175.s: After four years in a service band and marriage, he took a steady job in Chicago and stopped playing, wishing to return.
175.q: Well the only thing about my, I just was sorry that I just stopped playing, period. Because I don't think there's anything else that I would rather do than play.

176.t: Pensacola station, Mariana, and the Bunky club job
176.s: They place Pensacola and Mariana and recall working at Bunky's nightclub out on Highway 71, around the late 1940s into the Korean War period.
176.q: When you had a hemorrhage. Mm-hmm. You remember now? We, we, let's see, must have been around about, we've been around about 40, 45, something like that. Right, 45, 46, something like that.

176.t: 24 years at Luchenbach's and going to Bunkie in the war
176.s: Billie says she stayed at Luchenbach's about 24 years and went to Bunkie during the war.
176.q: I seen one of my club play time post the card the other day. Let me see if I can find that card. I had a other job cleaning up my shipping room.

177.t: Grandfather Napoleon Giles, Civil War drummer
177.s: Giles knows little of his grandfather Napoleon, a drummer in the Civil War, probably with the Union side; no dance music that he knows of.
177.q: Well my grandfather, he was a drummer in the Civil War. I don't know too much about him. I mean I remember him but so far as to sit down and talk with him, I don't know too much about speaking. Sure I understand. I heard that he was a drummer in the old Civil War. Would that have been with the

177.t: Who he played with around World War II
177.s: Jiles gives the order: Rene Parker, then Toker, then Albert Burbank around the war years.
177.q: Well, we played Artie Mellenburg, for Alec Baradot. I can't recall the name of the place. Was that Mellenburg? Alec Baradot.

178.t: Pearl Harbor and war-time playing at army posts
178.s: He recalls the WPA band at Jackson Barracks on Pearl Harbor Sunday and playing for soldiers and USO shows; he is not a sports fan.
178.q: I can tell you that I know that good as a book. We were playing at Jackson Barracks when I was in the WPA band. And you should have seen those soldiers' face how they changed because all of a while it was just draft. But then the country went into war then. Yeah, I was at WPA band. I was on a…

178.t: Where Dick Allen first heard him; Allen's Georgia roots and army years
178.s: Allen says he heard the band at Haydell's about 1950-51; talk drifts to Allen's Georgia hometown and where Ferbos and Dejan were stationed.
178.q: I was down here. Because I went to Washington, my son was at that edgewood, right outside of Baltimore,

179.t: Brothers and others in the Navy band during World War II
179.s: Bocage's brothers and many New Orleans players in the Navy band, such as Tats, Gilbert Young, Herbert Leary and Frank Fields, who visited his house daily.
179.q: Frank plays in your band. Well, Frank Fields was, uh... Get-off player when he went in the Navy, but after he got in there, he started playing bass tuba. See, and that from bass tuba, then he got on the string bass. All them fellas used to be by my house every day when they was at the... when they…

179.t: George Williams, Barney Gilbert and other Navy bandsmen
179.s: More Navy band members: George Williams, Barney Gilbert, Herbert Leary; what they played; most were from New Orleans.
179.q: from, uh... Yeah, George Williams. He come from Downersonville. George was, uh... George was, uh... head, uh... band man down there.

180.t: Called up in 1941 and taking his trumpet to the reception center
180.s: Back at the dance hall, drafted, and playing trumpet on the train and at the reception center.
180.q: And then, 41, I went back to work a few weeks, a few months or so, at the foreign dance hall, the same dance hall, see. Well, then Uncle Sam called me there, and I had to go in army. Well, after Uncle Sam called me in army, I went in army. I took my trumpet with me when I got in army. A lot of…

180.t: Army band at Eglin Field, special service and the replacement trumpet
180.s: Forming a band at Eglin Field, the engineer's fight song, special service in Virginia and the lieutenants buying him a trumpet.
180.q: Yes sir. So I'm coming to that now. So I left, I mean after these fellas, they took me and put me on KP one day, see, in the army, well every now and then I used to blow a tune, see, well they put me on KP. And the major, and then we missed the trumpet, he said, why is that fella playing that…

181.t: Military drill groups, brooms and gold-headed canes
181.s: Interviewer asks about rifle companies, broom and dumbbell brigades and gold-headed canes; Parker remembers none.

181.t: Mac's railroad work as a cook
181.s: Mac, Parker's neighbour, explains railroad tracks and tells how he became a railroad cook in World War II.
181.ch: Mac, railroads and the second line
181.q: No it wouldn't be because the tires are buried under the ground. It's leveled. The rail, they have to change the rail but they have to dig all that up and then they bury the tire back down.

182.t: Spanish-American War: troops leaving and the colored bands
182.s: Tom remembers at about 16 watching soldiers march to the ship, the colored brass band, light-skinned Creole musicians in white bands, old man Ulec's big band and Fess's brother John.
182.ch: Early bands and the city, c. 1898-1900s
182.q: Would it be a brass band? They had a brass band, but I didn't know who that band was. Led them from the, from the City Park I think it was. And led them to, they come on Espanade Street, but right on the wall there. It was 30th Street Ferry, and on the side they had a wall there and that's why the…

182.t: World War I draft and the armistice
182.s: Tom describes registering at 45, hearing the boats blow at peace, and the interviewer's chat about Johnny Gould and the Charles Street music shop.
182.q: No, the boats was blowing there. All the ships. There had plenty of ships in there and all the ships blowing. That should have been a big party then. Oh yeah, yeah. We was in the bed. I was in the bed. I listened to them. I said, I'm all right now. And they said, I don't listen no more. I was…

183.t: Induction into the Army and a year at home after discharge

212.q: Yeah they had a music program but they threw me out of it after about six months. There’s a whole story about how that happened and a weird teacher I had who really disliked me a lot, but not more than I disliked him.

212.t: Racism in the Navy: barred from Iceland
212.s: Service officially desegregated, but black sailors were kept off the ship in Iceland; his protest nearly got him in the brig.
212.q: Yeah. But they had their ways of getting a message across. For instance we couldn’t go to Iceland. We did a North Atlantic cruise and we went to Oslo and Kiel, Germany and Southampton in England, Rotterdam. And we were scheduled to go to Iceland at the end and they wouldn’t let the black sailors…

213.t: Army, Columbia, The Record Changer and meeting Monk at Alfred Lion's
213.s: After the Army he returned to Columbia, edited The Record Changer with Bill Grauer, and met Monk at the Lions' home.
213.ch: Monk, the Army and learning the job
213.q: Fine. Okay. The world has gone on to other forms of waylaying people. I mean I’m not old enough to have been around when the press gangs were kidnapping sailors and putting them on ships in the harbor, but this is almost it. But no the point is so what I’m saying is it’s a combination of a certain…

213.s: He describes night incendiary raids on Japan, flying over burned Tokyo, and his view of the bomb.
213.ch: Monk, the Army and learning the job
213.q: I was on Guam. I was a navigator radar operator on B-29s. I did a lot of dropping of bombs on Japan, which I’m resolutely not proud of for the rest of my life, so—

214.t: Avoiding the draft, Frankie Carle's band and induction
214.s: City College study delayed the draft; after the Kenton offer fell through he joined Frankie Carle, then was inducted in 1957.
214.ch: Early road bands and the Army
214.q: Well there was a three-month tour with that band to mostly the southwest. And I went on that tour and we were playing Texas A&M and a cadet came up with a note from my parents and it said, “Lanny call home regarding induction notice.”

214.t: Seventh Army Symphony and jazz band in Germany
214.s: In Germany he played in the Army symphony and an 18-piece jazz band with Eddie Harris, Don Ellis and Cedar Walton.
214.ch: Early road bands and the Army
214.q: they call them in Germany, and then we had a jazz show, an 18-piece jazz band that did six months over there. And I couldn’t have been any more fortunate. Along with myself it was Eddie Harris and Leo Wright and Don Ellis and Cedar Walton. So it was really playing with good musicians and also the…

215.t: Joining Vaughn Monroe at 17 before the draft
215.s: He joined Monroe in 1943, was drafted in April 1944, and got his job back after two years of service.
215.ch: Vaughn Monroe band and the army
215.q: Oh yeah. I was just 17, I just got out of high school and I was about to be drafted as soon as I turned 18, you know they were taking them right after 18. You were in the Army in two weeks.

215.t: Army service in Manila and listening to V-discs
215.s: He did little but play basketball and music in Manila, and heard Nat King Cole and big bands on V-discs.
215.ch: Vaughn Monroe band and the army
215.q: I was a PFC, I did nothing but shoot baskets. We had nothing to do. The war was over. We were sitting around Manila doing nothing.

216.t: Draft notice and winning a spot in the West Point band
216.s: Finishing his master's at Michigan State, he got his draft notice and auditioned for the West Point band, then studied with Russianoff and Regni.
216.q: Yeah well actually I was a little older than that because I think that was — I went in the Army in 1967. And I was there for three years, ’67 to ’70. But yeah, I was going to get drafted. And I already had, well I was finishing up my master’s degree at Michigan State and was getting ready to get…

216.t: Mustaches as protest at West Point
216.s: Band members grew mustaches as a small protest against Vietnam and the draft until a surprise inspection.
216.q: Yeah we did. You’ve got to remember, in that era, you know that many young people did not think it was a good thing what we were doing in Vietnam. And also it was the idea of the draft and there was a lot going on and a lot of protests and marches and all kinds of stuff. And we kind of felt a…

217.t: About three months with Teagarden, then the Army
217.s: Drafted into the infantry, he played glockenspiel in the 104th Division band for about two and a half years, then was discharged at Camp Carson.
217.q: Well I tried to get in the band. But they needed cannon fodder. They put me in the infantry. And I went through basic training and then I ended up in the 104th Division and I got in a band with the 104th Division. I was playing glockenspiel in the marching band.

217.t: First job back in East St. Louis at Bowman's
217.s: After discharge he took the train to St. Louis and played piano at Bowman's restaurant.
217.q: I got out of the Army and let’s see, I was down in the Mojave Desert on maneuvers. I ended up in Colorado Springs at the Camp Carson. And that’s where I got my discharge. And I took the train back to St. Louis from Colorado Springs, and my first job was in East St. Louis at a place called Bowman’s.…

218.t: Hospital stay and conducting an Army swing unit in Germany
218.s: After an injury he ended up conducting another band in Germany, turning a military unit into a swing band and show.
218.q: Ouch is right. But that caused me to have damaging results down there. And these guys found me in this hospital and they transported me to the band that was supposed to get me, but that band was leaving to go to the United States. This was in Germany. And this band was going home. But I didn’t want…

218.t: Segregation in the service and thoughts on civil rights
218.s: The Army was segregated; he reflects that civil rights change cost black jobs and that time would have solved it.
218.q: Definitely at the time I was in it was segregated. But I didn’t know it. I mean to me I had always lived like this. But I lived in the ghetto neighborhood, I didn’t realize anything then. I don’t know where my mind was. None of this bothered me.

219.t: Combat engineers, playing for officers, V-disks and the end of the war
219.s: Wein enters the Army in January 1944, avoids combat, plays officers' dances, finds V-disks in England and weeps with relief at the atomic bomb.
219.q: Sometimes you did, yeah. Because the war had started and there were a lot of sailors and they would get drunk and the SPs and the MPs would come in there. I remember once they hit a guy over the head and the blood spurted up to the ceiling. But this wasn’t the way I made my living, I was still a…

219.t: What the Army taught him; music wherever he went
219.s: The Army made him stand on his own; musicians in every camp and on the troopship kept him going.
219.q: Oh everybody did. But the thing I learned in the Army that was, hey, you were only yourself. You were not Dr. Wein’s son. You were not a nice Jewish kid from a middle class family. Economics, background, nothing meant anything except you, yourself. And you had to compete with the other guy. Now the…

220.t: Early arranging and touring with Josephine Baker
220.s: Wess recalls first arrangements in 1940 and his Army band, which toured North Africa with Josephine Baker.
220.q: Yeah. Well I’ve been writing. I think I did my first commercial arrangement in 1940 I think, for the old entertainer, I don’t know, you probably never heard of Fifi D’Orsay from Canada. I did an arrangement on “Alouette” for her. Years, years, years ago. And I did a couple of things while I was…

220.s: The band had special authorization and recruited professional musicians exempt from basic training.
220.q: Well we had a big band. We had special authorization for 55 pieces, and the Army band was only 28. But our band leader was a friend of President Roosevelt’s. So we had special authorization and he used to recruit professional musicians who were on the road and about to be drafted. And he had a deal…

221.t: Merchant Marine service and the Murmansk run
221.s: He served two or three years, carrying ammunition before America declared war, and later received veteran status.
221.q: Well actually we were in the war before America declared war. We were, they was keeping it quiet, but we were actually making the Murmansk run for the Ammunition Department, by way of, via Calcutta. And the public, America didn’t know it. Nobody knew it.

221.s: While in service he walked up and sang with a group in Calcutta, singing blues like Wynonie Harris; Teddy had been there with Buck Clayton.
221.q: I was trying to sing like the Ink Spots then. But that night I sang like Wynonie Harris. blues.

222.t: High school jazz combo during the war
222.s: Only in senior year did he play, in a student combo at variety shows and veterans' hospitals in 1945.
222.ch: Growing up in the Bay Area
222.q: But I didn’t play drums in high school because there was no orchestra. There was just a marching band for the football games and so forth. So I didn’t play anything in high school except maybe in my senior year some of the students organized a little jazz combo and they were searching frantically…

222.t: College years: too young for the draft, drums again, jazz department
222.s: He graduated at 16, skipped the draft, played percussion in the college bands, and students organized jazz study.
222.ch: Growing up in the Bay Area
222.q: No. No I didn’t. I graduated from high school when I was 16 so actually I was too young for military service for World War II. I went to college and played drums again in college.

1.t: Cab Jivers, the draft call and the band's missing heartbeat
1.s: Barker was expected to play rhythm only, played in the Cab Jivers, and when called for induction found the band raggedy without him.
1.q: at him, how he begged for his job after telling me he can’t respect nobody that can’t play no . . . Cab wasn’t going to let me play no solos. You understand? Even if I could play.

1.t: Russell Smith, the trumpeter, and the Veterans Association's help
1.s: Milt tells how Russell Smith, a veteran of Jim Europe's band, was thrown out by his wife and the Veterans Association got him half of the house; Danny praises him.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: He and I were kind of tight. He always kept his little bottle with him. Always sharp. Always got a good word. Always clean. Helluva trumpet player. He played that horn til the ....(?)., right with them young cats that's blowin'. And it was a pleasure; a pleasure to know the man.

223.t: V-12 program, Great Lakes boot camp and the USS Pasadena
223.s: He enters the Navy officer program at Boulder, flunks out, goes through boot camp and serves on the cruiser Pasadena, where he plays in a poor ship band.
223.q: Exile, yeah. To be away from L.A., where I thought everything was happening, to be exiled to Boulder, Colorado, was just terrible. I always had that in the back of my head, and it kept me from having more fun there. But it was pleasant. I did well. I was studying mechanical engineering and a few…

223.t: Navy contemporaries: Duane Tatro and length of service
223.s: He recalls Duane Tatro and a future Kenton bass trombonist from the Great Lakes band and confirms about two years of service.
223.q: When I was in boot camp, there was another tenor player. I tried out for the band when I was in boot camp. The Great Lakes Naval Station had an official jazz band. I tried out for it and didn‟t make it. The guy that was there, his name was Duane Tatro. Later on he became a composer and he wrote a…

224.s: Douglas, a music student, came back from Europe a nervous wreck; Vin was also drafted.
224.q: Yeah. But even before that, he studied. He went in the Army. The Army tore him up. When he came out of the Army, he was no good. He still went to school.

224.t: How Haynes stayed out of the Army
224.s: He claimed an ulcer to be rejected, was rejected again during Korea, and was teased as Sergeant Roy Haynes on the radio.
224.q: Oh, good question. I love that. I learned how to stay out and was proud of it. There was another musician – because I was getting pretty popular around Boston. A lot of bands would come from New York. If they needed a drummer, at one period I was usually the drummer that they would get. They had a…

225.t: How World War II affected the band
225.s: Johnson says the war affected all music and travel but cannot say how, and Carter had no personnel problems.
225.q: Lida, I believe that the war and the whole world climate, if you will, was [affected]. [It] affected all phases of life including music, including jazz, and including – how could it not? It was such an important part of history and it had such a dramatic impact on our lives, on our psyche, and on…

225.t: Overseas with Oscar Pettiford's quintet entertaining troops
225.s: The Korean War quintet with Pettiford, Rudy Williams, Howard McGhee and Keeter Betts, and Pettiford's temper.
225.ch: Jazz at the Philharmonic and Count Basie
225.q: The answer to that question, Lida, is intertwined with the answer to the question of what year was it that I went overseas with Oscar Pettiford and a quintet to entertain servicemen in the Korean Conflict. We did so. Oscar Pettiford was the leader of this group, and it included Rudy Williams on…

226.t: Rejected by the Signal Corps, then rejected at induction
226.s: He was turned down for the Signal Corps because he was black, and at induction in 1945 said he would kill a top officer and was rejected.
226.q: I was called up for the draft. Actually, I tried to enlist, because I was thinking in terms of what I would do – always, everything I did, really, if you look at my whole history, everything that I tried to do was in terms of thinking what this would do, or what I could do to maintain a decent…

226.t: World War I as a child and the 1919 Chicago race riot
226.s: He knew of the war only from a soldier-suit photograph; during the 1919 riot his father and uncle stayed home and the family stayed in the neighborhood.
226.q: No. I think you mentioned that to me when we were talking before. I was aware of it, because I remember having a picture taken with me with a soldier suit on – with a little suit outfit with the soldier’s hat and all of that. Most kids maybe were Scouts or something, but I had this picture of…

227.s: Mandel says the draft board lost his registration and he never heard from them again.
227.ch: Venuti, Billie Rogers and Henry Jerome
227.q: Yep. They lost it, I wish we lived in that, well, you say you wish you lived in that pre­ computer age now, something like that, they can still lose stuff on computers but then they really lost it, ‘cause I was sweating it out. I just never heard from them again after I registered.

227.t: Straight onto the road with Venuti and the wartime generation
227.s: Right out of high school Mandel joins Joe Venuti because musicians are scarce in wartime, and talks about Al Cohn, Getz and Zoot Sims coming up young into bands.
227.ch: Venuti, Billie Rogers and Henry Jerome
227.q: No, I didn’t I went right on the road with bands, I went with Joe Venuti, immediately when I got out of high school I was with Joe Venuti, I mean immediately.

228.t: Fascination with Hitler and the Second World War
228.s: McLean describes Hitler's charisma, the Nuremberg rallies, Skorzeny's rescue of Mussolini and German jet technology.
228.ch: Copenhagen recordings, interests and views on the music
228.q: Yeah man, they sent for him. He came in. He said, I want to find the Duce. Find him, and find a way to get him here, get him out of there. So he posed as a champagne salesman, took a couple of his men with him and went down and hung around down in Italy, trying to find out where they were keeping…

228.t: Memories of the Depression and World War II
228.s: He had no sense of the Depression as a toddler and remembers wartime cartoons of Hitler at age eleven.
228.ch: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
228.q: No, not at all. I used to be up and down 135th Street, but I had no realization of it being a depression or anything, because I was a little baby boy at that point. I had my area that I could play in, because my godfather, Norman Cobbs, lived in the Y. We lived, my mother – the first place we…

229.t: Pearl Harbor, driving a cab and the crossing home
229.s: After the Pearl Harbor attack he drives a cab, then returns in June 1942 on an Army transport, and briefly tries Chicago.
229.ch: Hampton band, Honolulu and the war years
229.q: In Hawaii. So they were told that they couldn't quit until the war was over, but I knew that they were freezing the jobs in

229.t: San Francisco, Carl Johnson's band and the shipyard
229.s: He returns to Los Angeles in October 1942, joins Carl Johnson, and is let go after falling asleep from shipyard work by day.
229.ch: Hampton band, Honolulu and the war years
229.q: No. I think I had about a half a dozen gigs. Finally I figured that wasn't the place for me and I ended up back in Los Angeles, in October, 1942.

230.t: Being inducted seven times and never serving
230.s: Barnet went through draft induction seven times in New York without ever being taken, which led him to disband his band and move to California.
230.q: Well, I don't know. They kept calling me back and calling me back, but they had me in various -- I was in 1-A three times, and on every occasion I was -- something happened. They changed the -- they said, "No, you shouldn't be in 1-A." You should be here or there, and then the last time the war got…

230.t: Strobe-light tricks, USO physicals and Buddy De Franco the gentleman
230.s: A USO doctor found the band members unfit; Barnet says De Franco was orderly, unlike others, and stayed until the draft-driven breakup.
230.ch: Sidemen, mixed bands, the Apollo and Lena Horne
230.q: Oh, we had a thing that we did in a strobe light, where we had some trick instruments that were painted with this substance that glows in the dark with a strobe light. Well, they would smear it on their nose and on their cheeks and they'd look like clowns up there, and everybody is laughing, you…

231.t: World War I: no war material in the act, and too young to enlist
231.s: He did not add war material to his act and was only 15 when the war was on; he says no one specific shaped his development.
231.ch: The 1920s road: dance style and management
231.q: Well, the gag that they used on little bits concerning the army. It wasn't going out doing an act concerning the army, the war or nothing like that. They'd do bits of the army that you wouldn't ordinarily do just dry long so. You got to build it like you build a sketch of anything. They do the…

231.t: Soldiers surround him at the bus
231.s: As the only black and only American entertainer in the show, he is confronted by soldiers until security and the bus driver come out.
231.ch: Germany, Buck's death and ideas about life
231.q: I'm the only American entertainer. I'm the only black in the show, in this show, this revue. For entertainment I'm the only black and the only American-speaking person in the crowd, too, there. You know, they all were German.

0.t: Hearing of Pearl Harbor in a Philadelphia hotel with Basie's men
0.s: Caldwell, Dickie Wells, Jimmy Rushing and Don Byas heard the news on the radio on an off Sunday.
0.ch: Philadelphia, Atlantic City and the war years
0.q: that they call (unintelligible). Basie was in Philadelphia at that particular time, and we were -- Dickie Wells and I went around to a place called the Pet Shop, where all the musicians and performers used to go and you could buy whiskey there, you know, under the table. So it was on a Sunday, and…

0.t: The 8th Illinois National Guard band at about sixteen
0.s: He joined the 370th Eighth Illinois Infantry National Guard band, stationed in Chicago, and got good reading and concert training.
0.ch: National Guard band and first jobs in Chicago
0.q: That was the 370th Eighth Illinois (unintelligible) infantry National Guard band. And some of us fellows. And Dornell Howard was in that band too.

232.t: Harold Iller, the white replacement for Luther West
232.s: Fields hires white Harold Iller from Minneapolis after Luther West is inducted, at the Happy Hour, from where he called Love.
232.ch: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
232.q: That was in the forties. Early forties. That was after we had been to New York and everything because we had good booking then, but I was getting enough money that I would travel on the train sometimes. It was World War II, the gas was rationed, so I know it was in the forties, and so I would…

232.t: Touring the northwest for Pops McElroy
232.s: During the war Goosby is in the Portland shipyards; Fields tours there under Pops McElroy's ballroom bookings.
232.ch: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
232.q: So anyway, as I said we played there several times, but then years passed and went on and we didn't hear anything about Enid because I just happened not to be in that area, but during World War II, a lot of the okies migrated to the coast, and Dewey happened to go into the shipyard of Portland.

233.t: Wartime foundry work and plans to buy a dump truck
233.s: Turned down for the army over his knees, Monk saved to start a trucking business, encouraged by a neighbor with a dump truck.
233.q: Well, it came later for me, so far as the music. I continued doing what I was doing. What I was doing, I was doing it very well but it didn't have the same meaning...it wasn't what life was about. I had strong thoughts at that time, really really strong thoughts of...Prior to that, to show you how…

233.t: Buddy back from the army playing piano
233.s: Buddy returned from Kansas City service in his late teens playing impressively.
233.q: Pretty much. I was amazed when he came back from the army playing the piano the way he was. Because he had time to come in. He had come home on a little furlough, because he was stationed down in...He didn't go overseas or anything. He was stationed in Kansas City. He'd come home, like for a…

234.t: Army band service playing bass drum
234.s: Gil says he tried to avoid overseas service and played bass drum in an Army band because the Army did not recognise his piano.
234.ch: First bands, Ennis, Thornhill and the Army
234.q: Tried to keep out of the most of (Army?) infantry, (LAUGHTER). I was in the you know, tried to keep from being shipped overseas at that time.

234.t: Jazz and fear of sexuality: a publisher's reaction in 1955; records in the Army
234.s: Gil says objections to jazz are a fear of sexuality. A publisher called his arrangement dirty in 1955, and soldiers objected to his records.
234.ch: Miles Davis stories and what jazz means
234.q: Sounds funny, but it's basically a fear of sexuality. All of it. I remember one time I took an arrangement up to a publisher ( for an album ?) called 'Easy Things to Remember'. Rodgers and Hart tune. 'Easy Things to Remember'. I had it written like this. (PLAYS PIANO). Kind of like this. (PLAYS…

235.t: Deciding to leave Earl Hines in wartime flux
235.s: He did a couple of dances with Hines in New York, and with musicians going into the service and bands in flux, took the chance to change.
235.q: : of things. I think they were dances, if I can remember. And, you know, it was during war time and there was transition and people would go in and out of different bands and nobody was really stable, you know what I mean. So, from what I understand, somebody was going in the service and whatnot…

235.t: Drafted at San Antonio and quickly released
235.s: Inducted with one eye, he sought special service but was let out after two or three months while stationed in San Antonio.
235.q: Well, I went in the service but but you see I only have one eye and so they took me in, but then I applied for a special service, you know what I mean, because I'm a musician and I didn't have any other skills, other than music. So they said

236.t: Woody Herman's band, the Army and returning to Woody
236.s: He quit Goodman for Woody Herman's cooperative band, was drafted for three years, and rejoined Woody on discharge until the band broke up.
236.ch: Goodman, Woody Herman and the Army
236.q: : And then I finally got a chance to go with Woody Herman, so I quit. And it was just like goin'...jumpin' into Heaven to go with Woody Herman. That's why ....(?). ... became one of my best friends. And Hazel Scott was the final on the stage. She had Big Sid Catlett; I got to know him when I was…

236.t: Army NCO club band; Dick Libertini; Bob Preston
236.s: He played at an Army NCO club and mentions Dick Libertini and Bob Preston.
236.q: That's where I met...there was this guy...he was on Broadway, a very talented guy. He's out in California now. I can't think of his name.

237.t: The invitation to play for President Truman
237.s: Presidential staff heard them at Milton's, a telegram summoned them to Washington, and the Statler held bourbon from the president.
237.ch: Learning drums and recording on the Coast
237.q: That's right, but the greatest deal was when we played for the president, and that was -- oh, man, that was something, boy. I thought the guys was joking. He had some of those little stenographers, photographers, all of them listening to us out at Milton's, you understand me, about six of them,…

237.t: Playing Truman's inauguration with Julia Lee
237.s: Lovett and Julia Lee were invited to Washington; Smith works out it was 1945 and that they were still together then.
237.q: Yeah, she started at the Cuban Room. That was before.

76.s: Zutty joined the Navy because he admired the clean-looking sailors; his mother had to sign and Marge says he also loved travel and adventure.
76.ch: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
76.q: She had to sign for him to go. She didn't want him to go, he wanted to go. He enlisted but, he was only seventeen years old. But he liked that idea of the uniforms and all that and the travel. To see, travel and......

76.t: Spoiled and free: his mother's attitude
76.s: His mother let him do what he wanted during the war; Marge says he was spoiled but carries no chip on his shoulder.
76.ch: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
76.q: Yes, see it didn't leave him with a bad taste in his mouth. I think that's why he's been so nice all through the years.

238.s: The group dated to early 1941 and worked in San Diego, where she was when Pearl Harbor was attacked.
238.ch: Four Chocolate Drops, San Diego and Club Royal
238.q: So it had to be around the early part, you know. The early part of '41, I imagine. Because we worked at Curran's and then we went to San Diego, and we worked at Curran's seemingly, and then we went back to San Diego, and then we came back to Curran's, I think, if I remember correctly. But anyway --

238.t: Commuting to San Diego and the Pearl Harbor blackout drive
238.s: She worked six days a week in San Diego, visiting her young son, and drove home in the blackout after refusing the owner's offer to stay.
238.ch: Four Chocolate Drops, San Diego and Club Royal
238.q: Yeah, and we were off on Monday, so we would leave San Diego, and this was before freeways, for folks that don't know anything about doing it the hard way. We used to have to leave San Diego -- we'd have to leave home, rather, like on Mondays, for instance, and we'd go back not on Monday, but…

239.t: Danny Williams's band goes to Kentucky State; Pearl Harbor ends it
239.s: After Fambro, Jones played with Danny Williams's band, taken to Kentucky State to bring in collegians; the war dissolved the program around 1941.
239.q: No, no, not at all. Because his music was -- it was the same thing, different. Completely different. He had another kind of an imagination, you know? Oh, getting back to him, what I -- I'm trying to pull these things together. Fambro and the other guys, after we'd been together for awhile, and then…

239.t: How the Stuff Smith Trio avoided the draft: Stuff's act and Jones's heart murmur
239.s: Stuff drank water and vomited on the psychiatrist's desk, John Levy feigned craziness, and Jones was rejected for his heart murmur.
239.ch: Stuff Smith stories, Wes Montgomery and singers
239.q: Oh, okay. Well, Stuff had -- well, he wasn't dangerously insane or anything like that, but he had just come out of -- Kankakee, Illinois, you know.

79.t: Will Vodery's attempt to launch a group; drafted
79.s: Will Vodery admired Babe's voice and Joe's trumpet and backed a group that played college dates until the draft for World War II interrupted.
79.ch: The 1940s: small groups, Teddy Wilson and Ethel Waters
79.q: Yeah, well, he loved Babe's voice and he was trying to set up some things, you know. So, we were introduced and he heard my trumpet playing and he liked my trumpet playing so we got something to go. He knew the people to talk to. So we tried. He had a couple of dollars so we tried.

79.t: Turning down a Coca-Cola overseas tour
79.s: Thomas, afraid of flying, planned to go by ship until Babe pointed out the ocean was mined, and he dropped out of the Coca-Cola overseas tour.
79.ch: The 1940s: small groups, Teddy Wilson and Ethel Waters
79.q: What happened, Eddie Condor, we had done some things at Town Hall, at Carnegie Hall, you know ... with the Coca-Cola people. And, what the hell, I needed the money. It sounds good. We had a good group of musicians there. I think it's going to be nice and quiet. She disrupted my idea altogether. ...…

240.t: Working on the SS President with Pierson and Paul Barbarin until the Army
240.s: He worked about two years on the boat under Eddie Pierson, then with Paul Barbarin until entering the Army in April 1941. He also once filled in on piano for John Handy.
240.q: And then Pierron gave it up and I think he went into his other little business or something and Paul Barberant took the band over. And I worked with Paul Barberant I'd say about two years or so, maybe more. But anyway I worked with Paul Barberant until I went right in the Army. That was in 41 in…

241.s: Russell had not known he played Bourbon Street; Valentine says it was before the war, when everything was cheap.
241.ch: Luck, tricks and the Bourbon Street job
241.q: Yeah that was before the war, that was before the war. Everything was really, you know what I mean, cheap then. Yeah. Yeah that was, you see that was after the first war, you see, after the first war, you see.

242.t: WPA dates and playing for servicemen at 1420 Canal Street
242.s: He clarifies he joined the WPA band around 1941-42, playing for sailors and soldiers at 1420 Canal Street during the war.
242.q: That's right, because we used to play for the sailors and the soldiers at 1420 Canal Street.

243.t: Three and a half years in the Navy band
243.s: Breaux says he was in the Navy for three and a half years in a band with Bill Humphrey and Clyde Kerr.
243.q: I was in the Navy for three and a half years. I was in the Sam band with Bill Humphrey and Clark Kerr, Magnus Kruster, we all was in the Sam Navy band together.

244.t: New Orleans musicians passing through the Bay Area
244.s: Few old friends came through, mostly Navy bands at Treasure Island during the war.
244.ch: Day jobs and Bay Area gigs
244.q: Not many really out here now that I grew up. There's one Tom Johnson. He's not playing anymore at the time. But he's out here. He came out here pretty. A lot of them came out with the bands, with the Navy band during the war. And they had a lot of New Orleans bands at the Treasure Island that came…

245.t: Army band in Kansas City and France under Amos White
245.s: He joined Amos White's army band in 1918 in Kansas City, went to France, and was switched to clarinet.
245.q: Yeah. And, uh, we had a 32, I think it was a 32 piece band. We formed a band in, in, uh, Kansas City, Missouri. And we went to Hoboken, New Jersey. We went over in, uh, England. See? We crossed the English Channel and went over in France. It was our Envoy Doon, Le Havre, and Paris, France, you…

246.t: Memories of the Civil War and Spanish-American War
246.s: Glass says he remembers the Civil War battle shooting around the French Quarter.
246.q: Do you remember the Spanish and American War? Yeah. Well, I remember the Civil War, too. What went on there? Shooting and gun on.

247.t: Gumbo band during the Spanish-American War and the Pickwick and Boston clubs
247.s: He joined an ear-playing band at about 27 or 28 around the Spanish-American War, called a gumbo band, and played the Pickwick and Boston clubs and with Charles Hippolyte and Piron.
247.q: Oh, you mean, how old you mean? Well, I was a young man. I was about... Let me see. Don't ask me a little bit. Well, I was quite blind, you know. I knew how to play bass, but they had a bass player. You know? Were you about 20 years old at this time? 30? Well, I'll tell you. What was the bass? 27,…

248.t: Drafted for the First World War and the night of dime banks
248.s: Dawson was drafted but a letter after the armistice said he was not qualified; on the eve of leaving he serenaded all night and spent his dimes.
248.q: I was drafted in that, uh, first, uh, that, uh, third world war, I think it was, uh, in 19... that was, that's before the war, war, war broke out in 19, 19, 1917. Uh-huh.

249.t: His first band and the draft
249.s: His first band included Copeland, Maurice Durand, Charlie Bernard and Joe Watson; he left for St. Louis and was drafted around 1916-17.
249.q: Yeah, the clarinet player was named, he died, too. And the bass, the banjo player was named Bernard, Charlie Bernard. Yeah. I can't think of the clarinet player name, good as I know him, too. All of them is dead, all of them. Maurice was living there. Yeah, Maurice. He was down there when Ricard…

250.t: Machine shop business and the Coast Guard in the war
250.s: The war draft pulled his business staff; he served in the Coast Guard, where he sat in with service bands but could not get in one.
250.ch: Bands and bandleading in New Orleans
250.q: That's about the time I left Joe's Inn and the war came on. Yeah. We had the little business and before you know it all of the personnel that actually ran the business was in A1 classification with the draft board. I was the last one so I got a little deformity until I got somebody broken in to run…

251.t: Picketing and integrating the Texas military bases
251.s: Albert says he walked picket lines at big stores and, using officer contacts, helped integrate bases through the Goodwill Society.
251.ch: Civil service, Keyhole club and civil rights
251.q: I was also responsible for integrating most of the bases because I fought the civil rights here. I picketed the Jaskis, walked the pickets, the biggest store in the state of Texas. The handy andy stores, the biggest chain stores in the state of Texas. I walked the picket line. What about all of…

252.t: Opening and the Spanish-American War song Over the Garden Wall
252.s: Allen opens the session at 1926 Harmony Street, 3 Sept 1960, and asks about the song Over the Garden Wall; Diggs sings it as a Spanish-American War song.
252.q: Yeah. Well, I'll tell you, it's been quite a while. Because I heard the last of it was in, when was I in Milwaukee, in 40-something. That was the last, but that was when during the Spanish-American War. Over the Golden Wall, the sweetest girl of all. I'll never forget the night we met over the…

253.t: Using a plastic reed during the war
253.s: Hall explains he switched to plastic reeds because cane reeds were hard to get and warped in wartime.
253.q: Well, I tell you the reason why I used a plastic reed is because I had to use it because during the war you couldn't get no reed. You see, you could buy a reed but you had to buy so many of them to get a good one. And those that you would get a regular reed, it was made so long that it was all…

254.s: They place Prohibition after World War I and recall everyone celebrating the armistice, with no work done at the Harrahan railroad.
254.ch: Reel 2: carnival, Prohibition, funerals and clubs
254.q: Got on that train that morning, got to the, out to the Harrahams and ready. Turn around, come on back. No, they didn't be there. Nobody worked that day.

255.s: As the tape runs out he mentions leading his own three-piece sax groups with vocals during the war.
255.q: Yeah, that's where we rehearsed, right there. Yeah, it's right there. Yeah, it's right there. There's only about another minute left down here, half a minute. Is there anything else? I think we've covered most of your life. Is there anything else you'd like to add? Well, I'll-

256.s: He marched through the district, recalls its closing, and again poses as a midget.
256.q: Yeah. And I went back there one night, and my mother beat the diggers at me. I used a pair of long pants, and that's what I said. That was when I started posing as a midget, you know, putting black marks on my hair, and my head looked like wrinkles. And the cop thought I was a schoolboy, and he…

257.t: Freddie Kohlman, Jack Willis and Sam Dutrey; the Omaha GI club
257.s: He has worked on and off with Freddie, Jack and Sam for over twenty years, from Robichaux days to a wartime little band in Omaha and Evansville.
257.q: Yeah. Well matter of fact, Freddie Coleman, Jack Willis, Sam Dutra, we've been working together off and on for about the last 23, 24 years.

258.t: Army base shows during the war
258.s: He played army bases for three months, flying from base to base, one night for officers and one for rookies.
258.q: Well during the war, political or, well, I would say this is military, I think. I played army bases three months. And we used to fly from base to base. We always stayed in one base two nights. First night for the officer we played and the next night was for the rookies. Next day we were flying out…

259.t: The Liberty Band at the time of World War I
259.s: Vincent says the first band he organized was the Liberty Band, around 1918, and tells how Maurice and others joined and the group changed.
259.ch: Liberty Band, marriage and the Depression
259.q: He said who was you playing with in World War One? World War One, that's when they had the Liberty Band. That's the first band I organized, you know, for the Liberty Band.

260.t: Moving to California, wartime service and the New Orleans reunion
260.s: Both men now live in California; Ray went into service for about three and a half years after the Crosby band broke up in 1942. They recall a riverboat reunion in New Orleans with Doc Souchon the previous October.
260.q: Yeah, well, in 42 is when the Crosby band broke up and I went to service for about three and a half years. And then when I came out again, I got a home there myself, see? Yeah. So we have our homes out there in California now. Yeah. But I still like New Orleans.

261.t: Going to Los Angeles in 1941 and the Army in 1943
261.s: Verrett was in California in 1941, then was called into the Army in 1943 and returned to New Orleans.
261.q: Well, I was there in 58. 58. Yeah, I've been out there 58. See, during 1940, that's when I went 41 out there. I worked out with all the four shit, but then I went on the base, you know, because they'd stay out of the Army. But in 43, they called me in the Army. Anyways, I said, I went in the Army…

262.t: Marriage in 1910, Spanish-American War and World War I
262.s: Bailey married at 21 in 1910, recalls no Spanish-American War, and says he was scheduled for the draft in World War I.
262.q: Well, he'll be back then. Let's see. It's the birth certificate, you know. Now, do you remember this? I got married in 1910. I got married in 1910.

263.t: Townsmen band, Army service, and first meeting with Bunk Johnson in New York
263.s: He plays in the Townsmen swing band, serves in Army bands in Kentucky and Indiana, then goes to New York, sits in with Bunk Johnson, plays the Town Hall concert and records for Rudi Blesh in 1946.
263.ch: Army years and joining Bunk Johnson
263.q: worker in Towson as a result of that training and later went to work in an investment bank down Redwood Street but oh that's when I joined the Towson they they had a very good swing band in Baltimore it was the most popular band not only in Baltimore but I'd say several states around really what…

264.t: Army service and return to New Orleans, Floyd Hunt
264.s: After the 1943 records Zardis went into the Army for three years, returned about 1946, played at Mississippi City and joined Floyd Hunt in Denver.
264.q: Well, I stayed in the Army. I got in, it was about three years I stayed over there. And I got back around here around forty-six. I'll be a little before forty-six, but in that three years' time, you know.

265.t: Growing up in the Irish Channel; Army in 1917
265.s: He grew up in the Irish Channel, where one club paraded until 1917, then went into the Army.
265.q: I was brought up in the Irish Channel. That's around Diamond and South Peter. Enunciation Street, Chappatula Street, St. Thomas Street.

11.t: Looking for Wade Whaley; digression; 1918 draft and France
11.s: Searching for Wade Whaley, a muddled aside about a drummer and band picture, then his move from LA and 1918 draft.
11.ch: Sid Leprotti and the So Different band
11.q: Yeah, when he left here he went to San Jose. And the next time I heard he went to San Diego. Because I was down in Los Angeles. I was told that he had a little cigar stand and whatnot. And I went all up and down Central Avenue. And nobody knew nothing about him.

266.t: Tape equipment banter and a visit to the Air Force Museum
266.s: Banter about the age of the recorder, which leads to Jones's visit to the Air Force Museum near Dayton while working in Ohio with the Mac Stitt band.
266.q: Well, you got around Ohio, that's right. Yeah, with the Mac Stitt Band. We were working there at some short-lived jazz club called the New Farm Club. And on one of our days off, my wife and the kiddies and I packed up and went out to the Air Force Museum. Which has nothing to do with jazz, I…

267.t: Battiste as musician, the Korean War breakup and going to Detroit
267.s: Ford praises Battiste, then explains the Korean War ended the Johnson Brothers and he went to Detroit to stay with his Uncle Percy, where music work was not enough.
267.q: He's one of the smartest, well one of the best musicians I know. Aside from financial things, I mean he's a national down-to-date musician. Because we were in a little Army Reserve band he was in also, where I learned a lot. This guy was a professor at Dillon and he had the band in charge and we'd…

39.t: Leaving Hampton and teaching school bands in Florida
39.s: After finishing Hampton in May 1916 Brown played in Norfolk, then took a Florida job teaching school bands until the Army intervened.
39.q: Not very long. Not very long. I'll tell you why. Because I finished Hampton in May of 16. Well, I went right to Norfolk and played in the Paris theater. And it wasn't very long before I got a letter from Hampton, offered me two school jobs. One in Topeka to teach school bands. That's really what I…

268.s: Turner served only briefly in 1943, being over age.
268.ch: Day job, war and Bocage's band
268.q: Oh, you were just in for a very short while. Very short while. Oh, I see. And then you started back to the book.

269.s: Questions about the 1877 Canal Street battle; as a child she did not go about the city.
269.q: Well you see, children didn't go about like the children now. You couldn't pick yourself and go where you want.

270.t: Spain talk and shore leave rules
270.s: Talk of Franco's Spain, then going ashore and trusting the crew.
270.q: You know, you had time to do it. Yeah. Oh. So, like I said, when we get to Tower, where we're going to be in two days? You know, I think most of two days. It'll be a Saturday, a Sunday, a big stop time. Well, everybody had a chance to go out and have a little fun. And then sometimes if it's a…

271.t: Steckler's band ends; Ramis's string trio
271.s: Steckler's band broke up when members joined the army in the Spanish-American War, leaving Ramis's three-piece string band.
271.ch: Early string bands and first jobs
271.q: they disbanded. And, and, and, and the, uh, Spanish-American war why one or two of the fellow signed up and went to the army and the band, why just disbanded and they was never reorganized. So let's see, they had another band. I believe that was O'Ramus' band. That was three pieces. Guitar, bass,…

272.t: Reel change and return to a repair-department job
272.s: A second reel goes on; Lizana says he came back to New Orleans and held two or three jobs, one in a repair department.
272.ch: Back from service and early jobs
272.q: He couldn't join the sports services and he couldn't make the grades. And he's a piano player.

273.t: Jones's bands: Army, the Tin Roofers and joining the Straws
273.s: Jones played in reading and Army dance bands, then Dixieland with Moose, Norman and Gene as the Tin Roofers. John heard them at the jazz club and Jones joined the Straws in October 1958.
273.q: Well, I played a little bit with bands in Boga Loosa, reading bands. And then when I was in the Army, I played with the band, naturally, you know, the dance band. And played around with guys a little bit. But actually, I didn't really start playing with Dixieland until Moose called. I go to school,…

274.t: Joining the Supreme Band after school
274.s: Right after World War I Labat auditioned on violin for leader Paul Maurice and joined, staying until the members died.
274.q: It's something like that name, too. Well, to make a long story short, I was near a week from school. This fellow Paul Maurice, he was the leader of the band, leading with Clarinet, you see. And they came around, I read music, pretty good at the time, just out of school. And they brought some music…

22.t: Piron's 1915 band, the ODJB's silent films and war work, and Clarence Williams's arrival
22.s: La Rocca adds that Piron played string-based ragtime in 1915, lists the ODJB's films, society dates and wartime entertaining, and says Piron sent Clarence Williams to him in New York in 1923, arguing Black players followed the ODJB.
22.ch: Piron, Clarence Williams and the ODJB repertoire
22.q: Well you mentioned Pierron's band and what type of music they play. I forgot to mention it was in the year about 1915. I think Pierron then used mostly string instruments. And he played regular conventional ragtime like I had right on records that was of that date of error. There's some things I'd…

275.t: USO show in freezing Abilene, Texas
275.s: On a USO tour at an Abilene army camp there was no lodging in snow; a juggler was heckled.
275.q: Yes, I remember that. I like to froze to death. We were appearing at the army camp in Abilene, Texas, and it was 15 below zero and snow about knee deep. And when we arrived there, well, there was no place for us to stay as the army camp was overcrowded. The town was about 40,000 population and…

276.t: Sailing, the Marine Hospital and travels in the northern states
276.s: Nash recalls sailing on ships, two months in the Marine Hospital after operations, and places he visited from New Haven to San Francisco.
276.q: I mean, it made it nice out there. People seem to be so friendly in Toastable, you know. Where I was. Where was I? In New Haven? No. I was in New Haven. I was in New Haven too. I used to sail on a ship from North of New Haven. I was telling her after I got off the ship, I stayed in the Marine…

43.t: Glover Compton and returning to New Orleans
43.s: Talk of Glover Compton and his wife Nettie Lewis, with whom she worked. She then went home to New Orleans after the war.
43.ch: Bucktown, Chicago and the cabaret years

277.t: University of Chicago and the Cakewalking Babies
277.s: After the Navy he came to Chicago on the GI Bill; Steiner and he list the Cakewalking Babies' members.
277.ch: University of Chicago and the Cakewalking Babies
277.q: G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Well, I came to the University of Chicago after I got out of the Navy. I got out of the Navy in 1946. And my friend Dan Gerald, who I had played with in Boston and who we had a mutual interest in jazz, he was at the University of Chicago. So I came here under the G.I. Bill of Rights.…

45.t: Playing with Armstrong at Pete Lala's, then leaving for Los Angeles
45.s: Williams played little with Louis Armstrong, who left for the boat; Williams played around until going to Los Angeles in 1919, narrowly missing the draft.
45.ch: Buddy Petit and Sam Morgan years
45.q: A little, very few. I didn't play many. See, because I left, you see. I must play about one or two, because I left, you see. After we played Pete Lollars, after that 1916, you know, rave. Well, we went in Pete Lollars, you see, about 17 and the war started, come out, you know, broke out. Mm-hmm.…

278.s: He went into the Army in January 1963 and heard Irma Thomas's million-seller while in service.
278.q: Right. That must have really disrupted things. A bit, yes. I was, by that time I was ready to go to the Army. I had been deferred a couple of times before then. And one time I was out because my left foot was in a cast from putting on trampoline shows. I had an accident. But I had been deferred a…

279.t: Revival of 1946, solo piano and the Maritime Service
279.s: He began solo piano around 1941-42, then served in the Maritime Service band 1943-45.
279.q: Well, of course that brought us up to pretty much up to the time of 1946 when all the revival of jazz came back. From there on, why it was really, I guess a story that everybody's been talking about now.
