280.t: Being drafted in 1940 with Morand and Horace Malcolm
280.s: Williams registered in the first draft with Herb Morand, Horace Malcolm and Tom Taylor but did not serve because he had six dependent children.
280.q: Six children at that time. Yeah. I was in the first draft of the United States. Yeah. Horace Malcolm, me, Moran, we were all around the same. Moran didn't go for it. Moran was a great big guy, this big, he's too big, you know, too big. That time they wasn't taking big men.

281.t: Dating Oliver's arrival and the military school band
281.s: Interviewer dates the Oliver engagement to about 1918; Spanier says he played cornet and bass drum in a school band outside Chicago.
281.q: That was the cornet. I was playing the cornet and the bass drum in the band. Where was that school? That was at Marysville, right outside of Chicago.

282.t: Army service in France: entertaining troops and hospital stay
282.s: He joined an entertainment unit with New Yorkers playing violin for hospitals and the YMCA, was ill for months, and played no blues or jazz.
282.q: Well when I went in, I didn't fool around playing over on this side at all and when we went to the other side, I started playing. I got, we met a band in the orchestra right in the Army and they made us go with the entertaining department. Well then we stayed in Paris, France a good while. We used…

283.t: Small bands in Gulfport and Pensacola and a wartime steak club
283.s: He left town for Gulfport and Pensacola with small bands, including a club that served black-market steaks.
283.ch: Return to New Orleans and Sharkey
283.q: Yeah, with Bow Boy? No, Bow Boy, he owns a club. Oh. My Sarah, that owns a building, generally, Wright still owns a building, adopted Bow Boy when he was a kid, see? But he's a good lawyer, he was a big lawyer at one time. Yeah. Well, anyhow, after that, I went out of town, I went to Gulfport,…

284.t: Cleaning shop work and Sidney Desvigne
284.s: During the war he worked at his brother-in-law's cleaning shop until Sidney Desvigne hired him for two years on guitar.
284.q: Yeah. So, uh, after, after getting out of that band, it's when the war, you know, when the war was beginning there in full room, man, I, uh, went on and my brother-in-law, and we all call him Cuckoo, but his name is, uh, Todd.

285.t: Buddy Bolden's band and Home Sweet Home in 1898
285.s: He tells how Buddy Bolden's band played Home Sweet Home on a Spanish-American War transport and soldiers jumped overboard.
285.q: Buddy Bolden. Well, Buddy Bolden came after my, oh, he was ahead of my time. Buddy Bolden, I think, was in his heyday. One I can remember around, well, heard of him, heard a lot about him. But I think he went insane. Yeah, that's right.

286.t: Eight years with Papa Celestin, second trumpet, until the Navy
286.s: Russ joined Celestin around 1939 as second trumpet, with Henry Franklin discussed; he entered the Navy on 5 September 1942.
286.q: Yeah. No, I stayed on trumpet, so, I played with Papa Celestine from 1939, I think, in 1939, or 1940, something around, actually, 1939. Helping Celtics, and that's used for it. And, uh, I go to Papa Celestine. But most of my band work with Papa Celestine, which, you know, do a high, Clown's Hall,…

287.t: Leaving Chicago in 1941 and joining George Lewis
287.s: After 13 years away he left Chicago when war was declared, quietly leaving his job to his drummer, and came home to play with George Lewis' band.
287.q: Yeah. Well, I left when this country declared war. So I hadn't been home in 13 years at that time. My mother and father was living, so I decided to come home. I thought maybe I would be drafted, but I missed the draft by a couple of years. So I had a nice job playing on the north side in the…

288.t: Reel change; why he stayed south; the bank and Pullman porter work
288.s: Charles refused offers to go north, left the bank in 1918 and worked as a Pullman porter until the armistice.
288.q: I couldn't see going up north. The man was sent for me twice and I refused. Yeah, I couldn't see going nowhere but right there in New Orleans and I stayed there.

289.t: Church music, war work and the road into the music business
289.s: He grew up on church music, worked in aircraft plants in Los Angeles and Buffalo during the war, then returned to open a nightclub.
289.q: Well, in that particular time, most things you were listening was church music, you know. I played choir, the lady who played for the choir, you know. Because in them days, rock and roll wasn't happening, the blues wasn't happening, not to the young people had to go to church, you know, and that's…

290.t: How long the Nola Band lasted and dating by the war
290.s: Hard to date; the Nola Band lasted until he quit in 1934; he never went to war.
290.ch: Nola band, day job and nightclub work
290.q: Forty years, forty years ago, thirty years ago, it was kind of hard to remember. Especially the way this thing used to go, you know, you'd play with this band tonight, tomorrow night, playing some other band, you see.

291.t: Navy bands and the colour bar on rank
291.s: In the Navy he returned to clarinet and played classical and operatic music, but Black musicians could not rise above second-class rank. He describes the three kinds of Navy bands.
291.q: And that's about as high as you could go, no matter who you was, you couldn't go anymore in first class. The prejudice was so strong here.

292.t: Tom Brown, Nick LaRocca and a poem for her grandson
292.s: Dick Allen asks about local bandleaders; she does not recall them and reads a poem for her grandson in the Navy.
292.q: No, I was living here two years. I lived on the Louisiana Avenue Annunciation before this. I lived on Sixth Street for quite some years. I don't know exactly how long. I lived there, Goodwire on the 16th Constance.

293.t: Army in France in World War I
293.s: He reached France after the war ended, was the only French speaker in his company of 250, and played boogie-woogie blues on an organ in a boxcar.
293.q: In them new chemists and the dancing down. Yeah. And I had an organ in the... I had an organ in the boxcar where he was living in the boxcar. On all of them? On an organ. Mm-hmm. And I used... I used to... I shot them blues, them boogie woogie blues. Mm-hmm. Boogie woogie blues. Right. So played…

294.t: Military service, wartime and the disguised German records
294.s: Military service from 1938 ended his listening. In 1944-45 he found German-labelled records in a house in Germany that turned out to be Benny Goodman jazz.
294.q: Um, it was very, very nice, uh, time until, uh, 38, because it was, uh, the time when comes clothes over Europe, and I began my military service, and that was the end of my music, um, interests. Of course, not, uh, exactly, uh, interest, but no possibility to hear except military music. As you can…

295.t: Seven bands before World War I and their names
295.s: He ran up to seven bands until the first world war, named Reliance, Tuxedo and Lane, with split bands going out under the Lane name; some men were drafted.
295.q: Yes, I've had the lawyer candidates, both. Son and father playing lots of jobs with me, but the first time when, when I first organized, they played, especially the old man. He was with me. He was one of my members of the first, first band. Now, I had, uh, all together, I used to master seven bands…

296.t: Batiste De Leo and musicians in the Spanish-American War
296.s: De Leo went to war on alto and switched to trombone; the interviewer's uncle Louis was a musician in 1898.
296.q: he was playing he was playing let's see he was playing alto when he went to war but he got over there he took a trombone he took a baritone with good on both of them

297.t: Navy band service 1942-45 and return to New Orleans
297.s: He played in the US Navy band in California and McAlester, Oklahoma from 1942 to 1945, then returned to his job at the Athletic Club and spot jobs.
297.q: while he was in the service, did you keep playing then? I mean. I kept playing, but I was. Did you work with them, through that period? There's different bands, but I played with the United States Navy Band in the Navy for three years. Yeah? Uh. What was that, here? Well, that's in, uh, Los…

298.t: Where he worked when World War II started
298.s: Worked in the Quarter, with George Williams on Napoleon Avenue, Popeye's and Club Arlington with Billy and De De.
298.q: I think I was in the quarters. I think I was in the quarters. I think I was in the quarters of World War II. Uh, it wasn't that the last round, though.

299.t: Leaving Don Raymond's band for World War II service
299.s: He left Don Raymond's band for the service about ten months after the war began.
299.q: And they tried to fake them. Well I think I took more interest in the instrument when I went to the service. I left Don Raymond's band going to service. That was World War II.

300.t: Playing in Virginia and giving up trombone
300.s: Humphrey recalls switching from trombone and playing with combos and a bigger band around Charlottesville.
300.q: Oh, when I stopped, uh, I stopped in just about to see... I shipped about... ...45. Something like that. When we were... When we were... When I stopped playing trombone, then, I went to playing piece and... ...played a little piece of violin, a small combo over there. Where was that? So Sam took…

301.t: Joe Robichaux band, Lunsford and the war
301.s: After Desvigne he joined Robichaux, recalls its record personnel, the band became Lunsford, broke up when the draft took members, then Freddie Coleman.
301.q: Well I know he had a small outfit then. I forget that you were all known. Yeah, I know. I was quite a large man. There was Gene Porter, Gishard, Ransom Nolens, Eugene Ware, Bucket, and then Joe.

302.s: Russell wraps up; Oxley mentions circuses and army service in Europe and the Pacific; the tape note says he had to play Preservation Hall.
302.q: Well, I'll tell you, I would have to think. There's a lot of things, I mean, like different circuses and so forth like that. I mean, like different things I could talk about. I'll tell you what I said, but it takes you time to think. Yeah, I know, that's right. You were with circuses then too.

15.t: How he came to play cornet: the Army
15.s: He learned bugle and trumpet in the Army, which he entered underage as a drummer, and says he picked up other instruments by doing.
15.q: Yeah. I found I could play a bugle. And I learned I'd play a trumpet at the Army.

23.t: Keep America Out of War convention and Marxism
23.s: Perhanis asks about Rose's politics. Rose was a delegate to the 1938 anti-war convention in Washington and calls himself a classical Marxist and economic determinist.
23.q: Well, it was what it says it was. That it was a coalition of groups of people in America that were eager to block the entrance of the United States into World War II. Are you pacifistic? Am I a pacifist? No, I'm a revolutionary socialist. I'm an orthodox Marxist.

58.t: Dating the Bronze Mannequins road show with Charles Taylor
58.s: Allen asks about the Bronze Mannequins; Punch says it was Charles Taylor's show, shortly before World War II when Chicago work slowed.
58.q: Well, I started in that, I say, I don't know, the time, things got kind of slow there in Chicago, and I went out on the road with them. See, it must have been around, it wasn't in the 40s, before the 40s.

303.t: World War II work at Higgins and USO shows
303.s: Brother Tom a Marine; Jeff built boats at Higgins while doing 285 USO shows a year; Jackie Blaine singer.
303.q: the Marines, but he was in the Marines, and he was a drill sergeant at Parris Island. He was also lightweight boxing champion of the United States Marine Corps in World War I. I was too young for World War I, and when World War II came, I was already married, and we had a child, and so I worked…

304.t: Wood's background, Army service and early exposure to jazz
304.s: Born in Richmond in 1928, drafted in 1951, taught at Tulane and JMU; recalls Lead Belly records, Mister Jelly Roll, and meeting drummer Paul Barbarin at his first parade.
304.q: I was born in Richmond, Virginia in 1928, and with the exception of the years that I spent in New Orleans as a graduate student in the late 1950s, I've lived in Virginia almost all of my life. I was in the Army for a while, but other than that, I am a lifelong resident of Virginia. I'm on the…

305.t: Why Dixieland faded in the war and spread to other cities and colleges
305.s: White bands left or broke up at Pearl Harbor; Dixieland declined nationally in the forties, then returned and spread to other cities and colleges.
305.q: Well, it was not that so much, it's not a question of lack of interest, as if the Dixieland bands, the white bands, all left New Orleans. And, to put it bluntly, the Dixieland bands that remained in New Orleans at the time of Cleo Harbor, well, they just broke up automatically. And, Oscar Celestan,…

306.t: Chris Kelly's country origins, Army draft and marriage; closing
306.s: Edna says Chris worked the fields, was drafted, and married her after the Army. The interview closes.
306.q: Hmm. Hmm. Hmm. Hmm. Hmm. I can't remember anything more. I can't remember. Okay. Well, that's nearly the whole of that. Just a whole thing right there.

307.t: The H&J Tavern and Russell first hearing him
307.s: Thomas switched to Boehm clarinet while at the H&J Tavern in World War II; Russell recalls hearing him there in 1943 on George Lewis's advice.
307.q: Well, that was when I was playing at the H and J Tavern. Now, it was during the war, World War II I believe.

308.t: The Navy dance band and ad-lib drumming
308.s: He compares the Navy band to outside bands, notes the men were rated musicians, and returns to ad-libbing breaks.
308.q: Oh, yeah, well, maybe better. Yeah. They're a bigger band, yeah. They did a whole lot. Oh, yeah. They were well together, yeah. Nice arrangement.

309.t: When his father stopped playing; the two-banjo bands with Harry
309.s: His father quit around World War I; Julius and a rival banjoist played opposite ends of a band with alternating solos.
309.q: It must have been around in the, World War I. My daddy wasn't old enough to go to, no, my daddy had, I think it was 18 to 45, that, in World War I, they were taken from 18 to 45. Where Cal was too young, and my daddy was about a year or two years too old. So, it was around 50, they could stop.…

310.t: Brunswick work, Kansas boyhood, and Army band service in World War I
310.s: After a recording check, Brewster explains his name, says he ran Brunswick's foreign-release recordings with Glenn Miller and the Dorseys working for him, then recalls his barber father, learning trumpet by ear, the Sears cornet, enlisting in the National Guard band, and Chief Ballardi.
310.q: yeah discuss give me your name first and we'll see if it works Brewster, Lauren M Brewster mm-hmm and you told me what M was for before what year was what what M is for what the M stands for well my mother my grandmother was named me Morris but she spelled it M-A-U-R-I-C-E so Maurice oh yes but it…

311.t: Staying out of the Army and the Metropolitan Life elevator job
311.s: He was not drafted; he tells how he started on the Metropolitan Life elevator and, after three years, argued his way to a clerical job and a career there.
311.ch: Metropolitan Life and the Alley band
311.q: No I didn’t because at the time I had a couple of kids, I’m going to say essential and a non-essential industry. And I worked at the Metropolitan in those days and I was a flunky, what was I doing? Well the first job I had at the Metropolitan, I’ll tell you a story if you don’t mind, a little short…

312.t: After graduation: Army, Czech and the Washington scene
312.s: Joining the Army language school, banjo at Monterey, Washington bands and the Federal Jazz Commission.
312.q: As a matter of fact no. After I got out in ’58 I found myself in a position of possibly being drafted. And so I joined the Army so I could go to the language school. And I did that, and I picked the language that I thought would land me in Germany, where I wanted to go, and they sent me to Fort…

313.t: V-discs and the Army in the Philippines
313.s: Army Special Services sent V-discs overseas and Avakian smuggled some home.
313.q: Oh definitely. The Army Special Services, which was the branch that took care of morale and so forth, managed to get even V-discs over to the Phillipines and I copped a few for myself which I wasn’t supposed to do, and hid them in my barracks bag and brought some back home actually. And V-discs…

314.t: Not a composer, and dropping out of music school
314.s: He says he writes tunes but never studied composition and left music school after a week to avoid Korea.
314.q: I mean I write some tunes. But I never studied composition and I never studied counterpoint. I went to music school but it was trying to get out of the Korean War, and I lasted a week in music school and I dropped out. But I didn’t want to go over to Korea. And it was just ending right about that…

315.t: Dave's upbringing, World War II and the lost history book
315.s: Chris and Dan discuss Dave's Christian Scientist mother and cowboy father, his war experience with Patton's army, and the story of the history book found in a used bookstore.
315.ch: Dave and Iola: faith and values
315.q: Yeah and Judeo-Christian ethical morality thing was strong in his blood. You know? And Grandma Bessie was a Christian Scientist and it was a very wacky religion and Grandpa Pete believed in baked beans, stars, and rattlesnakes. But you combine those two — and you know World War II was a deep…

316.t: Air Force service, shot down and prisoner of war
316.s: Flying missions over Germany, shot down on the seventeenth, crew killed, and survival in a prison camp.
316.q: Well I always was fascinated by airplanes when I was a little kid growing up, and my father had been in World War I and he was in the infantry. And he suffered terrible. I mean he never was wounded but he had terrible experiences in World War I in the mud. As he says he slept in the mud, and I…

317.s: Jimmy had grown up around Jo Jones, Ben Webster, Lester Young and Chico Hamilton, who were in the service with him; Jeannie had stayed in Canada and the Midwest.
317.ch: Meeting in Buffalo and early careers
317.q: And I had just come back from California, not too long beforehand. And so that was kind of a habitual thing. After the gig was over and the pack up, and as Papa Jo Jones would say, “With our mutual armies we’ll move out smiling.”

318.t: Navy band at St. Mary's pre-flight school and Great Lakes
318.s: He enlisted, played in a Navy band with Marshall Royal and Jerome Richardson, worked clubs in civilian clothes, and recalls Clark Terry at Great Lakes.
318.q: Oh yeah. Well actually I enlisted and I was in the band with a bunch of the guys, you will probably know the names, Marshall Royal, Jerome Richardson, Jackie Kellso, who is with the Basie band right now playing lead alto. We were stationed up at Oakland at the St. Mary’s pre-flight school. There…

319.t: Saxophone, drums and the Army band
319.s: He tries alto sax, learns drums from a friend, finds asymmetrical jazz drumming hard, and plays trap drums in the Army band.
319.q: So I played that a little bit, didn’t really like it, and didn’t have an opportunity to get into any music on it, because the stuff we were playing, the parts weren’t very interesting. And by this time I’d become interested in jazz. And in high school this same teacher had formed a little swing…

320.t: Royal Observer Corps service in World War II
320.s: Dance served in the Royal Observer Corps in East Anglia, heard V-discs at American bases, then found bebop rude on returning to New York in 1946.
320.ch: War years and return to New York
320.q: In 1935 I joined the Royal Observer Corps. And I was in that until 1945. It was attached to the RAF. We were — there was immense air traffic in England after the Battle of Britain. We joined the Royal Observer Corps because we thought we could get out of the infantry and go into it, but we were…

321.t: Army band at Fort Wadsworth and learning woodwind repair
321.s: He was drafted in 1969, got into a Staten Island fort band, and learned woodwind repair with Saul Fromkin, which later helped with Woody Herman's horn.
321.q: not getting a teaching gig, and I got my draft notice right away, in 1969. So but I auditioned in Indianapolis, figuring that’s close enough to Ohio, maybe I can hang in there, you know a six hour drive and whatever. And the guy in Indianapolis was very great. He had me sit in, the audition was…

322.t: Miles Davis in Seattle, then joining George Benson
322.s: His inner voice story: in army uniform he heard Miles in Seattle, fled, then was told to get with a giant and joined George Benson in January 1968.
322.ch: Army, Miles Davis and George Benson
322.q: Oh yeah, man. See the internal voice, oh my God we could talk four hours about that. Again, I know I talk a lot but let me, let me tell you about the internal voice. Back in the army, stationed in Fairbanks, Alaska. Now around this time I’m 20 years old, right? So at one point I’m trying to figure…

323.t: Ice show and the NBC Symphony, no military service
323.s: Declined Fred Waring; skipped service; Sal Francella got him into the ice show, then Toscanini's NBC Symphony audition.
323.q: family, stayed there, and I got a telegram Whiteman wanted to join Fred Waring, but I declined. I don’t know what happened.

324.t: Army service: K.P., the Eighth Armored Division and the camp band
324.s: Gibbs describes boot camp punishment, being made a tank driver, then being put in an Army band in Dallas on drums and vibes, never rising above corporal.
324.q: I was very young and I couldn’t talk, I used to box. I wanted to be a fighter. And there was one, you know when you first go in they send you to I think Fort Dix, the big camp where before they send you out to wherever you’re going to go, they get thousands of guys there and all you do is walk…

325.s: Asked about the profanity on 'Nuclear War', Gordon says a changed band was keeping up with the times.
325.q: Yeah, well you know all things change in time you know. That was a different band than — you know these guys like a lot of them had passed away and the band turned over, and things changed. So you know that record really was keeping up with current trends. Okay? It’s not like Sun Ra was a I don’t…

326.t: First break: wartime shortage and the Auburn Knights
326.s: With the good players in the Army, teenage Green gets hired; the Auburn Knights hear him in Mobile and he joins them for a semester.
326.q: Well it might have been when World War II broke out. All the good guys went into the Army so they had to hire us kids to play.

327.t: Draft lottery and conscientious objector claim
327.s: With a draft number of 49 he files for conscientious objector status, with Billy Taylor's letter and a draft board hearing.
327.q: Yeah. And my number was 49. My number was up. So I was going to Vietnam. And I went through the whole thing of going down and the whole draft thing and taking the test, and couldn’t bring myself to lie or do stuff that —

328.t: Brothers in Army bands during World War II
328.s: His brothers served in Army bands overseas and the family never doubted they would return.
328.q: Well all my brothers went in the Army. And of course they were all in bands in the Army. You know that was very lucky for them. But they saw also some of the war action too, some of them did, and they told me about how it was and everything. But they did a lot of studying, being in the Army bands,…

329.t: Choosing drumming and playing in the service band
329.s: Never considered anything else; joined the service to get in a band, learned to read there.
329.q: Well I never did anything else. So I never thought of it, never thought of it. Just loved it. I never thought of ever doing anything else. Ever. I just loved it. When I went in the service, I figured well I’ll go in, I’ll be a gunner, you know. But they eliminated them gunners, in the 50s, they…

330.t: Army service in Alaska, Hawaii and Fort Lewis
330.s: He played in Army bands, never went to Korea, and played cello to see off troop boats.
330.q: I went to Alaska and I went to Hawaii. I played “Rhapsody in Blue” in Hawaii. And up in Alaska we didn’t do very much of anything. But I was in Ft. Lewis, Seattle, mostly, playing for generals and captains, and that kind of stuff. No, I didn’t go to Korea but I played off a lot of guys. When I was…

331.t: War years, family circumstances and segregated minstrel shows
331.s: His father's background and modest income, and playing in minstrel shows for servicemen; the local audience was segregated.
331.q: Well of course I was in school and my father did not have much formal schooling, I think he had to quit when he was about eight years old and go to work. He came from a community in Indiana, Kokomo, and he had to go to work in the foundry there. And then he sort of migrated from Indiana to…

332.t: American songs in Britain and wartime
332.s: American standards reached England and France via cover versions, and the Glenn Miller Army Air Force Band came during the war.
332.ch: Opening and early jazz in England
332.q: Yeah, quite a few of them did. I mean a lot of them made it further than anywhere else on the continent. I mean in France you get songs like “Ces Petit Choses” which is “These Foolish Things,” you know, and I mean they sang them with French lyrics. Quite a lot of the songs found their way over…

333.t: Singing on the radio the night World War II ended
333.s: At the Hotel Lincoln with Hawkins, an announcer interrupted to say the war had ended; he wonders if a recording survives.
333.q: Well I swore I’d never talk about it because people, you know people may say that — right now — I think about it, the night, and I could tell you, the night that World War II ended. It was ABC. And there was a lot of things happening. We were in the Hotel Lincoln. As you know, the Hotel Lincoln was…

334.t: American servicemen, jazz clubs and Richard Wyands
334.s: Americans came to Japanese jazz clubs; Richard Wyands toured with him having never met.
334.q: Yes. Many Americans came to jazz clubs. And they enjoyed our playing jazz. And these people, an American musician came to Japan. Richard Wyands.

335.t: Replacing Gap Mangione in 1968 and landing an Army band post
335.s: Joe took Gap's chair, was drafted, jammed with the 173rd Army Band at induction and stayed two years; his father's band teaching saved others in WWII.
335.q: Yes. I took his place when he enlisted in the army, I took that gig, which only lasted a matter of months because I was drafted very quickly. This was 1968, right? But I got through my military service fortunately and came home and went back with Gap and then went out with Woody’s band.

336.t: Drafted in 1963 and playing in an Army band
336.s: Drafted August 1963, he ended up in an Army band; discussion of enlisting versus draft.
336.q: Well I was drafted. It was pre — it was 1963. In fact, I was thinking about that today. Today is August the 8th, and it’s Benny Carter’s 95th birthday, which is — I played with Benny Carter twice and — my idol you know. But today I thought August the 8th, that’s the day I got drafted many, many…

337.t: Drafted: Bolling Field Air Force Band and the concert tone
337.s: Drafted in 1946, he got to Bolling Field in Washington; Major Howard sent him out until he learned a concert tone, and he worked as librarian before the dance band.
337.q: Yeah. Well what happened is after I played around with June Bug and Primo, then I got drafted and the war just ended. The war ended July 1945 and I just turned 18 around that time in September. I forgot what it was — no before that. Because I went in the service in 1946 and came out in 1948. So the…

338.t: How the Coconut Grove fire kept him out of military service
338.s: His fire experience and supporting his parents got him out of the draft; he then lost the NBC job and opened the Eddie Condon Club in 1945.
338.ch: New York, NBC and Eddie Condon's
338.q: Well the Coconut Grove helped me get out of there. It wasn’t a help in the fire, but it did get me out of going in the service. And they were all ready to take me until I told them that I didn’t think they were being real nice to me about it. I had gone through the fire and everything else, after I…

339.t: Army plane landing-gear scare and scorpions at Corpus Christi
339.s: Flying to an Army camp with Basie, the plane cannot lower its landing gear; after a scorpion-plagued show, Lewis and Wendell Culley take the train.
339.q: Yeah, you know we had some Army camps to do. We had to ride in the Army planes, you know the ones with two tails you know, and that big thing in the middle. So we got, one day we got on this thing going to one of the camps, and it was noisy, this thing was so noisy you couldn’t hear. Now Billy…

340.t: Draft pressure, teaching at Baker Hall, and his brother in Vietnam
340.s: A draft board clerk warned him about Canada; a friend steered him into special-education teaching at Baker Hall to avoid the draft, while his brother served in Vietnam.
340.q: that time, and guys like Dave Roll and Bobby Weiss and those guys, “How come you didn’t play with the ABA?” They didn’t have an ABA. And it turns out I couldn’t go to the college. I had a scholarship from all of them and I wanted to go to McGill, because I spoke a little French, because to me that…

341.s: Members prioritize Diva around Broadway, wedding bands and other work; the lead trumpeter joined the Army blues band.
341.q: Yeah. I think people make it a priority because they like it and as we were saying before there’s not loads of places where you can get a chance to express yourself playing jazz. A lot of people in the group play Broadway shows, a lot of them play in wedding bands, some have their own bands, but…

342.t: Drafted into the Army band at Fort Dix
342.s: Drafted in 1962 after drug problems, he played in the Fort Dix band, then moved to Field Artillery to escape the officers' ceremonies.
342.q: Yeah. Well I played a little bit. I played in an Army band but I was — by the time — I got drafted into the Army. I was living in New York as a young man and having problems with drugs, and hit sort of like a rock bottom. And when I got drafted, there were like all soldiers and I wanted to get out…

343.t: College, being drafted, and the 158th Army Band
343.s: He lost his clarinet scholarship, worked in a steel factory, was drafted, played clarinet in the band at Fort Knox and practiced bass in the basement.
343.q: Here’s what it was. I am now in college. That’s another story as to how I got there. I still don’t believe how I got there. It was the blessings of God, the Gods of music. But anyway I had, as a clarinetist I had entered college on a clarinet scholarship, right? And the moment I entered the school,…

344.t: Air Force band in Fairbanks, Alaska
344.s: Special Services band, jazz clubs six nights a week in 1956 territorial Fairbanks, pianist Roger Fleming, early discharge.
344.q: Is that right? Oh that’s great. But I’ll tell you I always wanted to do this you know. And when I was in the service, sitting in Alaska in the barracks, in Fairbanks, and it was 50 below zero outside, and we’d have the records on and we’d play jazz all the time.

345.t: Drafted from Woody Herman's band and serving in Korea as a cook
345.s: His family was little affected by WWII; McKenna was drafted in 1951, failed MP training, served in Korea as a cook, then returned to work with Boots Mussulli and Charlie Ventura.
345.q: Well I had a lot of uncles that were in the service on my mother’s side. And I don’t think we were greatly affected by it, no.

346.t: Army in Heidelberg and Muhal's big band rehearsals
346.s: In the Army in Heidelberg he met Karl Berger, Albert Mangelsdorff, Bent Jaedig and Nathaniel Davis at sessions; he then describes Muhal's big band at the C & C Lounge where members wrote for the band.
346.ch: Army, Chicago and the new music
346.q: Absolutely. He’s totally right on that. You know. Totally right. But I go way back with Karl Berger. When I was in the Army in Heidelberg, Germany, there was a K-54 and Karl Berger was down there with the musicians down there — Albert Mangelsdorff was there, Bent Jaedig, the great tenor saxophonist…

347.t: Joining the Marines and wanting to be a hero
347.s: He joined the Marines and Army as a challenge, driven by a wish to be outstanding.
347.q: A challenge. Just strictly a challenge. Same thing in the Army. It’s a challenge. I always wanted to be — now this is weird — I always wanted to be a hero. Hero to me meant somebody who was way above everybody else, for whatever reason. When I was a little boy I wanted to be a fireman. I thought…

348.t: Army service, then Tommy Dorsey, Les Brown and the move to Fox
348.s: Three and a half years in service taught him writing and flute; afterward Dorsey in 1946, Brown 1948-50, and Fox in 1950.
348.q: It was one of the most gratifying, and I’m sorry to say nicest, supposed to be — in the military and I just had a ball because I learned how to write, how to arrange, and I learned how to play flute from one of the fellows in the band and it was great. There were great musicians from the west…

349.s: He was not drafted and felt left out as friends went overseas.
349.ch: Early gigs and the war years
349.q: Right a military base to get knowledgeable about how to fight. And it got to me. I felt kind of left out like you know. The guys said, “Man don’t worry about it, don’t worry, you’ll get your chance, don’t worry about it.”

350.t: Refusing to define himself by political labels; American identity and Air Force years
350.s: Murray declines to discuss how black Americans define themselves, calling it political confusion, and says he defines himself as an American. He recalls being a college teacher before being drafted in World War II.
350.q: I’d prefer not to talk about that. I think it’s a lot of confusion about that that’s based on political maneuvering and has very little to do with an actual historic basis for definition. The stuff I’m interested in, defining my role as an American and the ways that the idiom that I grew up in add…

351.t: The war's end and taking his family west with Barnet
351.s: Marty was not political; he was with Barnet at war's end and took his wife and baby daughter to California.
351.q: Well to tell you the truth, in my youth I wasn’t very intelligent. All I had in my mind was playing the piano. I didn’t think politically, I didn’t think musically — well musically actually just for the band that I was playing with. And I didn’t know what was going on in the world actually. I…

352.t: Returning veterans, jazz concerts and booking big bands
352.s: Veterans took younger students under their wing and organized the jazz concert; bands booked via Willard Alexander played the gymnasium.
352.q: They did and they were very helpful. I found them just great. They’d take the younger students under their wing. I remember particularly the jazz concert here. The older men who had returned wanted that music and they got the concert together. But I was part of it. And they didn’t have to. I was…

353.t: Starting out during and after World War II
353.s: She was still in school during the war, her father kept her out of clubs, and she began playing sorority dances in 1948-49.
353.q: Well see I was still in school then. I didn’t really start until ’48, that’s when I got out of high school. But see I wasn’t playing then. My father wouldn’t let me come in the clubs, that was taboo. You know at that age. I got started really like in the early 50s, and the late — oh ’48, ’49 is…

354.t: University of Michigan and the 75th Infantry Division Band
354.s: Drafted from Michigan into the 75th Infantry Division Band at Fort Leonard Wood, where he learned from better players and that there is only good and bad music.
354.q: I was in the marching band before that at the University of Michigan, on a scholarship, a music scholarship. And I got drafted out of there, and of course I knew how to do all that stuff and I ended up in the 75th Infantry Division Band, Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri. The old joke is that if they…

355.t: Air National Guard band, then dropping out of USC and UCLA for music
355.s: He enlisted in the Air National Guard band during Vietnam, found USC unwelcoming to his ensemble, and on Chuck Berghofer's advice committed to music.
355.q: But back to your question, so there was music all around me and I knew it’s what I wanted to do from a very early age I guess. Now I had to — I went into the Air National Guard band based in Van Nuys, actually I did a year in street clothes because the Vietnam War was raging and there wasn’t enough…

356.s: His time in the 503rd Air Force Band at Lackland and Edwards AFB, with Bill Berry and Monty Budwig, mostly playing music.
356.ch: Los Angeles, college and the Air Force
356.q: Well it’s strange. There’s guys in there that make a career of the military, and they’re great guys. They’re not like me at all though. But I had fun. All we did was play, so I was in the 503rd Air Force Band. First I was a permanent party Lackland AFB, which is a boot camp where everybody goes to…

357.t: Army service as a radio operator
357.s: A classification specialist made him a high-speed radio operator at Southeast Signal School for two years during the Korean War, thanks to his radio jingle job.
357.q: I was a radio operator. I was fortunate to have, they called them Classification Specialists, who would interview you, as you are interviewing me, and determine how I would best serve Uncle Sam. It was the time of the Korean War and so you would think that they would exercise a little more wisdom…

358.t: Avoiding military service and the G.I. Bill
358.s: He was never drafted, being married with a child, and credits the G.I. Bill with upgrading music.
358.q: No. No I was not in the military. When the next war came around, and I think it was the Korean War maybe, they were drafting — they were not drafting fathers — I mean they were not drafting husbands, and I had just gotten married. Then they started not drafting fathers and I had just had a kid. And…

359.t: Spanish flu and an Italian centenarian's memories of wartime
359.s: He compares the pandemic to the Spanish flu and recounts a very old Italian teacher saying people never felt today's anxiety during the wars; Shearing's wartime England is similar.
359.q: I think that we were lucky that a hundred years went by and didn’t have such a big pandemic going on. Because I think the last event that this, even that can be considered similar to this was the Spanish flu, even though back then I think the numbers of people that died was unbelievable. Like more…

360.t: Pearl Harbor, shipyard welding and trying to enlist
360.s: He heard of Pearl Harbor outside a theater, became a first class welder on landing ships, and was refused by the Marines because of his exemption.
360.q: Oh yeah. Yeah, yeah. I was on Center Avenue going to the Roosevelt Theater. There was a Roosevelt Theater right on Center Avenue, and I never did get to the show because the news came over the air and they blasted it.

361.t: Strip joints, Air Force, Las Vegas and Woody Herman's advice
361.s: Early hard living, Air Force piano, Vegas work with Ventura and Herman, and Herman's advice to leave.
361.q: because everybody was working at Kodak Park or going to college and becoming a doctor or this or that. And here’s a guy, my brothers are studying to be doctors and here I am playing in a strip joint, playing piano in a strip joint, wondering where my next paycheck would be coming from. And I had…

362.t: Jazz history in Japan and growing up after the war
362.s: Early Japanese jazz and Shanghai, his generation's rock tastes, and the postwar generation's lack of war memory; his father's view that the army was crazy.
362.q: Yeah, yeah. I read the history of jazz in Japan. They, in the book, said even before World War I, already Japanese jazz singers existed. And at that time they went to Shanghai. Because Shanghai was a colony of England, or something like that.

363.s: Denied deferment, he served two years doing clerical work in the tank corps, practised alone, and found the band had lost ground.
363.ch: Discovering jazz and the trad band
363.q: Yeah. But our name was on the poster, our name was on the tickets, you know, we were going to really do it. So there you are.

364.s: Radio operator in Korea in 1952; Bobby Hackett calls him on his return, audition at Lou Terassi's, and touring.
364.q: Yeah. I was there from ’51 through ’53. No I was in Korea for all of ’52 that is. I took — I was a radio operator. And I went over there and did radio. And when I got out I sat home and it was like March of ’53. And I’m sitting home and I’m not knowing what to do with myself. And the phone rings.…

365.t: Army Special Service at Fort Lewis and gigs in Seattle
365.s: He served at Fort Lewis 1944-46 playing parades, and worked steadily with Tooty Boyd in Seattle and Portland.
365.q: Oh lovely. I was in Fort Lewis, Washington from 1944 to 46, and I was with a Special Service Unit. And we didn’t have to do too much except play for the parades on a Saturday. The rest of the time I was in Seattle.

366.t: Army service, Engineer Battalion and the Air Force Band
366.s: Sol's wife got him transferred from the 297th Engineer Combat Battalion to the Fort Dix band.
366.q: Well luckily, again for my wife, Monk, originally I was in an outfit called the 297th Engineer Combat Battalion. I don’t know if you know what that is. They are the infantry but they build bridges. Before the regular infantry came along, we used to build a bridge called the Bailey Bridge. So here…

367.t: Snooky leaves Basie to join Gerald; draft and Great Lakes band
367.s: Snooky left Count Basie to join his friend Gerald in California; he was found physically fit but never drafted, and they recall the Great Lakes and St. Mary's Pre-Flight bands.
367.q: The guys couldn’t understand that. They say, “where you going?” “Look,” I say, “I’m going out to California.” They say, “You going to California for what?” I say, “I’m going to join my friend. He’s got a band, Gerald Wilson.” They said, “are you kidding? You’re going to leave Count Basie?” I say,…

85.t: Armed forces broadcasts and the wartime band's changing personnel
85.s: He was asked to do forces broadcasts and record for Capitol; the draft took players and younger modernists came in.
85.q: One thing that I’ve learned is never volunteer. So I was approached and asked to do it, and we did. No, we didn’t volunteer. But, I mean, we did display our willingness to do it, you know.

368.t: Touring Europe with Dorsey and the Air Force, and Buddy Rich on the plane
368.s: Dorsey's band flew with the Air Force; he describes the B17 and Buddy Rich getting sick on a plane ride.
368.q: Oh yeah, that’s right. We traveled to different places. Yeah, that was in conjunction with the Armed Services. We played, yeah the way he worked, he had a deal with the Air Force whereby he would play three or four civilian jobs and then he’d play two or three Service jobs on a ship or on a Service…

369.t: The wartime entertainment tax and her wiggling at the piano
369.s: A tax claim on her wiggling was settled by the union as long as she kept playing; she says critics were women pianists with flat behinds.
369.q: I don’t remember that. Unless it was on me. They claimed that I wiggled when I played and there should be a tax on it, you know. So the union says, “Well, she can wiggle as long as she keeps playing the piano.” Some of the women pianists were kind of jealous.

370.t: Army service, marriage in Las Cruces and discharge
370.s: Alfred was drafted and sent to El Paso; Gordon flew out sick, they married in Las Cruces, and he was discharged for eyesight and they returned by troop train.
370.ch: Alfred Lion and early Blue Note
370.q: That was some trip. I was a mess. I’ll tell you. But I pulled myself together, and we got married. Again, that’s three times we got married.

371.t: Sunshine Gardens in Saginaw and jobs in Flint and Lansing
371.s: Small joints with Choker Campbell and Jimmy Parker; the date is 1941, when Jones was turned down for service for flat feet.
371.ch: Early bands and the road to New York
371.q: Well, Sunshine Gardens was one of those little joints. You have to call it a joint because it was. They had a band there; we used to work there occasionally.

372.t: Draft status and the psychiatrist who spoke Yiddish
372.s: He recalls being told in Yiddish by a psychiatrist he would not be drafted because of his eyesight.
372.q: Well I was actually told in Yiddish by the psychiatrist not to worry, I won’t have to go in, supposedly, because of my eyesight. I don’t know why he spoke to tell me that in Jewish, but . . .

373.s: An arm injury and a Latin School alumnus doctor got him a 4F in the draft physical.
373.q: . . . 18 or so. I had had several operations on my left arm, one of them because the doctor had left some stuff in there when he operated. I went for my draft physical and seemed to pass it until we got to the last doctor in line. I didn’t deliberately do this. I’m not saying I’m sorry about it. I…

374.t: Time at Wilberforce and being drafted
374.s: He explains his time at Wilberforce, clarifies he was drafted rather than enlisting, and recalls his romantic wish to be a Marine.
374.q: They called me up – the Army called me up. I was nearing 18. I was at Wilberforce once, and then I left, worked for six months, got myself together, and went back to Wilberforce, and then I was there for two years, not exactly going to school, because Wilberforce was a place that attracted people…

375.t: The union man's spacecraft blueprint and Walter Davis
375.s: At 18 a union collector showed his family a blueprint to build a craft; Shorter later asked a physics professor about it; Walter Davis wanted to build the spacecraft.
375.q: of, in the electrical storm. Then he asked me to go with him to Alaska, to the DEW Line (I was DEW Line when I was in the Army) to witness the Aurora Borealis with Whitney Streiber and some other scientists. But I couldn’t go. I was going on the road. Then he got married and moved to Japan. I’m…

376.t: Becoming a guitarist and playing for GIs after liberation
376.s: He studied Django records and harmony, left university, and after liberation played cafes and GI clubs with a rhythm section.
376.q: During the War, you know, a little bit. And then I became… quickly I became a good guitar player. Studying from those records of Django. Django was a fantastic… The records of Django Reinhardt were fantastic. Well, I never got that velocity, you know. He was… But uh… see, the harmonica, as…

377.t: Lester Young leaving: not fired but drafted
377.s: Basie denies that he fired Lester over a missed Friday the 13th recording, saying Lester and Jo Jones both went into the Army.
377.ch: The band, its players and singers
377.q: Lester went to the Army and then when Lester came out of the Army, Lester said that he would try a little thing of his own.

26.t: Germany at the outbreak of war, 1939
26.s: Greer describes the Hamburg station full of soldiers, 1939.
26.q: it was something else. Oh, man, I saw the Second World War jump off. We were there when the second World War jump off. The later years, you know. We went back to play a European

67.t: A short job at a New London beer joint
67.s: Albertson asks for missed stories and he recalls a brief wartime job near the submarine yards with Wayman Carver.
67.q: There's was a little job I had up in New London, Connecticut, with Tiny -- Tiny whatever his name is, little job didn't mean anything, it was just doing -- during the war and submarines were being built up in New London.

378.t: Back on 52nd Street; the draft takes Shorty, Hank and Rowles
378.s: Billie sang with them again at a 48th Street fish place, but the draft took Shorty Rogers and Jimmy Rowles, and Hank Kahout went to Cleveland.
378.ch: War years, Goodman and Woody Herman
378.q: But we did some more dates, I forget what they were. Then we went back into the 52nd Street again. And, we had a pretty good show going then, I don't remember who it was, but Billie was back in with us.

379.t: Arrivals: Machito's army service, Rene Hernandez, bongos and Tito Puente
379.s: He dates the arrivals and departures of key players, including Rene Hernandez and Tito Puente.
379.q: No, '46, no-no, '40 -- beginning of '45, because (inaudible) Rene play with the band in Miami. He could have played in New York in '45, when he got here. The union (inaudible).

380.t: Avoiding the draft by staying 1A all through the war
380.s: Callender never mentioned his military school and was never called, while friends like Bumps Myers went into the Army.
380.ch: Youth, the road and arrival in California
380.q: Years later...I guess it's all right to tell it now... But when the War started, I never did tell them I went to ROTC school. See, I was officer material, but I never put that down. For whatever reason, I was in 1A the whole duration of the War and never got called. I was on a 21-day furlough and…

381.t: No military service: turned down for stuttering
381.s: He was rejected for the draft because of his stutter, but played army camps with Lucky.
381.q: Although, during the time of the war, I was with Lucky Millinder there, and we played at many army camps and navy bases during the war because that was the only way that we were able to get gas. (CUT)

382.t: The wartime slump in recording and swing 'nipped'
382.s: Poor material and the recording ban; Maxine says swing was nipped during the war.
382.ch: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
382.q: records made but they were poor. You had poor material, you know, the material that recordings were made out of was just not available.

383.t: Big bands visiting Tuskegee and Hinton meeting Wilson's mother
383.s: Wilson says a nightclub owner brought Ellington and Cab Calloway's bands to Tuskegee, where his mother met many musician friends.
383.q: Well, that very well could have been -- because during the second world war, there was a man named [Bulls] who had a nightclub off campus there at Tuskegee, and he brought many of the big bands who were traveling, who would play there in Tuskegee. I know that Duke Ellington played there, and Cab --…

93.t: Jonathan Nichols and the Dancing Doughboys
93.s: Green names his last protege Jonathan Nichols, who was Pete Nugent's protege, and Nugent's This Is the Army choreography team.
93.q: Well, they were the choreographers of "This is the Army." It consisted of Pete Nugent, (unintelligible) Lee, and the now Timmy Rodgers.

94.t: Houston the night after Pearl Harbor
94.s: In Houston, servicemen were ordered back to base and the club emptied.
94.ch: New York, Dallas and Kansas City
94.q: Yes. We switched from there to Houston and I was there in Houston when the Japanese struck Pearl Harbor and I remember that day -- no, the following day that the whole City of Houston was populated by servicemen, soldiers, so that night when we went to work and it was almost midnight before we put…

72.t: World War One draft: put in a cage as a supposed slacker
72.s: In Birmingham he was displayed as a slacker, then found too young for the first war and too old for the second.
72.ch: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
72.q: Yeah. I think during that time... I think I was in Birmingham, Alabama. What year it was, I don't know. It was round about... Anyway, I think I was around Birmingham. Eighteen or nineteen years old, somewhere

384.t: Paul Lavalle's letter about jury duty and the City Service Band
384.s: A 1952 letter from Lavalle asks a court to postpone Morehouse's jury service because he was a featured soloist on the weekly City Service broadcasts.
384.ch: N'goma drums and the scrapbook clippings
384.q: spaghetti and hot sausages. The clipping continues on the other side but he's got it folded over. So I can't read it and I don't want to undo his scrapbook. Along with a photograph of the City Service Band of America, conducted by Paul Lavalle, there is a copy of a letter written by Paul Lavalle on…

385.t: The Cookery and West End dispute with Phil Schaap
385.s: He explains a dispute over playing a club, and an off-tape note about faking a twitch to dodge the draft.
385.q: - Yeah I played there. We had a misunderstanding. Static, as you might say -- whatever you want to call it. I didn't knock off join in knockin' off or don't playin' the joint, or picketin' it -- whatever you want to say -- goin' on strike against it came the new owner had -- the guy wanted me to…

386.t: Carnivals, road shows and soldiers' stories in Waco
386.s: He recalls carnivals, minstrels and road shows, marching bands at the start of World War I, and soldiers' tales while he shined shoes.
386.q: Now what happened about the traveling shows, when I was about eight, in Waco, which we were still living in Waco, we used to have carnivals and they would have road shows and minstrels and things like that. But a kid seven years of age is not going to have an opportunity to learn... when I say to…

387.t: Bill Finegan: meeting and Army oddities
387.s: He knew Bill from the Army band days and Wolpe's lessons.
387.q: He used to live in Tenafly, which is not far from here and he was assigned to the Cap Shanks. I met him early on in the Glenn Miller, but only in passing. I was introduced to him, we talked a bit, but it was never very much. When it came to Shanks, somehow we would spend evenings together. I would…

388.t: Called up for the draft and then exempted
388.s: Leeman gives up his Woody Herman job and apartment for induction at Fort Dix, but a new rule exempts fathers over thirty and he does not go.
388.q: Well, we can go back over lots of things, but ... I was taken in the draft, to go into the Army, so I had all these songs that became so great with Woody -- I had rehearsed, like --

389.t: Visiting Venuti's wartime band in Miami
389.s: During wartime shortages Venuti hired two girl saxophonists from the union and laughed through their poor playing; Challis explains his hiring problems with 4-F musicians.
389.q: So we went over there, the dances ran there. There was this service place, the Air Force place, where all the guys, the enlisted men were there, and draftees and they'd come dancing in this place, and it started at 8 o'clock and finished off at 12:00. No real late stuff there.

97.s: Scott takes a civil service job during the war while gigging weekends.
97.ch: Reel 2: touring, shows and the war
97.q: Well, (inaudible) the '40s now. The United States went to war, war broke out. Well, the fellows weren't doing very much work, and those fellows that had quit from the big bands, they were all getting jobs downtown as messengers. One musician worked at a chemical bank, and he had -- what do you call…

78.t: Leading the 732nd Military Police Band at Camp Desplaines, 1942-43
78.s: Louis Armstrong turned down bandmaster of the Joliet camp band under Wayne King and recommended Horace. He led a 42-piece band including Fats Waller's saxophonist Jackie Fields, and got letters from draft-eligible musicians.
78.ch: Army band, Lena Horne, Billie Holiday and the 1950s
78.q: camp in Joliet, Illinois, and they needed a leader that would be made bandmaster, you know, so this is exactly what happened. So I played all the service clubs and what not, and we had this great 42 piece band.

98.t: DeLisa sidemen and the wartime draft
98.s: Sonny Cohn, Johnny Board, Harlan Floyd, Cy Touff, Dennis Farnon and Earl Washington played in the band, which had high turnover from the draft; Saunders was 4-F.
98.q: Well, we had so many of them. The boy who at one time, it was about six of my ex-men in Basie's band. Johnny Board was in there.

13.t: After Hines: day jobs and Sax Crowder's band
13.s: He worked wartime day jobs and a small West Side band.
13.q: Yeah, that was -- well, I had two. Driving for Chicago Service Lines and CTA and working in the alcohol denaturing plants.
